paragraphs.text: ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

First, we thank the Lord. Anything clear in these pages came from Him, not from us. We pray He keeps pouring wisdom into our hearts so we can serve His Church well. We pray you finish this course more awake, more steady, and more in love with Jesus, not more scared of the headlines.

This book took a long time. Not because God was slow, but because we wanted to get it right. It started when God put a passion for prophecy on Larry’s heart. He preached it for six weeks from the pulpit, Bible open, quizzes ready, teaching what the Lord had given him. Pastor Rocky took that foundation, grew it into twelve lessons, and added the depth and study tools you see here. The sermons became a class. The class became a book. All of it is for the glory of God.
FAMILY AND LEGACY

We owe a lot to our father, James Kaslov. He did not write these pages, but you can feel him in them. For years he pressed prophecy, especially how Scripture speaks to what is happening in the world and in the news. He put that heart in us. He taught us to read the Bible until we could see God’s signature on the page. He answered our questions, called us out when we got sloppy, and kept pointing us back to Christ. Dad, thank you.
OUR MINISTRY PARTNERS
To Pastor Angelo and Soldiers for God Ministry in Dallas, thank you for opening the classroom door. This material was preached, tested, and sharpened with real believers before it ever went to print.
To Pastor Anthony, our overseer, thank you for leading us and guarding what we teach. Your wisdom and support have helped us more than we can say. We love you, Pastor.
TO THE STUDENTS

This book is for every student who will walk these twelve lessons, read, write, take the quizzes, and ask hard questions. We built it for you. SFGM Ministries built this course to wake up the body of Christ and get us ready for the coming King. Thank you for taking God’s Word seriously. May this study make you ready, not proud. You are the Bride of Christ. Live like you believe the Bridegroom is coming.
PREFACE

About one out of every four verses in the Bible is prophecy. That is not a side topic. That is a fourth of the Book God breathed. Still, in many churches today, it is one of the least taught subjects. For many believers, prophecy has become either a scare show or a seminary fight, something to fear or avoid. That was never God’s design.
Scripture says it plainly:

“And I fell at his feet to worship him. But he said to me, ‘See that you do not do that! I am your fellow servant, and of your brethren who have the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.’” (Revelation 19:10, NKJV)

From Genesis to Revelation, prophecy is not about charts for the sake of charts. It is about Jesus. Every promise that came true, every feast God set, and every sealed scroll points to the same truth: the Bridegroom keeps His Word, and He is coming back.

When Scripture says the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy, it means prophecy is more than God telling the future. It is God showing us a Person. The Holy Spirit uses prophecy to pull back the curtain of time so you can look straight at Jesus.

If you only read prophecy to build timelines, you end up with dry bones. When you see that Jesus is the heart of it, those bones come to life. Prophecy shows that Jesus runs human history and holds the future of your family in His hands.

Here is the simple truth: if prophecy was right every time about the past, you can trust it to be right about the future. God does not get a partial grade. When you look back and see history land exactly where God said it would, centuries ahead of time, you realize faith is
not a blind jump into the dark. It is trust in a God who speaks ahead of time and then does what He said.

In the first century, believers did not carry a New Testament under their arm. They had the scrolls of the Old Testament prophets and the living words of the apostles. When they stood before kings, judges, and angry crowds and said Jesus was the Messiah, their proof was prophecy. They bet their lives on it. His life, death, and resurrection matched what God had already written.

This course is built the same way. SFGM Ministries is a local church giving clear Bible teaching, and this book is a rescue mission for the Word. We will look at the text, look at history, and let the evidence speak. The lessons follow God’s timeline in order, as closely as the teaching allows: from the first word of Genesis, through the first coming of Jesus and the long Church Age, to the Rapture, the wedding, and the thousand-year Kingdom.
In these twelve lessons we have five big goals.

First, we will open the parables Jesus told in His last week in Jerusalem. They are more than stories. They are courtroom prophecy, showing how the care of God’s kingdom was taken from the leaders who rejected Him.
Second, we will walk God’s calendar: the feast days of Israel and the eras of the Church. We will show the prophetic design hidden inside them.

Third, we will tear down the deception of Replacement Theology, the teaching that says the Church permanently replaced Israel. We will show where that idea came from, how it was written into church practice in the days of the Council of Nicaea, and how it tried to cut the Church off from its Jewish roots.
Fourth, we will study one word Jesus used: escape. We will show from Scripture how God takes His people out of danger before His wrath falls.
Fifth, we will look at ancient wedding customs from the Bible and from our own living Roma tradition. They paint a clear picture of the Rapture.

Along the way, we will prove from history that God’s prophecies come true, from the first word of Genesis to Daniel’s countdown. We will watch Israel come back to life as a nation, and we will look ahead to the thousand-year Kingdom of Christ and the New Jerusalem.

This study is for two kinds of readers. If you are new to end-times teaching, we will explain every hard word in plain English and keep going. If you already know prophecy well, you will still find history, Hebrew word studies, and honest confrontation with bad teaching. We are not talking down to you. We are talking straight to you.
You are the Bride of Christ. The Bridegroom is coming. Let us prepare.
HOW TO USE THIS BOOK
This is a twelve-lesson course: one lesson a week for twelve weeks. Treat it like a real class.
Study one lesson per week. Do not rush, and do not skip ahead. Give the Holy Spirit room to speak, and let the text settle in you.
Each lesson begins with a Memory Verse. Learn it during the week.
Keep a notebook nearby. At the end of each lesson, choose one Journal Essay prompt and write 300 to 500 words in your own words. Include Scripture and show how it applies to your life.
Complete the ten-question quiz after every lesson. Ask your local church teacher for the quiz, or go to sfgmboston.com to submit answers online and listen to the lesson audio.
After you finish all twelve weekly quizzes and pass the final exam (ask your teacher or visit sfgmboston.com), you will receive a Certificate of Completion from SFGM Ministries.

Read Before You Begin and The Timeline first, and come back to the Timeline often. Near the end of each lesson you will find a Chapter Summary and Key Verses to review, followed by the Journal Essay Prompts.

At the back of the book you will find a Glossary of hard words and a list of Sources. If you are not sure you belong to Jesus, the chapter right after the Conclusion, How to Be Ready, will show you how to settle it.
Before each lesson, ask the Holy Spirit for a clear mind. Ask Him to help you see what God already wrote, not what culture, denomination, or fear wants you to see.
Before You Begin
Three Things to Consider Before Taking This Course

Before you open Lesson 1, stop and think about three things. Why does prophecy matter so much? Can we really know what season we are living in? And why does it feel like the world is walking away from God? Settle these three questions first, and the rest of the book will make more sense.
1. THE PLACE OF PROPHECY IN THE BIBLE
Some people think prophecy is a small corner of the Bible, a topic for experts. The numbers say the opposite.

Bible scholar J. Barton Payne counted every prophecy in Scripture in his Encyclopedia of Biblical Prophecy. He found 8,352 verses of prophecy out of the Bible’s 31,124 verses. That is about 27 percent, more than one verse out of every four.

The return of Jesus alone fills page after page. Bible teachers such as Tim LaHaye counted about 318 times the New Testament speaks of the Second Coming. They point out that only one subject gets more attention: salvation itself. That makes the return of Christ the second most taught subject in the New Testament.
Think about what that means. God did not hide prophecy in a footnote. He wrote it into a fourth of His Book. Something that big is not optional for a believer.
“And so we have the prophetic word confirmed, which you do well to heed as a light that shines in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.” (2 Peter 1:19, NKJV)
Peter calls prophecy a light in a dark place. You do not need a flashlight at noon. You need it at night. The darker the world gets, the more we need the prophetic word.
2. RECOGNIZING THE SEASONS

A farmer knows the seasons. He does not need a calendar to tell him spring is here. He sees the buds on the trees, feels the warmer air, and knows it is time to plant. A good father knows his son’s footsteps on the stairs before he sees his face. When you know someone, you recognize them coming.
God expects His people to know His seasons and to recognize His Son’s coming.
Jesus scolded the religious leaders of His day because they could read the weather but not the times:

“When it is evening you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’; and in the morning, ‘It will be foul weather today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ Hypocrites! You know how to discern the face of the sky, but you cannot discern the signs of the times.” (Matthew 16:2–3, NKJV)

Jesus Himself was standing in front of them, and they missed Him. When He wept over Jerusalem, He told them why judgment was coming: “because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19:44, NKJV).
The Bible praises people who understood their season. When David was becoming king, the tribe of Issachar sent men “who had
understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do” (1 Chronicles 12:32, NKJV). They read the moment and acted.
Jesus gave us the same lesson with a fig tree:

“Now learn this parable from the fig tree: When its branch has already become tender and puts forth leaves, you know that summer is near. So you also, when you see all these things, know that it is near—at the doors!” (Matthew 24:32– 33, NKJV)
No one knows the day or the hour. Jesus said that clearly. But He also said we can know the season. Paul put it this way:
“But you, brethren, are not in darkness, so that this Day should overtake you as a thief.” (1 Thessalonians 5:4, NKJV)
A thief surprises people who are asleep. A believer who is awake and watching will not be caught off guard. This course is meant to help you read the season you are living in.
3. THE GREAT FALLING AWAY
The Bible says that before the end, many people will turn away from the faith.
“Let no one deceive you by any means; for that Day will not come unless the falling away comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition.” (2 Thessalonians 2:3, NKJV)

Some people read this verse and ask, “Doesn’t the Antichrist have to show up before Jesus comes for His Church?” Look closely. “That Day” is the Day of the Lord, the time of God’s wrath on the earth, not the Rapture. The “man of sin” is the Antichrist. Paul says Someone is holding him back right now: “only He who now restrains will do so until He is taken out of the way” (2 Thessalonians 2:7,

NKJV). Many Bible teachers believe the One who restrains is the Holy Spirit, working through the Church. When the Church is taken out, the restraint is lifted, and the man of sin can be revealed. In Lesson 10 we will see that God takes His people out before that Day of wrath begins.
Paul warned Timothy about the same thing:

“For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires, because they have itching ears, they will heap up for themselves teachers; and they will turn their ears away from the truth, and be turned aside to fables.” (2 Timothy 4:3–4, NKJV)
Jesus asked a hard question: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He really find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8, NKJV).
Look at what has happened in America within one lifetime.
When Gallup asked Americans in the 1950s and 1960s, “Do you believe in God?” 98 percent said yes. In 2022, only 81 percent said yes, the lowest number Gallup has ever recorded.

In the 1980s, about 8 percent of Americans said they had no religion at all. By 2025, Gallup found 24 percent, about one in four adults. The Pew Research Center found 29 percent in its 2023–24 study, up from 16 percent in 2007.

Gallup also found that church membership dropped from 70 percent of Americans in 1999 to 47 percent in 2020. For the first time in the history of that survey, fewer than half of Americans belonged to a church.

In about forty years, the share of Americans with no religion has tripled, from about one in twelve to about one in four. That is not a slow drift. That is a falling away, and it is happening in front of us.
This is not a reason to fear. It is a reason to wake up. The falling away is one of the signs God told us to watch for. When you see it, you know the season.
WHY THESE THREE THINGS MATTER

Prophecy fills a fourth of the Bible, so God wants you to know it. Jesus expects you to read the season, so you cannot shrug it off. And the falling away is happening now, so there is no time to waste.
Open your Bible, open your heart, and let us begin.
The Timeline
God’s Plan in Order

This page shows the whole story of Bible prophecy in order, from the Cross to eternity. Each step has a key verse and the lessons where you will study it. Come back to this page whenever you need to see where you are on God’s calendar.
Step What Happens Key Verse Lesson
1. The Cross Jesus dies, is buried, and rises again, right on God’s schedule.
1 Corinthians 15:3–4
2. The Church Age
The long “valley” between the two comings of Christ. Jews and Gentiles are saved by grace. Daniel’s clock is paused. Israel is reborn as a nation in 1948.
3. The Rapture
Jesus comes in the air and takes His Bride, living and dead, out of the earth before the wrath. In heaven, the Bride stands before the Judgment Seat of Christ, and the wedding takes place.
1 Thessalonians 4:16–17
4. The Treaty A world leader confirms a seven-year covenant with Israel. Daniel’s final week begins.
Daniel 9:27 4
5. The Tribulation
Seven years of judgment, called the time of Jacob’s trouble. In the middle, the treaty is broken and the abomination of desolation stands in the temple.
6. The Second Coming
Jesus returns to the earth with His saints, ends the battle of Armageddon, and stands on the Mount of Olives. Israel looks on the One she pierced and turns to Him.
Zechariah 14:4–5
7. The Millennium
Jesus reigns from Jerusalem for a thousand years. Satan is locked away.
Revelation 20:4–6
8. The Final Revolt
Satan is released for a short time and gathers the nations. Fire from heaven destroys them, and Satan is thrown into the lake of fire.
Revelation 20:7–10
9. The Great White Throne
The unbelieving dead are judged. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire.
Revelation 20:11–15
10. The New Jerusalem
A new heaven and a new earth. God lives with His people forever.
Revelation 21:1–4
Three things to keep in mind as you read:
The Rapture and the Second Coming are two different events. At the Rapture, Jesus comes for His Bride. At the Second Coming, He comes with His Bride.
No one knows the day or the hour of the Rapture. But God has shown us the order of events and the signs of the season, so we can live ready.
The Bible does not say how much time passes between the Rapture and the treaty. The seven years are counted from the day the treaty is confirmed, not from the Rapture.
Lesson 1
The First Word
Before Creation, the Cross Was Already in View
MEMORY VERSE
“No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself.” (John 10:18, NKJV)
THE FIRST WORD: BERESHIT
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” (Genesis 1:1, NKJV)

Most people read the Bible only on the surface. They skim the English for history or a little encouragement. But ancient Hebrew works differently from English. It has layers, and those layers fit together in a way God meant us to notice.

Every letter in the Hebrew alphabet works in three ways at once. First, it is a letter with a sound. Second, it is a number: Aleph stands for 1, Bet for 2, and so on. Third, it began as a picture, a small drawing that tells a story under the surface of the text.

The very first Hebrew word of the Bible is Bereshit, said Beh ray SHEET. In English Bibles it reads, “In the beginning.” On the surface, it announces that God made the heavens and the earth. Under the surface, the old pictures inside the word point to who did
the making, and how that Maker would one day lay down His life on a cross.
Bereshit is spelled with six Hebrew letters: Bet, Resh, Aleph, Shin, Yod, and Tav.
THE PICTURES INSIDE THE WORD
Here is how the oldest form of each letter has been read:
Bet is a picture of a tent or house. It means family or home.
Resh is a picture of a head. It means the chief, the first, or the firstborn.
Aleph is a picture of an ox head. It means God, strength, or leader.
Shin is a picture of teeth. It means to crush or destroy.
Yod is a picture of a hand. It means a deed or work done by the hand.
Tav is a picture of two crossed sticks. It means a mark, a sign, or a covenant. In its oldest form it looked like a cross.

Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and Tav is the last, the Hebrew A to Z. Jesus calls Himself “the Alpha and the Omega” (Revelation 22:13), the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. It is the same idea: He is the first word and the last word.

Where does “Son” come from? Put the first two letters together, Bet and Resh, and they spell bar, an Aramaic word for “son” (the usual Hebrew word is ben). Psalm 2:12 uses it: “Kiss the Son” (NKJV). So the word opens with the Son, then God (Aleph), then crushing (Shin), by His own hand (Yod), on a cross (Tav).
Read those pictures in order, and the first word of the Bible carries a message many Bible teachers have pointed out: the Son of God will
lay down His life by His own hand on a cross. No one would take His life from Him. He would give it.
Jesus said exactly that about His death:
“No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This command I have received from My Father.” (John 10:18, NKJV)
Before God created light, oceans, stars, or Adam, the story of the Cross was already pictured in the first word of His Book. Redemption was not a backup plan. It was the plan from day one.
“All who dwell on the earth will worship him, whose names have not been written in the Book of Life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.” (Revelation 13:8, NKJV)
THE FALL AND THE FIRST PROPHECY

In Genesis chapter 3, Adam and Eve crossed God’s boundary. Sin entered the world, and death came with it. God did not panic or scramble for a new plan. He stepped into the garden and spoke the first prophecy in human history. Bible teachers call it the First Gospel, the first announcement of the Good News.
“And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her Seed; He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise His heel.” (Genesis 3:15, NKJV)
God was speaking to the serpent. He was announcing that Satan would be defeated by a coming Savior, the Seed of the woman.
THE BRUISED HEEL AND THE CRUSHED HEAD
The same Hebrew word is used for both blows, but where they land makes all the difference. A bruised heel hurts, but it heals. It does

not kill you. A crushed head is final. God was telling Satan that the Cross would wound the Messiah for a short time through His death, but that same death would be the final blow against sin, death, and the devil.
Before Adam and Eve ever left the garden, the ending was settled. Prophecy is God telling you ahead of time what He has already planned, so that when it happens, you recognize His voice.

“Remember the former things of old, for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me, declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done, saying, ‘My counsel shall stand, and I will do all My pleasure,’” (Isaiah 46:9–10, NKJV)
THE PROOF IN THE CAVE
Every skeptic asks the same question: How do we know the prophecies were not written after the fact? Maybe later writers changed the text to make Jesus fit.
God answered that question in 1947 in the desert near the Dead Sea, at a place called Qumran.

A young Bedouin shepherd was looking for a lost goat. He threw a stone into an opening in a cliff and heard pottery break. He climbed into the dark cave and found tall clay jars holding ancient scrolls wrapped in cloth.
He had found the Dead Sea Scrolls, one of the greatest archaeological discoveries in history. Among them was the Great Isaiah Scroll, a complete copy of the book of Isaiah.
Scholars date that scroll to more than a hundred years before Jesus was born. It sat in the dry desert air for over two thousand years.
When scholars compared it to the Isaiah in our Bibles today, they found it was almost exactly the same. The differences were mostly

small spelling changes, the kind you find in any hand-copied book. The message, the words, and the prophecies about the Messiah were all there, written long before Jesus was born. God kept His Word safe in clay jars to show the world that the prophecies about Jesus are real and ancient.
THE SYNAGOGUE IN NAZARETH
In Jesus’ day, the Scriptures were copied by hand onto large scrolls. They were kept in a special cabinet in the synagogue and handled with great respect.

Luke chapter 4 tells us that Jesus went into the synagogue in His hometown of Nazareth on the Sabbath. Every Sabbath, the synagogue read from the Law of Moses and then from the Prophets. That day, the attendant handed Jesus the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. Jesus unrolled it, found the place, and read it out loud:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He has anointed Me to preach the gospel to the poor; He has sent Me to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed; to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” (Luke 4:18–19, NKJV)
The people in the room knew these words by heart. For centuries they had heard them as a promise for someday. They were waiting for a King who would come in the future.
HE SAT DOWN TO TEACH
Then Jesus did something every person in that room understood.
“Then He closed the book, and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all who were in the synagogue were fixed on Him.” (Luke 4:20, NKJV)
Today, that detail seems small. In Jesus’ world, it meant everything.

In a Hebrew synagogue, a man stood up to read God’s Word. He stood out of respect, because the words were holy. But when it was time to explain what the words meant, the teacher sat down. Sitting was the teacher’s place of authority. Standing meant, “I am reading God’s Word.” Sitting meant, “Now I will teach you what it means.”

Jesus spoke about this custom when He said, “The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat” (Matthew 23:2, NKJV). Moses’ seat was the place of the teacher who explained God’s Law. Archaeologists have found stone seats like this in ancient synagogues, such as one carved from black basalt at Chorazin, a town near the Sea of Galilee where Jesus taught.
Watch how often the Gospels show Jesus sitting to teach:
When He gave the Sermon on the Mount, “He went up on a mountain, and when He was seated His disciples came to Him. Then He opened His mouth and taught them” (Matthew 5:1–2, NKJV).
When the crowds pressed in at the lake, “He got into a boat and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore” (Matthew 13:2, NKJV).
At the temple, “He sat down and taught them” (John 8:2, NKJV).
On the night of His arrest, He told the crowd, “I sat daily with you, teaching in the temple” (Matthew 26:55, NKJV).

This is very different from what most of us see today. Most preachers stand behind a pulpit, raise their voice, and point to the crowd. A Hebrew teacher sat down, and his students gathered close around him to listen. He did not have to shout to have authority. The seat itself said, “Listen. The teaching is about to begin.”

So when Jesus rolled up the scroll and sat down, the room went quiet. Every eye was on Him. They expected the usual explanation of what the words might mean someday. Instead, He said something that shook the room:
“And He began to say to them, ‘Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.’” (Luke 4:21, NKJV)
ANOINTED: THE MESSIAH

When Jesus read, “He has anointed Me,” He was reading Isaiah’s Hebrew word mashach, which means “to anoint.” It is the root of the word Mashiach, which means Messiah, the Anointed One. In Bible times, kings and priests were not elected. They were set apart by having olive oil poured on their heads.
Jesus was telling His hometown, “I am the One this verse is about. I am the Anointed One. I am the Messiah.”

The word “fulfilled” comes from the Greek word pleroo. It means to fill something all the way to the top, or to bring it to completion. Jesus took a promise His people had treated as “someday” and filled it full of real history, right there in that room.
WHY THIS MATTERS

Luke chapter 4 sets the standard for this whole course. When God makes a promise, it must come true in real history. If Jesus said it was fulfilled, we are not free to shrink it into a nice idea whenever it gets uncomfortable.

The God who pictured the Cross in the first word of Genesis is the same God who promised to crush the serpent, kept His Word safe in clay jars, and sat down in Nazareth to say, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled.” He finishes the story He started.
God is not reacting to the world. The world is reacting to Him. When you understand that history is moving on God’s schedule, fear loses its grip.
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: Before time began, God planned the Cross, pictured it in the first Hebrew word of Genesis, promised the serpent’s defeat in the garden, kept the proof safe in the Dead Sea Scrolls, and sent Jesus to declare in Nazareth that the prophecy was fulfilled.
Three truths:
1. Hebrew has layers: Every Hebrew letter is a sound, a number, and a picture, and the first word of the Bible points to the Cross.
2. The Dead Sea Scrolls: The Great Isaiah Scroll proves the prophecies about Jesus were written long before He was born.
3. Prophecy comes true in history: When Jesus read Isaiah and sat down to teach, He declared that God’s Word was fulfilled in real time and space.
Key Verses: Genesis 1:1, Genesis 3:15, Luke 4:18–21, John 10:18, Revelation 13:8
JOURNAL ESSAY PROMPTS
Choose one prompt below and write a 300 to 500 word response in your study journal. Cite at least one Scripture from this lesson, write in your own words, and show how it applies to your life.

1. Beh ray SHEET: Explain the three layers of a Hebrew letter (sound, number, picture). How do the pictures in the first word of the Bible show that the Cross was God’s plan from the beginning, not a backup plan?
2. The Dead Sea Scrolls: Tell the story of the shepherd and the cave in your own words. Why does this discovery answer the critic who says the prophecies were written after the fact?

3. He Sat Down: Jesus read Isaiah 61:1–2 standing, then sat down to teach. Explain what sitting down meant in a Hebrew synagogue. Then look closely: Jesus stopped reading in the middle of Isaiah 61:2. Why do you think He stopped where He did? (Lesson 3 will answer this.)
Lesson 2
Prophecies Concerning Jesus
The Mathematical Signature of the Coming King
MEMORY VERSE
“But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to Me the One to be Ruler in Israel.” (Micah 5:2, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

Imagine a historian trying to write the life story of a world leader two hundred years before that leader was born. It cannot be done. No one could name the exact town of his birth, the price of his betrayal, the way he would die, or the man who would give him a grave. Human guesses about the future are vague at best.
Yet the Old Testament does exactly that. It gives over three hundred prophecies about the birth, life, betrayal, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, written centuries before He was born.
This is where faith stands on solid ground. Prophecy is not God guessing. Prophecy is God telling us ahead of time what He will do, then signing His name on history when it happens.

In Lesson 1 we saw that Messiah means the Anointed One, the King set apart by God. The prophets described that King in detail. In this lesson we will look at the text, check it against history, and do the
math. You will see why Jesus being the Messiah is not a hopeful guess. It is proven.
FOUR PROPHECIES AND THEIR FULFILLMENT

Centuries before Rome built a cross or minted a coin, the prophets of Israel drew a clear picture of the coming Savior. Here are four of the hundreds of details they wrote down, each one paired with the place in the New Testament where it came true.
1. The Birthplace: Micah 5:2
Micah wrote this about seven hundred years before Jesus was born.

“But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to Me the One to be Ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from everlasting.” (Micah 5:2, NKJV)

There was more than one Bethlehem in Israel. Another Bethlehem sat in the northern land of Zebulun (Joshua 19:15). So God was specific: Bethlehem Ephrathah, a tiny farming village in Judah. Out of all the towns on earth, the prophecy named one small village centuries ahead of time.

The fulfillment: “Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king...” (Matthew 2:1, NKJV). When King Herod asked the religious leaders where the Messiah would be born, they quoted Micah 5:2 to him (Matthew 2:4–6).
2. The Price of Betrayal: Zechariah 11:12
Zechariah wrote this about five hundred years before the night Jesus was betrayed.
“Then I said to them, ‘If it is agreeable to you, give me my wages; and if not, refrain.’ So they weighed out for my wages thirty pieces of silver.” (Zechariah 11:12, NKJV)

The prophecy did not just say the Messiah would be betrayed. It named the exact price. Under the Law of Moses, thirty shekels of silver was the price paid to a slave’s master when an ox killed the slave (Exodus 21:32). God’s Son was sold for the price of a slave.

The fulfillment: Judas asked the chief priests, “What are you willing to give me if I deliver Him to you?” And they counted out to him thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15, NKJV). Zechariah even said the money would be thrown down in the house of the Lord for the potter (Zechariah 11:13). Later, Judas threw the silver down in the temple, and the priests used it to buy the potter’s field (Matthew 27:3–10).
3. His Hands and Feet Pierced: Psalm 22:16
King David wrote this about one thousand years before the crucifixion.
“For dogs have surrounded Me; the congregation of the wicked has enclosed Me. They pierced My hands and My feet.” (Psalm 22:16, NKJV)

When David wrote these words, crucifixion was unknown in Israel. The Jewish way of executing a criminal under the Law was stoning. Centuries later, empires such as Assyria and Persia hung people on stakes, and centuries after that, the Romans made crucifixion a tool of public terror. Yet David described pierced hands and feet long before a Roman cross was ever built.

The fulfillment: After the resurrection, Thomas said he would not believe “unless I see in His hands the print of the nails” (John 20:25, NKJV). A week later, Jesus showed him His hands. On the night He rose, Jesus had already told the disciples, “Behold My hands and My feet” (Luke 24:39, NKJV).
4. Buried with the Rich: Isaiah 53:9
Isaiah wrote this about seven hundred years before the crucifixion.
“And they made His grave with the wicked—but with the rich at His death, because He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.” (Isaiah 53:9, NKJV)
Crucified men were often left on the cross or thrown into a common grave with other criminals. That would have been a grave “with the wicked.” But Isaiah said He would be with the rich at His death.

The fulfillment: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man and a member of the Jewish council (Mark 15:43), went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. He wrapped it in clean linen and laid it in his own new tomb, cut out of rock (Matthew 27:57–60).
THE MATH OF PETER STONER
Some critics say these fulfillments were just lucky coincidences. So let us do the math.

Peter Stoner was the chairman of the mathematics and astronomy departments at Pasadena City College. In his book Science Speaks, he and over six hundred of his students worked out the odds that one man could fulfill these prophecies by chance. The American Scientific Affiliation reviewed his work and found it sound.
Stoner looked at just eight prophecies about Jesus. He found that the odds of one man fulfilling all eight by chance are 1 in 10 to the 17th power. That is a 1 followed by 17 zeros.

His eight were these: born in Bethlehem, a messenger sent ahead of Him, riding into Jerusalem on a donkey, betrayed by a friend, sold for thirty pieces of silver, the money thrown down in the house of God for the potter, silent before His accusers, and hands and feet pierced. You have already read four of them in this lesson.
To help people picture that number, Stoner gave this illustration.

Imagine covering the whole state of Texas with silver dollars, stacked two feet deep. Now mark one coin with a red spot and mix it into the pile. Stir the whole state. Then blindfold a man and tell him he can walk as far as he wants across Texas. Anywhere he chooses, he can reach down and pick up one coin.
What are the odds he picks up the red coin on his first try? The same odds as one man fulfilling just eight prophecies by chance.
Jesus did not fulfill eight prophecies. He fulfilled over three hundred.
WHY THIS PROOF MATTERS
Remember the word from Lesson 1: pleroo, to fill all the way to the top. Jesus did not just match a few old predictions. He filled history full of what God had promised.
If God was right about every detail of the first coming of Christ, you can trust Him about every detail of His second coming.

History is not a random accident. It is moving on a schedule set by one Creator. When you know the Bridegroom keeps His promises on time, you can trust Him with your life, your family, and your future.
CHAPTER SUMMARY
One sentence: The odds against one man fulfilling even eight prophecies by chance are so great that the more than three hundred prophecies fulfilled by Jesus carry the signature of God.
Three truths:
1. Exact details: The Old Testament named the birthplace, the betrayal price, the piercing, and the burial of Jesus centuries ahead of time, and the New Testament records each one coming true.
2. The math: Peter Stoner showed that the odds of fulfilling just eight prophecies by chance are 1 in 10 to the 17th power, like finding one marked silver dollar in Texas covered two feet deep.
3. Trust for the future: Because past prophecy came true exactly, we can trust that future prophecy will come true exactly.
Key Verses: Micah 5:2, Zechariah 11:12–13, Psalm 22:16, Isaiah 53:9, Matthew 2:1–6, Matthew 27:3–10, Matthew 27:57–60
JOURNAL ESSAY PROMPTS
Choose one prompt below and write a 300 to 500 word response in your study journal. Cite at least one Scripture from this lesson, write in your own words, and show how it applies to your life.
1. The Silver Dollars: In your own words, explain Peter Stoner’s Texas silver dollar illustration. Why does it answer the claim that Jesus fulfilled prophecy by chance?
2. Psalm 22:16: Why is it important that David wrote about pierced hands and feet centuries before crucifixion was used? What does that tell you about who was guiding his pen?

3. Faith for Today: God was exactly right about the first coming of Jesus. How should that change the way you read the promises about the Rapture and the end times? How can it help you when you feel anxious?

chapters.title: Lesson 3: The Near and Far View

paragraphs.text: Lesson 3
The Near and Far View
The Mountain Peaks of Prophecy, the Olivet Discourse, and
the Third Temple
MEMORY VERSE
“Therefore when you see the ‘abomination of desolation,’ spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (whoever reads, let him understand)...” (Matthew 24:15, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

Imagine standing on a flat desert plain, looking at a mountain range fifty miles away. You see two tall peaks. From where you stand, they look like they are right next to each other, touching the same horizon.

You might think that if you climbed the first peak, you could step right across to the second. But when you drive across the desert and climb to the top of the first peak, you get a shock. A deep valley, miles wide, lies between the two mountains. You could not see it from fifty miles away, because distance squeezes everything together.
That is how many prophecies work. The Hebrew prophets often saw a near fulfillment and a far fulfillment in the same view, like two
mountain peaks with a hidden valley between them. Bible teachers call this the Near and Far View, or the Mountain Peaks of Prophecy.

If you do not understand this, prophecy will look like a pile of contradictions. In this lesson we will see how it works in Isaiah 61 and in Matthew chapter 24. We will also see why mixing up the peaks has led many churches to put the Church into Israel’s Tribulation, and why today’s headlines about Jerusalem matter.
TWO PEAKS, ONE VIEW
When the Old Testament prophets looked down the long hallway of time, they did not see history laid out like a calendar page. They saw it like a man looking at a mountain range from far away.
They saw Peak A: the Messiah coming as a suffering servant. Humble, riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), pierced through His hands and feet, led like a lamb to the slaughter.

And right next to it, sometimes in the very same sentence, they saw Peak B: the Messiah coming as a conquering King. Riding a white horse, His robe dipped in blood, ruling the nations with a rod of iron (Psalm 2:9), the same King John later saw in Revelation 19:11–16, bringing peace to the whole earth from Jerusalem.

From far away, the prophets could not see the valley between the two peaks. They did not know the two comings would be separated by about two thousand years. Peter says the prophets “searched carefully” when they wrote about “the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow” (1 Peter 1:10–11, NKJV). They saw both peaks but not the distance between them.

That is why so many religious leaders missed Jesus at His first coming. They were looking only for Peak B, a King who would crush Rome. They walked right past the suffering servant of Peak A. When Jesus did not bring political peace right away, they decided He could
not be the Messiah. They did not understand that Peak A had to come first.
THE FIRST EXAMPLE: WHERE
JESUS STOPPED READING
Go back to the synagogue in Nazareth from Lesson 1. Put the words Isaiah wrote next to the words Jesus read. Look closely at where Jesus stopped.
What Isaiah wrote: “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God...” (Isaiah 61:2, NKJV)
What Jesus read: “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” (Luke 4:19, NKJV)

Jesus stopped in the middle of the verse. He did not read “and the day of vengeance of our God.” He rolled up the scroll, handed it back, sat down to teach, and said, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”
Why did He stop right there? Because He was showing the Near and Far View in front of everyone.

The first half of the verse belonged to Peak A, His first coming as Savior. He came to bring grace, heal the brokenhearted, and set captives free from sin. That part was being fulfilled that very day.

The second half, “the day of vengeance of our God,” belongs to Peak B, His second coming as Judge, when He brings God’s wrath on a rebellious world. That part was not fulfilled that day, so Jesus did not read it.

Between two phrases of one verse, God hid a valley of time that has already lasted about two thousand years. That valley is the Church Age, the age of grace, when the door is open for anyone to be saved before the day of judgment comes.
THE SECOND EXAMPLE: THE THREE
QUESTIONS OF MATTHEW 24
Now let us see the same pattern in a whole chapter: Matthew 24, the most important prophecy in the Gospels.
Jesus and His disciples were walking away from the temple in Jerusalem. The disciples were amazed at the huge white stones and the beautiful buildings. Jesus stopped and said something shocking:
“And Jesus said to them, ‘Do you not see all these things? Assuredly, I say to you, not one stone shall be left here upon another, that shall not be thrown down.’” (Matthew 24:2, NKJV)
He was talking about the real temple standing in front of them. Then they climbed the Mount of Olives, where they could look across the valley at the temple.

“Now as He sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to Him privately, saying, ‘Tell us, when will these things be? And what will be the sign of Your coming, and of the end of the age?’” (Matthew 24:3, NKJV)
The disciples asked three questions in one breath:
Question 1: When will these things be? They meant the destruction of the temple.
Question 2: What will be the sign of Your coming? They meant His return in glory.
Question 3: What will be the sign of the end of the age? They meant the end of the whole timeline.
In their minds, all three would happen at the same time. They squeezed the timeline together, just like someone looking at two peaks from far away.

Jesus answered with a near and far answer. He spoke about the near peak: the destruction of Jerusalem (Matthew 24:2; Luke 21:20–24). That happened in AD 70, when the Roman army under the general Titus broke through the city walls and burned the temple. According to tradition, soldiers pried the stones apart to get at the gold that had melted into the cracks. That was the near peak.
Then Jesus turned to the far peak: the Great Tribulation and His return in glory at the end of the age.
LET THE READER UNDERSTAND
As Jesus turned to the far peak, He pointed straight to the book of Daniel and added a short warning.

“Therefore when you see the ‘abomination of desolation,’ spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (whoever reads, let him understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.” (Matthew 24:15–16, NKJV)

Look at the words in parentheses: “whoever reads, let him understand.” Mark’s Gospel includes the same warning (Mark 13:14). It is like a flashing light on the page. Slow down. Pay attention to who this is for.

The abomination of desolation is a future event. The Antichrist will walk into a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, stop the sacrifices, and demand to be worshiped as God. The Antichrist is the coming world ruler who sets himself against Christ. Lesson 4 shows where he comes from.

Now notice who Jesus is talking to. “Let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.” He did not say the church in America or Europe. He named Judea, the heartland of Israel. And He said, “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24:20, NKJV). The Sabbath rules were part of Jewish life in the land of
Israel. That detail tells you this part of the prophecy is aimed at Israel.
THE THIRD TEMPLE IN TODAY’S HEADLINES

For the Antichrist to stand in the holy place, there must be a temple standing in Jerusalem. That means a Third Temple must be built on the Temple Mount. King Solomon built the First Temple, and Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC. The Second Temple was built after the Jews came home from Babylon, and it was the temple Jesus walked in. Rome destroyed it in AD 70. The Temple Mount is the hill in Jerusalem where both of them stood.

This is why this lesson is not dry history. Open the news and you will see constant fights over the Temple Mount. There are organizations in Israel that have already drawn the plans for the temple, made the garments for the priests, and prepared many of the sacred items needed for temple worship. The work is underway.
The world thinks the fight over Jerusalem is just an argument over land. But a student of prophecy knows the world is being moved toward exactly what Matthew 24:15 requires.

The Third Temple does not start Daniel’s final countdown. As you will see in Lesson 4, a seven-year treaty with Israel starts the clock. But the temple must be standing for the abomination of desolation to happen in the middle of those seven years. When you see the preparations for that temple, you are watching the far peak come into view.
DO NOT PUT THE CHURCH
IN ISRAEL’S TRIBULATION
This is where Replacement Theology causes great confusion. It is the teaching that the Church has replaced Israel, and we will study where it came from in Lesson 7.

Because many churches believe the Church replaced Israel, they read Matthew 24, see the horrors of the Great Tribulation, and say the Church will go through it. They take a passage Jesus aimed at Israel and force the Church into it.
But when you keep the near and far peaks straight, you see something important: the Church is not in the Tribulation timeline of Matthew 24.

That does not mean Matthew 24 has nothing to say to us. Jesus’ warnings about the abomination of desolation, fleeing from Judea, and praying that your flight is not on the Sabbath are aimed at Israel during the Tribulation. But some of His words are for every believer in every age: watch, be ready, and learn the season from the fig tree (Matthew 24:32–44). That is why this book uses those verses for the Church. And “the elect” in Matthew 24:22 and 31 are the people who belong to God during those seven years, including the remnant of Israel.

Bible teachers call this teaching the Olivet Discourse, because Jesus gave it on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24–25, Mark 13, Luke 21). The whole Olivet Discourse is set in a Jewish world. The disciples asked about a Jewish temple. Jesus spoke of Judea and the Sabbath. The Church is a separate mystery. In the Bible, a mystery is not something no one can understand. It is a truth God kept hidden in the Old Testament and has now made known. Paul says the mystery is that the Gentiles “should be fellow heirs, of the same body” (Ephesians 3:6, NKJV). The Church is that mystery, and the Bride
will be taken home to the Bridegroom’s house before Daniel’s final seven years begin. You will study that rescue in Lessons 10 and 11.
Forcing the Church into the Tribulation mixes up the mountain peaks. It assumes that because two events appear on the same horizon, they must happen to the same people.
God does not mix up His plans. Israel goes through the refining fire of the Tribulation and comes out restored. The Church is delivered from the wrath to come.
NEXT: DANIEL’S SEVENTY WEEKS
When Jesus gave His warning in Matthew 24:15, He sent us to “Daniel the prophet.” He was pointing to one of the most precise prophecies in the Bible: the Seventy Weeks of Daniel.

To understand the near and far peaks fully, we have to go back to the Old Testament and find the countdown Jesus was reading. In the next lesson, we will open Daniel, count the years to the day Jesus rode into Jerusalem, see why the prophetic clock stopped at the Cross, and see how a seven-year treaty will start it again.
WHY THIS MATTERS FOR YOUR FAITH
When you understand the Near and Far View, the confusion clears. Bible prophecy is not a mess. It is a masterpiece.
Keep the near peak, the destruction of the temple in AD 70, separate from the far peak, the future temple and the Second Coming, and you see that God is right every time.

History is not sliding into chaos. It is moving on God’s schedule. The Bridegroom will protect His Bride from the day of vengeance. You can look at the headlines with clear eyes, knowing which peak is coming next.
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: The Near and Far View shows that prophets often saw near and far events side by side, which is why Jesus stopped reading Isaiah 61 in the middle of a verse, and why Matthew 24 separates the destruction of the temple in AD 70 from the future Tribulation and Second Coming.
Three truths:
1. Where Jesus stopped: Jesus stopped in the middle of Isaiah 61:2, showing that a valley of two thousand years lies between His first coming and the day of vengeance.
2. Three questions, two peaks: The disciples squeezed the timeline together in Matthew 24, but Jesus separated the near destruction of Jerusalem from the far sign of His return.
3. The temple in the headlines: The preparations for a Third Temple show the far peak of Matthew 24:15 coming into view.
Key Verses: Isaiah 61:1–2, Luke 4:18–21, Matthew 24:2–3, Matthew 24:15–20, Zechariah 9:9
JOURNAL ESSAY PROMPTS
Choose one prompt below and write a 300 to 500 word response in your study journal. Cite at least one Scripture from this lesson, write in your own words, and show how it applies to your life.
1. Let the Reader Understand: Why does Matthew 24:15 include the words “whoever reads, let him understand”? Why is it important to know who a prophecy is talking to before you apply it?
2. The Third Temple: Why must a Third Temple be standing for Matthew 24:15 to be fulfilled? What starts Daniel’s final seven years, and how does the temple fit into that time?

3. The Church and the Tribulation: Using this lesson, explain why putting the Church into the Tribulation mixes up the near and far peaks. How does knowing you are the Bride of Christ take away fear when you read end-times Scripture?

chapters.title: Lesson 4: The Seventy Weeks of Daniel

paragraphs.text: Lesson 4
The Seventy Weeks of Daniel
God’s Prophetic Stopwatch and the Restarting of the Clock
MEMORY VERSE

“Seventy weeks are determined for your people and for your holy city, to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make reconciliation for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy.” (Daniel 9:24, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

If you love watches, picture a Rolex Cosmograph Daytona on your wrist. It is one of the most famous watches in the world, built for timing races. Besides telling the time, it has a stopwatch, called a chronograph.

Press the top button on the side of the case, and the stopwatch hand starts sweeping around the dial. Press the same button again in the middle of a lap, and the hand stops. It freezes in place, holding the exact time, while something else happens on the track. Press the button a third time, and the hand picks up right where it left off and finishes the count. Only the bottom button resets it to zero.
That is how God’s prophetic calendar runs. It is driven by one of the most precise prophecies in the Bible: the Seventy Weeks of Daniel.
The clock ran, then it stopped, and one day it will start again right where it left off.

This lesson follows the three presses of the button: start, stop, and restart. In Lesson 3, Jesus pointed us to “Daniel the prophet.” Now we will read Daniel’s prophecy and look at the history that proves the stopwatch is real.

Before we start, a word of comfort. This is the lesson where many readers get lost, because it is full of numbers. We know it can be confusing. So here is the secret: you do not need to memorize a single number. There is no test on how many days are in 483 years. Don’t pay attention to the numbers. Pay attention to the proof. The numbers are only here to show one thing: God told Daniel when the Messiah would come, and He was right to the day.
If you remember only three words from this lesson, remember these: start, stop, restart.
THE ANGEL’S MESSAGE

Daniel was an old man living in exile in Babylon. He was reading the scroll of Jeremiah and realized that Israel’s seventy years of captivity were almost over (Daniel 9:2). As he fasted and prayed for Jerusalem, the angel Gabriel came to him with a message that lays out the shape of history. It begins with the memory verse at the top of this lesson.

Notice who the clock is for. Gabriel said the seventy weeks are for “your people and for your holy city.” Daniel’s people were Israel, and his holy city was Jerusalem. This stopwatch belongs to Israel. Keep that in mind, and the rest of the prophecy makes sense.
When English readers see “seventy weeks,” they think of seven-day weeks on a calendar. But the Hebrew word is shavu’im, which simply means “sevens.” Think of the word “dozen.” A dozen means
twelve, whether it is twelve eggs, twelve donuts, or twelve cars. In the same way, a “seven” is a group of seven. In Daniel 9, each “seven” is seven years. So seventy sevens is 490 years.
Here is the whole plan. Just follow the first column:
Button When What Happens
Start The king’s command to rebuild Jerusalem
The countdown begins: 69 weeks until “Messiah the Prince.”
Stop The week Jesus rode into Jerusalem as King
Jesus is “cut off,” and the clock stops after 69 weeks.
Paused About 2,000 years so far Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed, and the Church Age runs.
Restart A seven-year treaty with Israel The last week begins: the time of Jacob’s trouble.
Sixty-nine weeks are done. One week is still waiting. That is the whole prophecy. Now let’s press the buttons one at a time.
BUTTON 1: START

“Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the command to restore and build Jerusalem until Messiah the Prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublesome times.” (Daniel 9:25, NKJV)

The clock starts with “the command to restore and build Jerusalem.” The Bible records that command. In the month of Nisan, which falls in our March or April, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes of Persia, the king gave Nehemiah permission to go and rebuild Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:1–8).

Why does Gabriel say “seven weeks and sixty-two weeks” instead of just sixty-nine? Many Bible teachers believe the first seven weeks, 49 years, cover the rebuilding of the city, when “the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublesome times.” The other
sixty-two weeks run on until the Messiah comes. Put them together, and you have sixty-nine weeks.
Here is the short version. Gabriel gave Daniel a countdown. When you count it out, it lands on Palm Sunday, the very day Jesus rode into Jerusalem as King. That is the proof.
The steps below just show the work, like a math teacher who asks how you got your answer. If numbers make your head spin, feel free to skim them and pick up again at “Think about what that means.”
Step 1: Add the weeks. 7 weeks plus 62 weeks is 69 weeks.
Step 2: Turn weeks into years. 69 times 7 is 483 years.

Step 3: Use God’s prophetic year. Bible prophecy uses a year of 360 days, and the Bible proves it. In Revelation, the same period is called “forty-two months” and “one thousand two hundred and sixty days” (Revelation 11:2–3; 12:6; 13:5). Divide 1,260 days by 42 months, and you get 30 days a month, or 360 days a year. The Bible uses 30-day months as far back as the Flood. The waters rose on the seventeenth day of the second month, and the ark rested on the seventeenth day of the seventh month, five months later. Genesis calls that time 150 days (Genesis 7:11, 7:24, 8:4).
Step 4: Turn years into days. 483 years times 360 days is 173,880 days.

Step 5: Count the days. In 1881, Sir Robert Anderson, who later became the head of the detectives at Scotland Yard in London, did the counting. That’s right: a real-life detective checked Daniel’s math. In his book The Coming Prince, he started from the king’s command in the month of Nisan, 445 BC, and counted forward exactly 173,880 days, adjusting for leap years. His count landed on April 6, AD 32: Palm Sunday, the day Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey.

You may notice that 445 BC to AD 32 is only 476 years on our calendar, not 483. That is not a mistake. Our year has about 365 and a quarter days, and the prophetic year has 360. So 483 prophetic years, 173,880 days, add up to about 476 of our years. (There was no year 0, so from 445 BC to AD 32 is 476 years.)

Think about what that means. Imagine finding a letter written in the 1500s that named the very day something would happen this year, and then it happened right on that day. That is what Daniel’s prophecy did, and it was written more than five hundred years ahead of time.

Again and again during His ministry, Jesus had told people to keep quiet about who He was. He kept saying His hour had not yet come. But on that day He did the opposite. He rode into Jerusalem in a public, royal procession, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. He let the crowds wave palm branches and shout, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Matthew 21:9, NKJV).
Then, as He came near the city, He wept over it:
“If you had known, even you, especially in this your day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.” (Luke 19:42, NKJV)

“This your day.” Jesus held Jerusalem responsible for knowing the day. He said judgment would come “because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19:44, NKJV). The prophecy had been in their scrolls for more than five centuries.
BUTTON 2: STOP

“And after the sixty-two weeks Messiah shall be cut off, but not for Himself; and the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end of it shall be with a flood, and till the end of the war desolations are determined.” (Daniel 9:26, NKJV)

This is where God pressed the button on the stopwatch. The sixtyninth week ended when Jesus presented Himself as King. Days later, the Messiah was “cut off,” crucified, not for His own sins but for ours. So when this book says the clock stopped at the Cross, this is what it means: the count ran out the day He rode in as King, a few days later He was cut off, and the clock has stayed stopped ever since.
How do we know the clock stopped there and did not keep running? The Bible gives us two proofs.
Proof 1: The Order of Verse 26
Look closely at verse 26. It names two events that happen “after the sixty-two weeks,” after the sixty-ninth week is over:
First, “Messiah shall be cut off.” Jesus was crucified just days after the Triumphal Entry.
Second, “the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary.” The Roman army destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70.

AD 70 came almost forty years after the cross. A “week” in this prophecy is only seven years long, so those forty years cannot fit inside the seventieth week. Both events happen after the sixty-ninth week and before the seventieth. The text itself leaves room for a gap.
Proof 2: Six Promises Still Waiting
Go back to our memory verse. Gabriel listed six things God would do by the time all seventy weeks are over. Ask a simple question about each one: is it done yet?
The Promise in Daniel 9:24
Where It Stands Today
To finish the transgression Waiting. As a nation, Israel still has not turned back to her Messiah.
To make an end of sins Paid for at the cross. Israel as a nation will receive it when she repents.
To make reconciliation for iniquity
Paid for at the cross. Israel as a nation will receive it on her Day of Atonement (Lesson 6).
To bring in everlasting righteousness
Waiting. The world is still full of evil until the King reigns.
To seal up vision and prophecy
Waiting. Many prophecies, like the ones in this book, have not happened yet.
To anoint the Most Holy Waiting. Many teachers see this as the anointing of the holy place in the Kingdom.

Jesus paid for sin once and for all. “Now, once at the end of the ages, He has appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself” (Hebrews 9:26, NKJV). But look at the rest of the list. Everlasting righteousness does not rule the earth. Prophecy has not been sealed up. Israel has not turned back to God as a nation.
If the seventy weeks were finished, all six promises would be finished. They are not, so one week is still waiting to run. The clock stopped.
The Pause

You have seen God do this before. In Lesson 3, Jesus stopped reading Isaiah in the middle of a sentence, because the rest of the verse belonged to His second coming. Daniel’s clock has the same kind of pause.

Think of a football game. When a team calls a time-out, the game clock stops. The players are still on the field, and the game is not over. There is still time left on the clock, and when play starts again, the clock picks up right where it stopped. Israel’s clock has been in a time-out for about two thousand years, and seven years are still left on it.
The pause is the hidden valley we saw in Lesson 3: the Church Age. God paused Israel’s clock and opened a window of grace when Jews and Gentiles are saved together into one body.

During most of that pause, there was no nation of Israel on the map. Then in 1948, God brought Israel back into her land, and in 1973 He kept her alive through a surprise attack. In Lesson 9 you will study that story in detail. For now, know this: Israel’s return is a sign that the pause is ending and the final seven years are getting near.
A Quick Check
Take a breath. You have already learned most of this prophecy. Here it is in three lines:
Start: The king’s command to rebuild Jerusalem. Done.
Stop: Jesus rides in as King and is cut off. Done.
Restart: A seven-year treaty with Israel. Still waiting.
BUTTON 3: RESTART

“Then he shall confirm a covenant with many for one week; but in the middle of the week he shall bring an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of abominations shall be one who makes desolate, even until the consummation, which is determined, is poured out on the desolate.” (Daniel 9:27, NKJV)

Who is “he”? Look back at verse 26: “the prince who is to come.” His people are the ones who destroyed the city and the temple, and that was the Roman army. So this coming prince will rise from the people of the old Roman world. He is the coming world leader the Bible calls the Antichrist.
He will confirm a seven-year covenant, a treaty, with Israel. The day that treaty is confirmed, the stopwatch starts again, and the final seven years begin.
That agreement will give Israel security, and with it the freedom to do what we saw in Lesson 3: rebuild the temple on the Temple Mount and bring back the sacrifices.

But there is a trap. Gabriel warns that “in the middle of the week,” three and a half years into the treaty, the Antichrist will break his word. He will stop the sacrifices and set up “the abomination of desolation” in the temple, demanding to be worshiped as God. That betrayal starts the last three and a half years, the time Jesus called the Great Tribulation in Matthew 24.
THE TIME OF JACOB’S TROUBLE
The Bible gives these final seven years a name, and it is not “the Church’s trouble.”
“Alas! For that day is great, so that none is like it; and it is the time of Jacob’s trouble, but he shall be saved out of it.” (Jeremiah 30:7, NKJV)

God named this time after Jacob. And notice how the verse ends: “but he shall be saved out of it.” The trouble is real, but it ends in rescue. To understand why God allows it, look at what the name Jacob means.
In Hebrew, Jacob is Ya’aqov. It comes from the word for “heel.” Jacob was born holding his twin brother’s heel (Genesis 25:26), and

his name came to mean “heel-catcher,” the one who trips others up to get ahead. His brother Esau said, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times” (Genesis 27:36, NKJV). Jacob was a schemer. He leaned on his own tricks and his own strength.

But in Genesis chapter 32, Jacob was alone at night by a river, afraid, because his brother was coming toward him with four hundred men. A Man came and wrestled with him all night. Many Bible teachers believe this Man was the Lord Himself, appearing before He came as Jesus. The Man touched Jacob’s hip and put it out of joint. Broken and unable to fight, Jacob stopped struggling and simply held on, saying, “I will not let You go unless You bless me!” (Genesis 32:26, NKJV).
Then the Man asked him, “What is your name?” Jacob had to say his name, which meant admitting who he was: the heel-catcher, the schemer. And God gave him a new name:
“And He said, ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have struggled with God and with men, and have prevailed.’” (Genesis 32:28, NKJV)
Jacob walked away with a limp for the rest of his life. He could never again run on his own strength. He had to lean on God.

That is the key to the end times. Israel today is back in her land, but in many ways she is living like Jacob. Since 1948 she has survived by her own military skill, her own intelligence, and her own political plans, and most of her people still do not believe in Jesus.

God’s purpose for the final seven years is to bring the whole nation through that same wrestling match. The Antichrist’s treaty will be broken. Every human strength Israel trusts in will fail. The nation will be backed against the wall with nowhere to turn.
That is the time of Jacob’s trouble. It is a fire meant to break Jacob’s self-reliance so the nation falls into the arms of her Messiah and
cries out, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” Then the old character of Jacob will be broken for good, and the nation will be what God named her: Israel.

The Church was never named Jacob. The Church does not need to be broken out of rejecting Christ. The Church has already been washed in the blood of the Lamb and stands accepted as the Bride. To put the Church into Jacob’s trouble is to put the Bride into a wrestling match that was designed for someone else.
GOD HOLDS THE STOPWATCH

Some teachers say the Church replaced Israel, so the whole 490 years must have finished long ago. They squeeze the last seven years into the past and turn real numbers, a real temple, and real places into vague symbols. We will look at that teaching in Lesson 7. But Gabriel said the clock is for “your people and for your holy city.” Leave the clock with the people it belongs to, and the whole prophecy fits together.

God’s timeline is a masterpiece. The clock started with the command to rebuild Jerusalem. It stopped when the Messiah was cut off. It will start again when a treaty is signed with Israel. History is not drifting off course.

The same God who counted 173,880 days to the day Jesus rode into Jerusalem is holding the stopwatch for the final seven years. As the headlines about Jerusalem grow louder, you do not need to be afraid.
The Bridegroom is in control of the schedule, and He is preparing to take His Bride home before the final countdown begins.
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: Daniel’s Seventy Weeks are a 490-year plan for Israel that started with the command to rebuild Jerusalem, counted to the day Jesus presented Himself as King, stopped at the Cross to open the Church Age, and will start again when a seven-year treaty begins the time of Jacob’s trouble.
Three truths:
1. Start: Sixty-nine weeks of 360-day years equals 173,880 days, and that count runs from the command of King Artaxerxes to the day Jesus rode into Jerusalem as King.
2. Stop: Verse 26 places the cross and the fall of Jerusalem after the sixty-ninth week, and the six promises of verse 24 are not finished, so the seventieth week is still ahead.

3. Restart: A seven-year treaty with Israel will start the last week, the time of Jacob’s trouble, which God will use to break Israel’s selfreliance so she turns to her Messiah, something the Church, already washed in His blood, does not need.
Key Verses: Daniel 9:24–27, Nehemiah 2:1–8, Luke 19:41–44, Hebrews 9:26, Jeremiah 30:7, Genesis 32:24–30
JOURNAL ESSAY PROMPTS
Choose one prompt below and write a 300 to 500 word response in your study journal. Cite at least one Scripture from this lesson, write in your own words, and show how it applies to your life.

1. The Stopwatch: Explain the three presses of the stopwatch button in Daniel’s prophecy: start, stop, and restart. What event goes with each one, and how do verse 26 and the six promises of verse 24 show that the clock is paused?

2. Jacob’s Name: Explain what the name Jacob means and what happened when he wrestled with God in Genesis 32. Why is the Tribulation called the time of Jacob’s trouble, and why does that show the Church is not in it?
3. This Your Day: Jesus held Jerusalem responsible for knowing “this your day” (Luke 19:42). What does that teach us about paying attention to the prophecies that are still waiting to be fulfilled?

chapters.title: Lesson 5: The Parables of the King

paragraphs.text: Lesson 5
The Parables of the King
Courtroom Prophecy in the Last Week of Jesus
MEMORY VERSE
“The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief
cornerstone. This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Matthew 21:42, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION
Many people think the parables of Jesus are simple stories for
children: a lost sheep, a farmer planting seed, a son who runs away.
Some parables are gentle like that. But in the last week of His life, in the temple in Jerusalem, Jesus told parables that were not gentle at
all.
They were courtroom prophecy.
Picture a courtroom. A lawyer stands before the people who are accusing him. He does not shout. He tells a story. The story is so
clear and so fair that his accusers give the verdict themselves, and
then they realize the verdict is against them.
That is exactly what Jesus did in Matthew chapters 21 and 22. The religious leaders came to put Him on trial. By the end, they were the ones on trial, and they had pronounced their own sentence.
God has not canceled His promises to Israel, as you will see clearly
in Lesson 7. In this lesson we will see what did change when Israel’s leaders rejected their King. Jesus told them that the care of God’s
kingdom would be taken out of their hands. These parables show us how that happened, and they set the stage for the rest of this course.
THE CHALLENGE: BY WHAT AUTHORITY?
It was the week Jesus would be crucified. He had ridden into
Jerusalem on a donkey while crowds shouted “Hosanna!” He had driven the money changers out of the temple. Now He was teaching in the temple courts, and the leaders came at Him.
“Now when He came into the temple, the chief priests and the
elders of the people confronted Him as He was teaching, and said, ‘By what authority are You doing these things? And
who gave You this authority?’” (Matthew 21:23, NKJV)
This was a legal challenge. The chief priests and elders ran the
temple. In their eyes, Jesus had no license to teach there, and no right to clean out their marketplace.
Jesus answered with a question about John the Baptist: was John’s baptism from heaven or from men? They were trapped. If they said
“from heaven,” Jesus would ask why they did not believe John. If they said “from men,” the crowd, who believed John was a prophet, would turn on them. So they said, “We do not know.” And Jesus
said, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matthew 21:27, NKJV).
Then He told three parables. Each one was a case brought against
them.
THE FIRST CASE: THE TWO SONS
“But what do you think? A man had two sons, and he came to the first and said, ‘Son, go, work today in my vineyard.’ He answered and said, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he regretted it
and went. Then he came to the second and said likewise. And he answered and said, ‘I go, sir,’ but he did not go. Which of the two did the will of his father?” (Matthew 21:28–31, NKJV)
The leaders answered, “The first.” They gave the right answer, and it convicted them.
Jesus explained: “Assuredly, I say to you that tax collectors and harlots enter the kingdom of God before you” (Matthew 21:31,
NKJV).

The tax collectors and sinners were like the first son. At first they said no to God, but when John preached, they repented and obeyed. The religious leaders were like the second son. They said all the right words, “Yes, sir, we serve God,” but they never obeyed. When God
sent John, and then sent His own Son, they refused to go into the vineyard.
The point is simple. God is not looking for people who say the right words. He is looking for people who do His will.
THE SECOND CASE: THE WICKED TENANTS
The second parable is the center of this lesson.
“Hear another parable: There was a certain landowner who planted a vineyard and set a hedge around it, dug a
winepress in it and built a tower. And he leased it to vinedressers and went into a far country.” (Matthew 21:33, NKJV)

The leaders listening that day knew this picture. Seven hundred years earlier, Isaiah had sung a song about a vineyard. God planted it, protected it, and waited for good grapes, but it produced only wild grapes. Then Isaiah explained the song:
“For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are His pleasant plant. He looked for justice, but behold, oppression; for righteousness, but behold,
a cry for help.” (Isaiah 5:7, NKJV)
So when Jesus started talking about a vineyard, everyone knew He was talking about Israel.

But notice something important. In Isaiah, the vineyard itself was the problem. In Jesus’ parable, the vineyard is fine. The problem is the tenants, the vinedressers who were hired to take care of it. The tenants are the leaders.
The owner sent servants to collect his share of the fruit. The tenants
beat one, killed one, and stoned another. He sent more servants, and they did the same. This is the history of Israel’s prophets, who were rejected, beaten, and killed by the leaders of their day.
“Then last of all he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ But when the vinedressers saw the son, they
said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance.’ So they took him and cast him out of the vineyard and killed him.” (Matthew 21:37–39, NKJV)
Jesus was describing His own death, days before it happened. He would be taken outside the city walls and killed. The leaders wanted the vineyard for themselves, without the owner.
THEY PRONOUNCED THEIR OWN SENTENCE
Then Jesus asked the question that sprang the trap:
“Therefore, when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will
he do to those vinedressers?” (Matthew 21:40, NKJV)
“They said to Him, ‘He will destroy those wicked men miserably, and lease his vineyard to other vinedressers who will render to him the fruits in their seasons.’” (Matthew
They gave the verdict. They said the wicked tenants deserved to lose
the vineyard. They did not realize they were judging themselves.
This had happened once before in Israel’s history. After King David
took another man’s wife and had her husband killed, the prophet Nathan came to him with a story. A rich man with many sheep stole
a poor man’s only little lamb. David was furious and said, “As the Lord lives, the man who has done this shall surely die!” Then Nathan said to David, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:5, 7, NKJV).
Jesus did the same thing. He let the leaders announce the sentence, and then He showed them it was theirs.
“Jesus said to them, ‘Have you never read in the Scriptures:
“The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone. This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes”?’” (Matthew 21:42, NKJV)
That is a quote from Psalm 118:22–23. The builders were the leaders
of Israel. The stone was Jesus. They would throw Him away as worthless, but God would make Him the most important stone in
the whole building.
WHAT WAS TAKEN, AND WHAT WAS NOT
Then Jesus gave the ruling:
“Therefore I say to you, the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation bearing the fruits of it.” (Matthew 21:43, NKJV)
This is the verse people who teach Replacement Theology love to
quote. They say it proves God took everything from Israel and gave
it to the Church forever. But read carefully. Who was Jesus talking to?
The next verse answers that question:
“Now when the chief priests and Pharisees heard His
parables, they perceived that He was speaking of them.”
(Matthew 21:45, NKJV)
Jesus was not talking about the vineyard. He was talking about the tenants. The vineyard, Israel, stays the owner’s. What was taken
away was the job of caring for it, the leadership and stewardship of
God’s kingdom, from the leaders who rejected the Son.
And who received that job? A “nation bearing the fruits.” Peter later
used that same kind of language for believers in Jesus, both Jews and Gentiles, calling them “a holy nation, His own special people” (1
Peter 2:9, NKJV). The first people to receive that stewardship were Jewish apostles. Through them the gospel went out to the world, and the Church Age began.

This is a change of stewards for this age, not the cancellation of God’s covenants. Paul said so clearly: “For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29, NKJV). And Jesus Himself,
later that same day, told Jerusalem that her story was not over:
“For I say to you, you shall see Me no more till you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!’” (Matthew
“Till” means there is an end to the waiting. One day Jerusalem will welcome her King. You will see how that happens in Lessons 6 and 12.
THE THIRD CASE: THE WEDDING FEAST
The third parable moves from a vineyard to a wedding.
“The kingdom of heaven is like a certain king who arranged a marriage for his son, and sent out his servants to call those
who were invited to the wedding; and they were not willing to come.” (Matthew 22:2–3, NKJV)
The king sent more servants: “Tell those who are invited, See, I have prepared my dinner... Come to the wedding.” But the invited guests
made light of it. One went to his farm, another to his business, and
the rest seized the servants, mistreated them, and killed them (Matthew 22:4–6).
The king was furious. He sent his armies and burned their city (Matthew 22:7). Less than forty years later, in AD 70, the Roman army burned Jerusalem and destroyed the temple, just as Jesus had
warned.
Then the king said:
“Therefore go into the highways, and as many as you find, invite to the wedding.” (Matthew 22:9, NKJV)
The servants went out and gathered everyone they found, bad and good, and the wedding hall was filled. This is the Church Age. The

invitation that was refused by the leaders went out to the highways of the whole world. In this parable Jesus uses wedding guests to teach one point: the invitation goes to everyone. Elsewhere the Bible
pictures the Church as the Bride herself (2 Corinthians 11:2). One picture teaches the open invitation. The other teaches the love and the covenant, and you will see that in Lesson 11.
But the story has a warning at the end.
