“But when the king came in to see the guests, he saw a man there who did not have on a wedding garment. So he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding
garment?’ And he was speechless.” (Matthew 22:11–12, NKJV)
The man was thrown out. Jesus ended with these words: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14, NKJV).
What does “few are chosen” mean? Everyone is invited, but only those who accept what the King provides stay at the feast.
The invitation is free, and it goes to everyone. But no one gets into the wedding in his own clothes. Every guest must wear the garment the King provides. That garment is the righteousness of Christ,
received by faith. In Lesson 11, you will see how much the Bible says about the Bride’s wedding garment.
THE LAWYER SILENCES EVERY CHALLENGER
The leaders were stung, but they were not finished. They came back
with the hardest questions they could find, trying to trap Jesus in front of the crowd. One by one, He answered them.

The Pharisees asked if it was right to pay taxes to Caesar. If He said yes, the people would hate Him. If He said no, Rome would arrest Him. Jesus held up a coin with Caesar’s face on it and said, “Render
therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21, NKJV).
The Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection, asked a trick
question about a woman who married seven brothers. Jesus
answered from the Law of Moses that God “is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32, NKJV).
An expert in the Law of Moses asked which commandment was the
greatest. Jesus said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37, NKJV), and to love your neighbor as yourself.
Then Jesus asked them one question: “What do you think about the
Christ? Whose Son is He?” They said, “The Son of David.” Jesus asked how David could call his own son “Lord” in Psalm 110
(Matthew 22:42–45). The Messiah had to be more than a son of
David. He had to be David’s Lord, God Himself in human flesh.
“And no one was able to answer Him a word, nor from that
day on did anyone dare question Him anymore.” (Matthew
The courtroom went silent. The One they came to judge had judged
them, and no one could answer Him.
THE FIG TREE WITH NO FRUIT
One more scene from that week ties these parables together. On His way into the city, Jesus saw a fig tree covered in leaves.
“And seeing a fig tree by the road, He came to it and found
nothing on it but leaves, and said to it, ‘Let no fruit grow on
you ever again.’ Immediately the fig tree withered away.” (Matthew 21:19, NKJV)
The tree looked alive, but it had no fruit. That is a picture of the religious leadership of that day: lots of leaves, lots of show, but no
fruit for God. In Lesson 9 you will see that Jesus also promised a day
when the fig tree would put out new leaves again.
WHY THESE PARABLES MATTER FOR PROPHECY
These parables explain why there is a long “valley” of time between the first and second comings of Christ. The leaders rejected the Son,
so the care of the kingdom was taken from them, and the wedding
invitation went out to the whole world. That is the Church Age we live in now.
They also guard us against Replacement Theology. The vineyard was
never thrown away. The tenants were replaced, not the vineyard. God is still the owner, and He will still keep His promises to Israel.
And they warn us personally. Saying “yes, sir” like the second son is not enough. Showing up at the wedding in your own clothes is not
enough. God is looking for people who obey Him and who are
clothed in the righteousness of His Son.
CHAPTER SUMMARY
One sentence: In His last week, Jesus told courtroom parables that let Israel’s leaders pronounce their own sentence, showing that the
care of God’s kingdom would be taken from those who rejected the
Son and given to a people bearing fruit, while God’s covenant with Israel stands.
Three truths:
1. The tenants, not the vineyard: The vineyard is Israel. The wicked
tenants are the leaders who rejected the Son. Their stewardship was taken away, but the vineyard still belongs to God.
2. Matthew 21:43 does not cancel Israel: Jesus spoke to the chief
priests and Pharisees (Matthew 21:45), and He promised Jerusalem
would one day say, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 23:39).
3. The invitation and the garment: The wedding invitation went out
to the highways of the world, but every guest must wear the garment the King provides.
Key Verses: Matthew 21:23, Matthew 21:28–46, Isaiah 5:7, Psalm 118:22–23, Matthew 22:1–14, Matthew 22:46, Matthew 23:39
JOURNAL ESSAY PROMPTS
Choose one prompt below and write a 300 to 500 word response in your study journal. Cite at least one Scripture from this lesson, write in your own words, and show how it applies to your life.
1. The Courtroom: Explain how Jesus used the parable of the wicked
tenants to let the leaders pronounce their own sentence. How is this
like Nathan’s story to King David?
2. Matthew 21:43: Someone tells you this verse proves God replaced
Israel with the Church. Using Matthew 21:45, Matthew 23:39, and
Romans 11:29, explain what was taken away and what was not.
3. The Wedding Garment: What does the man without a wedding
garment teach us? Which son in the parable of the two sons are you
most like right now, and what needs to change?

chapters.title: Lesson 6: The Seven Feasts of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Lesson 6
The Seven Feasts of the Lord
God’s Calendar, the Nine Harvests, and the Numbers of
Perfection
MEMORY VERSE
“The feasts of the Lord, which you shall proclaim to be holy convocations, these are My feasts.” (Leviticus 23:2, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

When most people look at Israel’s religious calendar in the Old Testament, they think they are looking at a list of Jewish holidays, old cultural celebrations for one group of people. That is why many churches skip them. Many believers think of them as old rules that ended at the cross.
But read what God actually wrote. These days do not belong to Israel as her own property. God puts His own name on them. He calls them His appointed times.

In this lesson we will walk through the Lord’s calendar in Leviticus 23, look at the farming seasons of Israel, and see what the nine harvests picture. Then we will see how the first four feasts were fulfilled exactly at Christ’s first coming, why the next feast points to the Rapture of the Church, why the Day of Atonement points to Israel, and why the last feast belongs to all of God’s people together.
THE APPOINTED TIMES
Start where God starts.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: “The feasts of the Lord, which you shall proclaim to be holy convocations, these are My feasts.”’” (Leviticus 23:1–2, NKJV)
Look at who owns these days. God does not call them “the feasts of the Jews” or “Israel’s holidays.” He says, “These are My feasts.”
Two Hebrew words help us understand them:

Moed: The word “feast” translates the Hebrew moed. It does not mean a party. It comes from a root that means “to fix” or “to meet by appointment.” A moed is an appointed time, a set meeting on God’s calendar, where He plans to meet His people on an exact day.

Miqra: The words “holy convocation” translate the Hebrew miqra. It comes from qara, which means “to call out.” A miqra is a calling together, and it also means a rehearsal. Think of a dress rehearsal before a play.

For about fifteen hundred years, God had Israel rehearse these seven feasts every year, like actors practicing a play. The people thought they were remembering the past. God had them practicing the future. When the Messiah came, He stepped onto the stage and fulfilled the real event on the very days they had been rehearsing.

Think of a fire drill at school. The first time the alarm rings, everyone is a little scared. By the third or fourth drill, it is just a routine. Some students walk out slowly, talking with friends, because they know it is only practice. That is what happened to many in Israel. They rehearsed the feasts for so long that the feasts became routine. When the real day came, most of them missed it.
THE SEVEN FEASTS AT A GLANCE

THE NINE HARVESTS

The seven feasts follow the farming seasons of the land of Israel. God tied His calendar to the rain, the weather, and the crops. Many Bible teachers count nine harvests in Israel’s year, grouped into three seasons, and they see a spiritual picture in each one.
1. The Early Spring Harvests (Jesus and the First Believers)

The Flax Harvest: Flax was among the first crops ready in spring (Exodus 9:31). It was dried and combed into fine white linen. In Scripture, fine linen is a picture of the righteousness of the saints (Revelation 19:8). Right at the start of the year, God shows us the clothing He is preparing for His people.

The Barley Firstfruits: Barley ripens first after the winter rains (Ruth 1:22). It is soft and needs gentle handling. The first sheaf of barley pictures Jesus rising as the Firstfruits from the dead, and the saints who came out of their graves after His resurrection (Matthew 27:52–53).
The Main Barley Harvest: This pictures the first great wave of people who believed the gospel after the resurrection, gathered easily into the Lord’s barn.
2. The Late Spring Harvests (the Church Age)

The Early Wheat Harvest: Wheat is harder than barley. To separate the grain from its husk, a farmer dragged a heavy wooden board over it. The board had sharp stones underneath. In Latin this board was called a tribulum, and it is where our word “tribulation” comes from. Early wheat pictures the young Church, born into pressure and testing.

The Main Wheat Harvest: This harvest is celebrated at Pentecost. It pictures the worldwide harvest of the Church over two thousand years. The Church grows in a world of pressure and spiritual battle, but every true grain ends up safe in the Master’s barn.
3. The Summer and Fall Fruit Harvests (Israel and Judgment)
The Early Fig Harvest: In Lesson 5 we saw a fig tree withered for having no fruit, and in Lesson 9 we will see that in the Bible the fig
tree is a picture of Israel. The early figs picture the Jewish believers in the days of the apostles.
The Summer Fruit Harvest: Dates and pomegranates ripen slowly in the hot summer sun. This pictures the small Jewish remnant God has kept alive among the nations through the long Church Age.

The Olive Harvest: Olives do not fall gently into a basket. Workers beat them from the branches and crush them under a heavy stone press until the oil runs out. That oil lit the lamps in the temple. This pictures the crushing God uses to break His people’s self-reliance and bring out pure oil that shines in the dark.

The Grape Harvest: Grapes come at the end of the year. Workers throw them into a stone vat and stomp them until red juice pours out. In prophecy, this harvest never pictures believers. It is the “winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God” (Revelation 19:15, NKJV), judgment on a world that rejects Christ at the end of the age.
THE NUMBERS: SEVEN, FIVE, ONE, AND ONE
Bible teachers have long seen meaning in certain numbers in Scripture. Look at how the seven feasts divide.
Seven is the number of completion. God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh, finishing creation week. In the same way, there are seven feasts, one complete week of prophetic history.
Inside that seven, the feasts divide into three groups: five feasts for the Church, one feast for Israel, and one feast for all believers together.
Five is often called the number of grace, God’s undeserved favor. The five feasts tied to the Church show that the Church Age is an age of grace.

One feast belongs to Israel: the Day of Atonement. It is the day the nation will be made “at one” with God again. Later in this lesson you will see that this is exactly what the word “atonement” means.

One feast belongs to everyone: Tabernacles. It is the feast when God lives with all of His people at once, the Church, Israel, and the nations. “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men” (Revelation 21:3, NKJV).
THE FIVE FEASTS OF GRACE: THE CHURCH
Feast 1: Passover (Pesach)

Passover falls on Nisan 14, which is in our March or April. It remembers the night in Egypt when the blood of a lamb on the doorposts caused the angel of death to pass over Israel’s homes. That night was a real rescue from physical death.

Centuries later, the true Lamb of God came. Paul wrote, “For indeed Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us” (1 Corinthians 5:7, NKJV). Jesus became our Passover Lamb. John’s Gospel shows that Jesus was crucified on the day of preparation for the Passover, the same day the Passover lambs were being slaughtered (John 19:14). He shed His blood so that judgment would pass over everyone who trusts in Him.
Jerusalem was full of people keeping the holiday that week. Most of them were so busy with the routine of the feast that they missed the true Lamb dying on a hill just outside the city walls.
Feast 2: Unleavened Bread

This feast begins on Nisan 15, the next day, and lasts seven days. For a week, Israel ate flat bread made with no yeast. In Scripture, leaven, or yeast, is a picture of sin. Jesus fulfilled this feast while His body lay in the tomb. He was without sin, and God did not allow His
Holy One “to see corruption” (Psalm 16:10, NKJV). Because of Him, the Church stands clean before God.
The Search and the Hidden Bread
Two customs in Jewish homes today paint a beautiful picture of this feast.

The night before Passover, a Jewish father searches his house for leaven. This search is called bedikat chametz. By custom, he takes a candle, a feather, and a wooden spoon and walks through the dark rooms, checking every corner for crumbs. The candle finds the crumbs, the feather sweeps them onto the spoon, and the next morning the crumbs are burned. It is a picture of the Holy Spirit searching the dark corners of our hearts and clearing out hidden sin.

Then at the Passover meal, there is a cloth pouch with three pockets, sometimes called the matzah tash. Each pocket holds one sheet of unleavened bread. Many rabbis teach that the three stand for Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Watch what the father does. He takes out the middle piece and breaks it in half. He wraps one half in a white cloth and hides it. At the end of the meal, the children search for it. This hidden piece is called the afikomen, which means “that which comes after.” When a child finds it, the father pays a reward to get it back.

These customs grew up over the centuries, long after the time of Moses. But look at the picture they paint. Three pieces in one pouch: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The middle piece is taken out, broken, wrapped in white linen, hidden away, and brought back. That is Jesus: the Son, broken on the cross, wrapped in burial linen, hidden in the tomb, and brought back alive on the third day. Even the name fits the picture. “That which comes after” points to His coming again, and the reward the child receives points to the rewards Jesus will give at the Judgment Seat, which we will see in Lesson 11.
Feast 3: Firstfruits (the First Sheaf)

Firstfruits was celebrated “on the day after the Sabbath” during the week of Unleavened Bread (Leviticus 23:11, NKJV). Many Bible teachers understand this as the Sunday after Passover. The priest waved the first sheaf of barley before the Lord. It was a promise that the rest of the harvest would follow.

Jesus rose from the dead on that very day, the Sunday after Passover. Paul wrote, “But now Christ is risen from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20, NKJV). He was the first sheaf. His resurrection is God’s promise that everyone who belongs to Him will rise too.
Feast 4: Pentecost (Shavuot)

Count fifty days from Firstfruits, and you come to Pentecost, which falls in our May or June. “Pentecost” is Greek for “fiftieth.” In Hebrew it is Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, because Israel counted seven weeks to reach it (Leviticus 23:15–16). It celebrated the wheat harvest. On this day the priests did something unusual. They waved two loaves of bread “baked with leaven” (Leviticus 23:17, NKJV). Grain offerings burned on the altar had to be made without leaven (Leviticus 2:11).
Those two loaves picture the Church: Jews and Gentiles made into one body. The leaven shows that the Church, though saved by grace, still struggles with sin in this life.

Jesus fulfilled this feast exactly. “When the Day of Pentecost had fully come” (Acts 2:1, NKJV), the Holy Spirit fell on the believers in Jerusalem, and the Church was born. On the day Israel celebrated the wheat harvest, God began the great harvest of souls. Like wheat on a threshing floor, the Church was born into a world of pressure, so the true grain could be separated from the chaff.
Two Mountains, One Feast

Israel reached Mount Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt (Exodus 19:1), the same season as Pentecost. Jewish tradition teaches that God gave the Law at Sinai on the day of Shavuot. Put the two days side by side:
At Sinai, God gave the Law, and fire came down on the mountain. In Jerusalem, God gave the Spirit, and tongues of fire rested on the believers.
At Sinai, about three thousand people died after the sin of the golden calf (Exodus 32:28). At Pentecost, about three thousand people were saved when Peter preached (Acts 2:41).
Paul explained the difference: “for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6, NKJV).
Feast 5: The Feast of Trumpets (Yom Teruah)

Trumpets falls on Tishrei 1, the first day of the seventh month, which is in our September or October. God commanded “a memorial of blowing of trumpets, a holy convocation” (Leviticus 23:24, NKJV). It is the next feast on God’s calendar, the one still waiting to be fulfilled, and it pictures the Rapture of the Church.
Paul connects the trumpet to the gathering of the Bride:
“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” (1 Corinthians 15:52, NKJV)
“For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first.” (1 Thessalonians 4:16, NKJV)

Trumpets was the only feast that began on a new moon. The other feasts that fall on a set day come later in the month, when the moon is already shining. But on the night of a new moon the sky is dark, and most people are asleep. In Bible times, no one could be sure which day the new month would start until two witnesses saw the first thin sliver of the moon and reported it to the court in Jerusalem. Then the shofar was blown, and the feast began at once. That is why Jewish tradition calls Trumpets the hidden day. You knew the season, but you watched and waited for the signal. Many Christian teachers hear in it the words of Jesus: no one knows the day or the hour. In Lesson 11 you will see how this same phrase fits the ancient wedding.
That is exactly what Jesus said about His coming for His Bride: “But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but My Father only” (Matthew 24:36, NKJV).
The Hundred Blasts

The trumpet of this feast is the shofar, a ram’s horn. Israel first heard a trumpet like it at Mount Sinai: “when the blast of the trumpet sounded long and became louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him by voice” (Exodus 19:19, NKJV).
In synagogues today, the shofar is blown one hundred times on this day. The blasts come in sets of thirty, thirty, thirty, and ten, and they are built from four sounds:
Tekiah: One long, straight blast. It is the sound used to crown a king, declaring that God is King.

Shevarim: Three short, broken blasts that sound like sighing. The word means “breaks.” It is the sound of a broken heart and of repentance. “Turn to Me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12, NKJV).
Teruah: Nine or more quick, sharp blasts. It is an alarm, the sound blown when a city was under attack. It is a wake-up call.
Tekiah Gedolah: “The great blast.” One final blast held as long as the blower’s breath will last. It closes the service and stands for God’s complete victory.

Paul called the trumpet of the Rapture “the last trumpet.” An old Jewish writing tells a story about the ram God provided in place of Isaac (Genesis 22:13). It says the ram’s first horn was blown at Mount Sinai, and its other horn will be blown when God gathers His people at the end (Isaiah 27:13). The first trumpet sounded when God came down to meet His people on the mountain. The last trumpet will sound when He gathers them to Himself.

Some people ask, “Is Paul’s last trumpet the seventh trumpet in the Book of Revelation?” It is not. The seven trumpets in Revelation are blown by angels, and each one brings a judgment on the earth (Revelation 8–11). The last trumpet Paul spoke of is “the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16, NKJV), and it gathers God’s people instead of judging the world. It fits the Feast of Trumpets, where many teachers call the final great blast of the day, the Tekiah Gedolah, the last trumpet.
Apples and Honey

Trumpets is also the Jewish New Year, called Rosh Hashanah. How can a new year begin in the seventh month? Israel kept two calendars. Nisan begins the religious year (Exodus 12:2), and Tishrei begins the everyday, or civil, year. On this day Jewish families dip slices of apple into honey and pray for a sweet new year. Many see the round apple as a picture of a crown, the kingship of God. And the honey only gets on the apple when the apple is dipped. In the same way, the sweetness of God’s Kingdom comes to the one who is fully immersed in Him.
Trumpets also begins the Ten Days of Awe, ten days of looking back over the year and asking God for forgiveness. Those ten days lead straight into the Day of Atonement.
GOD KEEPS HIS CALENDAR
This is the heart of the lesson. Look at how the first four feasts were fulfilled.
Jesus was not crucified on a random day. He died at Passover.
He was not buried on a random day. His sinless body lay in the tomb during Unleavened Bread.
He did not rise on a random morning. He rose on Firstfruits.
The Holy Spirit did not fall on a random day. He came on Pentecost.

The four spring feasts were fulfilled on their feast days at Christ’s first coming. That shows us that God keeps His calendar. The fall feasts will not turn into vague symbols. They will be fulfilled too.

That is why we believe the Feast of Trumpets points to the Rapture. The next feast on the calendar is the trumpet, and the next event on God’s timeline is the trumpet call that gathers the Bride. Just as Pentecost opened the age of grace, the trumpet will close it.

But notice what God did with this feast. He built the waiting into it. Trumpets is the feast of the new moon, the day no one could name ahead of time. God does not want us setting dates. He wants us watching the sky like the witnesses on the hills, ready for the signal.
THE SUMMER GAP
After Pentecost, there is a long, hot summer of almost four months before the fall feasts. There are no appointed feasts during that time.

That summer gap pictures the long valley of the Church Age. The wheat has been gathered, the age of grace is underway, and Israel is in partial blindness. But when the trumpet sounds and the Church is caught up, the summer ends. God turns back to finish the last two feasts on the earth.
THE FEAST FOR ISRAEL
Feast 6: The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur)

The Day of Atonement falls on Tishrei 10, ten days after Trumpets, in our September or October. It is the most serious day of the year. God told Israel, “you shall afflict your souls” (Leviticus 23:27, NKJV), so it is a day of fasting, repentance, and humbling the soul. It was also the only day of the year when the high priest went behind the veil into the Most Holy Place, the room that held the Ark of the Covenant.
Leviticus 16 lays out what the high priest did on this day. Each step points to Jesus.
Step 1: The White Linen

“He shall put the holy linen tunic and the linen trousers on his body; he shall be girded with a linen sash, and with the linen turban he shall be attired. These are holy garments. Therefore he shall wash his body in water, and put them on.” (Leviticus 16:4, NKJV)

On every other day, the high priest wore beautiful robes of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet. On this day he took them off, washed his whole body, and dressed in plain white linen. He came before God not in majesty, but in purity and humility.

Jesus did the same. He did not come to earth in the robes of heaven. He laid His glory aside and came as a humble servant, clothed in human flesh. And like that white linen, His life was spotless, without a single stain of sin.
Step 2: The Two Goats
The high priest brought two goats to the door of the tabernacle and cast lots for them: “one lot for the Lord and the other lot for the scapegoat” (Leviticus 16:8, NKJV). One goat would die as a sin
offering. The other would stay alive and carry the people’s sins far away into the wilderness.

Jesus fulfilled both goats at once on the cross. He was the sacrifice whose blood cleanses us, and He was the scapegoat who carries our sins away. No lots were cast for Him. He chose both jobs Himself.
Step 3: The Cloud of Incense

Before he could go behind the veil, the high priest offered a bull for his own sins (Leviticus 16:6). Then he carried a pan of burning coals and two handfuls of incense into the Most Holy Place, “that the cloud of incense may cover the mercy seat that is on the Testimony, lest he die” (Leviticus 16:13, NKJV). The smoke was a screen between a sinful man and the presence of a holy God.

Jesus needed no smoke screen. He had no sins of His own to cover, so He offered no bull for Himself. When He died, the veil of the temple tore from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51). Now every believer can “come boldly to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16, NKJV).
Step 4: The Blood on the Mercy Seat

The high priest killed the goat chosen for the Lord and carried its blood behind the veil. He sprinkled it on the mercy seat, the gold lid of the Ark, to cover the sins of the nation for one more year (Leviticus 16:15–16).

“But Christ came as High Priest of the good things to come, with the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation. Not with the blood of goats and calves, but with His own blood He entered the Most Holy Place once for all, having obtained eternal redemption.” (Hebrews 9:11–12, NKJV)
In God’s eyes, the animal sacrifices ended the moment Jesus died and the veil tore. But the leaders in Jerusalem rejected Him, so the priests kept offering animals for about forty more years. The
sacrifices stopped only in AD 70, when the Roman army burned the temple to the ground.
Step 5: The Scapegoat

“Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions, concerning all their sins, putting them on the head of the goat, and shall send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a suitable man.” (Leviticus 16:21, NKJV)

The Hebrew word for “confess” here comes from yadah, which means “to throw” or “to cast.” The high priest did not tap the goat gently. He pressed both hands down hard on its head, as if throwing the weight of the nation’s sin onto it. Many see a picture of this in the soldiers who pressed the crown of thorns down onto the head of Jesus (Matthew 27:29). The place where sin was laid on the goat is the same place where the thorns of the curse were pressed into our Savior.

The King James Version calls the man who led the goat away a “fit man.” When Jesus grew too weak to carry His cross, the soldiers “compelled a certain man, Simon a Cyrenian... to bear His cross” (Mark 15:21, NKJV). Simon helped lead the true Scapegoat outside the city.

In the time of the second temple, the priests added a custom. They tied a strip of scarlet wool to the scapegoat and another to the temple door. The goat was led to a desert cliff and pushed over. Ancient Jewish writings record that when it died, the scarlet strip on the temple door turned white, a sign that God had answered Isaiah’s promise: “Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18, NKJV).
The Talmud, a collection of ancient Jewish teaching, adds something amazing. It says that for the last forty years before the
temple was destroyed, the scarlet strip never turned white again. Those forty years began about the time Jesus died on the cross.
Step 6: The Royal Garments

When the work was done, the high priest went back into the tabernacle, took off the white linen, and left it there. He washed again, put on his royal garments, and came out to the waiting people (Leviticus 16:23–24). The nation rejoiced, because their sins were covered.

When Jesus rose from the dead, He left His linen burial cloths behind in the empty tomb. John saw “the handkerchief that had been around His head, not lying with the linen cloths, but folded together in a place by itself” (John 20:7, NKJV). Then Jesus went back to heaven, where He sits in glory at the right hand of the Father as our High Priest and King.
Finished for the Church, Still Coming for Israel
If Jesus fulfilled every step of this day through His cross and resurrection, how can the Day of Atonement still be waiting? The answer is in the word itself.

The Hebrew word for atonement is kaphar. It means “to cover” or “to wipe clean.” The English word “atonement” was made popular in the 1500s by William Tyndale, one of the first men to translate the Bible into English. In his translation of Leviticus, he used a word built from “at one” for kaphar. Atonement is “at-one-ment,” bringing two people who have been separated back together as one.
Remember the near view and the far view from Lesson 3. This feast has a near peak for the Church and a far peak for Israel.
For the Church, the Day of Atonement is finished. When Jesus shed His blood and the veil tore, our debt was paid, and we were made one with God.

But in Leviticus 16, the Day of Atonement was given to the nation of Israel as a national day of cleansing. As a nation, Israel rejected her Messiah, and Paul says that “blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in” (Romans 11:25, NKJV). Israel and God are still separated. Her Day of Atonement is still ahead.
The prophet Zechariah shows how that day will come. At the end of the Tribulation, the nations will surround Jerusalem to destroy it. In Israel’s darkest hour, God will pour out His Spirit on her:

“And I will pour on the house of David and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and supplication; then they will look on Me whom they pierced. Yes, they will mourn for Him as one mourns for his only son, and grieve for Him as one grieves for a firstborn.” (Zechariah 12:10, NKJV)

The Hebrew word for repentance is teshuvah, which means “to turn back” or “to return home.” After two thousand years, the nation will turn back to God. The promise is clear: “whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32, NKJV).

Then the cleansing comes, just like the blood on the mercy seat: “In that day a fountain shall be opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness” (Zechariah 13:1, NKJV). God said, “I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day” (Zechariah 3:9, NKJV).

And just as the high priest came out in his royal garments, the Great High Priest will step out of heaven in glory. His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4), “And the Lord shall be King over all the earth” (Zechariah 14:9, NKJV).

See the difference between Trumpets and the Day of Atonement. At Trumpets, Jesus comes suddenly. To the sleeping world it will be like a thief in the night, but His Bride hears the shout and the trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16, 5:4). He does not touch the earth. He
catches His Bride up into the clouds. At the Day of Atonement, every eye sees Him. He stands on the earth, defeats Israel’s enemies, and the two separated parties become one at last.

Think of the olives, which are harvested in the fall. You cannot get oil from an olive by slicing it gently. You crush it. In the same way, during the Tribulation, Israel will be crushed under the weight of the nations. That pressure is meant to break her self-reliance. This is the time of Jacob’s trouble that we studied in Lesson 4. Out of that crushing will come the pure oil of repentance.
THE FEAST FOR ALL BELIEVERS
Feast 7: The Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot)

Tabernacles begins on Tishrei 15, five days after the Day of Atonement, in our September or October. God said, “The fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the Feast of Tabernacles for seven days to the Lord” (Leviticus 23:34, NKJV). It is the most joyful week of the year. God commanded, “you shall rejoice before the Lord your God for seven days” (Leviticus 23:40, NKJV).

Israel lived in small huts called sukkahs to remember that God “made the children of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:43, NKJV). For forty years in the wilderness, God lived among His people and took care of them.

The Old Testament also calls it the Feast of Ingathering (Exodus 23:16). It came at the end of the harvest year, when every crop was safely in the barns. The sweet fruits picture the joyful gathering of God’s people, at rest under Christ’s rule. The grapes, thrown into the winepress, picture the wrath of God at the Second Coming, clearing the earth of wickedness so the Kingdom can begin.
Water, Wine, and Light
By the time of Jesus, three great ceremonies took place at the temple during this feast. Ancient Jewish writings describe them.

The Water: Every morning, a priest carried a golden pitcher down to the Pool of Siloam while a crowd followed, singing. He filled the pitcher, carried it back up through the Water Gate, and poured the water out at the altar. The people were praying for the fall rains, and they sang the words of Isaiah: “Therefore with joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3, NKJV).

The Wine: At the same time, another priest poured out a drink offering of wine. The water and the wine were poured into two silver bowls at the corner of the altar, and both flowed down into the altar together. In Scripture, wine is a picture of joy and of a covenant sealed. Earlier we saw grapes in the winepress as a picture of wrath. The same fruit can show two things. Crushed in judgment, grapes picture wrath. Poured out as an offering, wine pictures joy. Jesus drank the cup of wrath for us (Matthew 26:39) so we could drink the cup of joy.

The Light: Every evening, the priests lit four giant golden lampstands in the temple court, each about seventy-five feet tall. The wicks were made from the worn-out clothes of the priests. The writings say the light was so bright that every courtyard in Jerusalem glowed. It reminded Israel of the pillar of fire in the wilderness, and it looked ahead to the day when “the Lord will be to you an everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19, NKJV).
Jesus at the Feast
John tells us that Jesus went up to Jerusalem for this very feast (John 7:2). Picture the scene: the golden pitcher, the singing crowd, the water poured out at the altar. Then Jesus spoke up:

“On the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink. He who believes in Me, as the Scripture has said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’” (John 7:37–38, NKJV)

John explains that Jesus was speaking about the Holy Spirit (John 7:39). And in the same temple court where the giant lampstands stood, Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life” (John 8:12, NKJV). The water and the light of the feast were pointing to Him, and He said so right in the middle of it.

The picture goes even further. At the feast, water and wine flowed down into the altar together. On the cross, when a soldier pierced Jesus’ side, “immediately blood and water came out” (John 19:34, NKJV). What the feast poured out on the altar, Jesus poured out on the cross.
A Preview on the Mountain

Jesus once took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. His face began to shine like the sun, and Moses and Elijah appeared, talking with Him. Peter blurted out, “Lord, it is good for us to be here; if You wish, let us make here three tabernacles: one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4, NKJV).

Why did Peter think of tabernacles? Many teachers believe this happened near the time of the feast, when every family in Israel was building booths. Peter saw the glory of Jesus and thought the Kingdom had come. He was seeing a preview of it. Just days before, Jesus had said some of them would see “the Son of Man coming in His kingdom” (Matthew 16:28, NKJV).
When the Feast Comes True
The water, the wine, and the light were a blueprint of the Kingdom and of eternity.

The Water: Zechariah says that in the Kingdom “living waters shall flow from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 14:8, NKJV). And at the very end, John saw “a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1, NKJV).
The Wine: The joy of the covenant is complete at the marriage supper of the Lamb, which we will study in Lesson 11 (Revelation 19:9).

The Light: The four lampstands burned out every year. In the New Jerusalem, “The city had no need of the sun or of the moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illuminated it. The Lamb is its light” (Revelation 21:23, NKJV).
No more drought. No more darkness. No more distance from God.

This feast is for all believers together. The Church will reign with Christ. Israel will be restored in her land, and as God promised, “the Lord will make you the head and not the tail” (Deuteronomy 28:13, NKJV). Even the nations will come to Jerusalem to keep it:

“And it shall come to pass that everyone who is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles.” (Zechariah 14:16, NKJV)

The Kingdom will not be an endless cloud with nothing to do. It will have a King, and His people will serve in His government. The Greek word for “church,” ekklesia, was the word Greek cities used for the assembly of citizens who met to run the city’s business. Jesus said the faithful servant will hear, “you were faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things” (Matthew 25:21, NKJV). Faithfulness in this life prepares a believer for his place in
the next. You will study the reign of Christ in Lesson 12, and you will see there how the thousand-year Kingdom is the Feast of Tabernacles come to life.
The whole calendar ends where God always wanted it to end, with Him living among His people:

“And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying, ‘Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them, and they shall be His people. God Himself will be with them and be their God.’” (Revelation 21:3, NKJV)
WHY THE CALENDAR KEEPS YOU STEADY
When you see how the feasts are laid out, you see that history is not a random accident.
Seven feasts: the complete plan of God.

Five feasts of grace: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Pentecost, and Trumpets. They belong to the Church. They give us our salvation, our clean standing, our resurrection power, our birth as the Church, and our rescue from wrath.
One feast for Israel: the Day of Atonement. It gives the nation her repentance and makes her one with God again.
One feast for all believers: Tabernacles. It brings God to live with all His people in the Kingdom.

Look at the design of the whole calendar. Passover paid the debt at the cross. Unleavened Bread laid the sinless Lamb in the tomb. Firstfruits promised our resurrection. Pentecost filled the Church with holy fire. Trumpets will call the Bride home. The Day of Atonement will bring Israel back to God. Tabernacles will bring God to live with His people forever.
God does not mix up His plans. The summer is closing. The trumpet is getting ready to sound. Stand on His Word.
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: The seven feasts of the Lord are God’s calendar of redemption: the four spring feasts were fulfilled exactly at Christ’s first coming, the Feast of Trumpets points to the Rapture of the Church, the Day of Atonement points to Israel’s national repentance, and the Feast of Tabernacles points to God living with all His people in the Kingdom.
Three truths:
1. Five, one, and one: Five feasts belong to the Church, one belongs to Israel, and one belongs to all believers together.
2. God keeps His calendar: The first four feasts were fulfilled on their feast days, so the last three will be fulfilled too, beginning with the trumpet on the day no one can name ahead of time.

3. Already and not yet: Jesus fulfilled every step of the Day of Atonement for the Church through His cross and resurrection, but Israel’s national Day of Atonement is still coming, when she looks on the One she pierced.

Key Verses: Leviticus 23:1–2, 23:24, 23:27, 23:34, Leviticus 16:21, 1 Corinthians 5:7, 1 Corinthians 15:20, 1 Corinthians 15:52, Hebrews 9:11–12, Zechariah 12:10, Zechariah 14:16, John 7:37–38, Revelation 21:3
