Lesson 7
Replacement Theology
The Battle for the Olive Tree and a Bloody Trail Through
History
MEMORY VERSE
“For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.” (Romans 11:29, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

Listen carefully. A false teaching has spread through a large part of the church world. This is not a small difference of opinion. It rewrites the Word of God, attacks the character of God, and blinds people to the end-times timeline.

This false teaching is called Replacement Theology. In seminaries it is sometimes called Supersessionism, which simply means one group takes the place of another. It teaches that because Israel’s leaders rejected Jesus, God canceled all His promises to the Jewish people, the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and handed them to the Church instead.
It claims God threw Israel away for good and replaced her with the Gentile Church. It gives all the blessings in the Bible to the Church and leaves all the curses on the Jewish people.

If you believe this, you are forced to believe that God breaks His promises. You are forced to believe He promises something to one people, then changes His mind and gives it to someone else. And if God can break His word to Israel, you have no reason to believe He will keep His word to you.
In this lesson we will look at what the apostle Paul actually wrote. Then we will follow a bloody trail through history and see where this lie has led.
THE OLIVE TREE
Open your Bible to Romans. Paul gave three whole chapters, Romans 9, 10, and 11, to one question: What is Israel’s place in God’s plan now?
In Romans 11, Paul warns Gentile believers not to become proud. He uses the picture of an olive tree.

“For if the firstfruit is holy, the lump is also holy; and if the root is holy, so are the branches. And if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive tree, were grafted in among them, and with them became a partaker of the root and fatness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you do boast, remember that you do not support the root, but the root supports you.” (Romans 11:16– 18, NKJV)
Here is what each part of the tree stands for:
The root is God’s covenant with Abraham, the patriarchs, and the promises God made to Israel.
The natural branches are the Jewish people, the physical descendants of Israel.
The wild branches are Gentile believers, saved by grace through faith.

Paul says some natural branches were broken off because of unbelief, and wild branches were grafted in. But he gives the Gentiles a sharp warning: do not boast. You do not hold up the root. The Jewish root holds you up.
The Church did not replace the tree. The Church was grafted into a tree with Jewish roots.

Paul ends the chapter by saying Israel’s blindness is partial and temporary. It lasts only until the full number of Gentiles has come in. And God can graft the natural branches back in, if they do not continue in unbelief (Romans 11:23).

“For I do not desire, brethren, that you should be ignorant of this mystery, lest you should be wise in your own opinion, that blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved... For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.” (Romans 11:25–26, 29, NKJV)
Irrevocable means it cannot be taken back. God’s promises to Israel cannot be canceled. God has not thrown away His people.

God made the same point through Jeremiah. He said Israel would stop being a nation before Him only if the sun, moon, and stars stopped shining (Jeremiah 31:35–37). Look up at the sky tonight. As long as it is there, God’s promise to Israel stands.

What does “all Israel will be saved” mean? It does not mean every Jewish person who ever lived is saved without Jesus. No one is saved without Him (John 14:6). It means the nation of Israel alive at the end will turn to Jesus as her Messiah, when “they will look on Me whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10, NKJV). You saw that day in Lesson 6. “The fullness of the Gentiles” means the full number of
Gentiles God is saving during this Church Age. When that number is complete, the Bride is taken home, and God turns again to Israel.
Verses People Use
People who teach Replacement Theology usually point to three verses. Here is what they really say.

Galatians 3:29: “And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise” (NKJV). Believers share in Abraham’s blessing by faith. Paul does not say God canceled His promises to Abraham’s natural children. In Romans 11, the same Paul says their calling is irrevocable.

Romans 2:28–29: “He is a Jew who is one inwardly” (NKJV). Paul is talking to Jewish people here. He is saying a Jew pleases God by a changed heart, not just by being circumcised. He is not saying Gentiles become Israel.

Galatians 6:16: “the Israel of God” (NKJV). Paul blesses “as many as walk according to this rule,” and then “the Israel of God.” The most natural reading is the Jewish believers in Jesus, the faithful remnant of Israel. Nowhere in the New Testament is the Church simply called Israel.
THE TRAIL OF THE LIE THROUGH HISTORY

If the New Testament is this clear, how did so much of the church get it wrong? When a false teaching takes over the pulpit, it soon moves into the halls of government, and from there into violence in the streets. Follow the trail.
Point 1: The Council of Nicaea, AD 325
The idea that the Church had replaced Israel began to show up in some church writings in the second century, such as the Epistle of Barnabas and Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho. But under the
Roman Emperor Constantine, contempt for the Jews was written into church practice.

For the first three centuries, the church was a persecuted minority with deep Jewish roots. Then Constantine saw that he could use Christianity to unite his empire. At the Council of Nicaea, the church set a date for celebrating the resurrection that no longer depended on the Jewish calendar. Christians were told to stop following the Jewish reckoning of Passover.
After the council, Constantine sent a letter to the churches. The church historian Eusebius preserved it in his Life of Constantine. Constantine wrote:

“It appeared an unworthy thing that in the celebration of this most holy feast we should follow the practice of the Jews, who have impiously defiled their hands with enormous sin... Let us then have nothing in common with the detestable Jewish crowd.”
That letter is clear evidence. The emperor of Rome and the church wrote hatred of the Jews into church practice to unite the empire. It pushed the idea that the Gentile Church was the new Israel.
Point 2: The Spanish Inquisition and the Expulsion of 1492
Once the church believed God had thrown away the Jewish people, the road was open for terror.
In 1478, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain set up the Inquisition. In 1483, the Dominican friar Tomás de Torquemada became its Grand Inquisitor.

Many Spanish Jews had been pressured into becoming Catholic, especially after mob attacks in 1391 killed thousands of Jews across Spain. The Inquisition hunted these converts, accused many of secretly keeping their Jewish faith, and tortured and burned many
of them. History calls this secret faith Crypto-Judaism, meaning hidden Jewish practice behind a Christian mask.
The church treated any trace of Jewish identity, feast keeping, or Sabbath keeping as an infection to be burned out.

On March 31, 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella signed the Alhambra Decree, also called the Edict of Expulsion. It ordered every Jew in Spain to convert or leave. Somewhere between 40,000 and 150,000 Jewish people were forced into exile, and they lost their homes and much of their wealth.
Point 3: Martin Luther, 1543

The Protestant Reformation did not cure this disease. Martin Luther rightly fought for salvation by faith alone, but he kept the lens of Replacement Theology. When the Jewish people did not accept his preaching, he turned on them with fury.

In 1543, Luther published a book called On the Jews and Their Lies. In it he told German princes to burn down synagogues, destroy Jewish homes, take away their prayer books and writings, forbid their rabbis to teach on pain of death, take away their safe travel on the roads, seize their money, and put them to hard manual labor.
The father of the Protestant Reformation used Replacement Theology to call for the destruction of a whole people. He claimed they were no longer God’s people.
Point 4: Hitler and the Holocaust, 1933 to 1945
Four centuries later, Adolf Hitler and the Nazis carried out the Holocaust. More than six million Jewish men, women, and children were murdered.
The Nazis did not have to invent hatred of the Jews. It was already sitting in German church pews. Nazi leaders praised Luther and reprinted his writings against the Jews. On the night of November 9

and 10, 1938, synagogues across Germany were burned. This night of terror is called Kristallnacht, “the night of broken glass.” November 10 was Luther’s birthday, and Martin Sasse, a Lutheran bishop in Germany, celebrated the burning as a fitting gift for it.

The Jewish people were not the only ones marked for destruction. The Roma and Sinti people, our Gypsy people, were hunted right alongside them. Historians estimate that between 220,000 and 500,000 Roma were murdered in the camps and killing fields. Our people call this genocide the Porajmos, which means “the devouring.”

Why did Hitler want the Gypsy people destroyed? The Nazis called the Roma racially inferior and “asocial,” and they hunted them by race, just as they hunted the Jews. But underneath that hatred is something deeper. The Roma and the Jewish people share something that empires hate. Both are built on close family, clear roles for men and women, deep history, and a strong commitment to keep their community separate from the corrupt ways of the world. Both refuse to be erased or melted into a godless state.

Because the Roma kept their own heritage, rules, and identity, the Nazis treated them as a threat. Just as Replacement Theology claimed the Church erased Israel’s identity, the Nazi state claimed it must erase the Gypsy identity.

Our people were rounded up, robbed, and murdered because their way of life stood against the godless system of the world. The same lie that says God can erase a people’s calling also says a government can erase a people.
Point 5: The Same Spirit in Today’s Headlines
If you think this trail ended in Berlin, look around. Turn on the evening news. Scroll through social media. You will hear the same old hatred, louder than ever.

When global media, secular universities, and activists call for the erasure of the nation of Israel, using clean-sounding slogans and global boycotts, you are not looking at a new political movement. You are looking at the same old spirit of Nicaea, the Inquisition, Luther, and Hitler in modern clothes.

The words have changed from religious language to political slogans. But the goal is the same: deny the Jewish people their right to their land and erase them from the earth. At the same time, the same globalist media attack any traditional community, including our church families, that refuses to let outsiders rewrite its faith, its roles for men and women, and its culture.
The disease is still alive, and it is preparing the world for the final showdown of the end times.
KEEP THE LINES STRAIGHT
If you do not understand this history, you will misread the end times. Replacement Theology scrambles prophecy because it takes the promises God made to Israel and forces them onto the Church.
When you read end-times Scripture, keep two lines straight.
First, Israel is still Israel. God’s promises about the land, Jerusalem, the temple, and the remnant of Jacob are still in force. They cannot be taken back.
Second, the Church is the Church. The Church is a mystery God is calling out of all nations during this present age. It is grafted into the root, but it has its own calling and its own future.

God has not changed His mind. The same God who kept the Jewish people alive through Nicaea, the Inquisition, the Reformation, and the Holocaust will keep every promise He made about their future. And the same God watched over our Roma people through the Porajmos.
Keep the lines straight, and prophecy becomes easy to read. And remember what God promised Abraham:
“I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” (Genesis 12:3, NKJV)
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: Replacement Theology is the false teaching that the Church replaced Israel, and history shows where it leads: from Nicaea to the Inquisition, to Luther, to the Holocaust, where up to half a million Roma were also murdered in the Porajmos.
Three truths:
1. God’s promises stand: Romans 11 teaches that the Church is a wild branch grafted into a Jewish root, and that God’s gifts and calling to Israel cannot be taken back.
2. The Porajmos: The Nazis hunted both the Jewish people and the Roma people by race, and both peoples hold to family, faith, and identity that empires cannot break.
3. The same spirit today: The hatred of Israel in today’s news and protests is the same old lie in modern language.
Key Verses: Romans 11:16–18, Romans 11:23–29, Genesis 12:3
JOURNAL ESSAY PROMPTS
Choose one prompt below and write a 300 to 500 word response in your study journal. Cite at least one Scripture from this lesson, write in your own words, and show how it applies to your life.
1. The Olive Tree: In your own words, explain Paul’s picture of the olive tree in Romans 11. Why does he warn Gentile believers not to boast against the natural branches?
2. The Porajmos: Why did Hitler target both the Jewish people and the Roma people? What do these two cultures share that makes godless governments see them as a threat?

3. Today’s Headlines: Look at the hatred of Israel and of traditional families in today’s news. How do modern slogans connect to the old lie of Replacement Theology? Why must a Christian keep the Bible’s lines straight when watching the news?

chapters.title: Lesson 8: The Seven Churches of Asia

paragraphs.text: Lesson 8
The Seven Churches of Asia
The Seven Golden Lampstands and the Map of Church
History
MEMORY VERSE
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with
him, and he with Me.” (Revelation 3:20, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION
When most people read Revelation chapters 2 and 3, they treat the
seven letters to the seven churches like old mail. Letters to seven churches in what is now Turkey, sent almost two thousand years
ago, and that is all. Many commentators see them only as history, or
as advice on how a local church should behave.
Those letters were written to real churches, and they still speak to every believer. But many Bible teachers see something more in
them. Read in order, the seven letters also form a map of church
history, from the apostles to our own day. This is the long valley between the Cross and the trumpet that we studied in Lesson 3.
That map was made famous by Clarence Larkin, an engineer who
became a Baptist pastor, in his 1918 book Dispensational Truth. Larkin and others noticed that when you read the seven letters in
the order Jesus gave them, they line up with the major eras of
church history.
The order itself is interesting. Picture a Roman mail carrier landing at the port of Ephesus. He travels north along the coast to Smyrna
and then Pergamos, turns inland to Thyatira, and then goes south through Sardis and Philadelphia to Laodicea. It is one continuous loop, the order of an ancient mail route, and it is the order of the
letters.

Keep one thing clear: Jesus is not speaking to unbelievers here. He is not talking to the Pharisees or to the godless world. He is speaking to His own Church. In Lesson 5 we saw Jesus as the Lawyer who silenced His accusers in the temple. Here the same Lord reviews the
case files of His own house. In this lesson we will open the Book of Revelation, then look at the lampstands, the overcomer, and each of the seven eras.
THE BOOK OF REVELATION
Before we read the letters, we need to meet the book they come
from. From here to the end of this course, we will read from Revelation more than from any other book of the Bible.
What the Name Means
The name comes from the Greek word apokalypsis. It means “an unveiling,” like pulling back a curtain or lifting the cover off something hidden so everyone can see it. Today many people use
the word “apocalypse” to mean a disaster. In the Bible it means the opposite of hiding. God is showing us what is coming.
Notice that the name is Revelation, not “Revelations.” It is one
revelation, and it is about one Person. The very first words tell us whose it is:
“The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show
His servants—things which must shortly take place. And He sent and signified it by His angel to His servant John, who bore witness to the word of God, and to the testimony of
Jesus Christ, to all things that he saw.” (Revelation 1:1–2, NKJV)
Who Gave the Book

Every book of the Bible is inspired by God (2 Timothy 3:16). But Revelation is the only book that opens by telling us it came straight from Jesus Christ Himself. Follow the chain in verse 1. God the Father gave it to Jesus. Jesus sent it by His angel to John. John wrote it down for the churches, and for us.

John was not writing his own ideas. He was the secretary. Again and again, Jesus tells him to write what he sees (Revelation 1:11, 1:19). The seven letters in chapters 2 and 3 are the words of Jesus Himself, given to John one church at a time.
Who Wrote It Down, and Where
John was the disciple Jesus loved, the same John who wrote the Gospel of John and three short letters. By the time he wrote

Revelation, he was an old man and the last of the twelve apostles still alive. The Roman government had sent him away as a prisoner to Patmos, a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea. He was there “for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ” (Revelation
1:9, NKJV). The early church leader Irenaeus wrote that John saw the vision near the end of the reign of the Emperor Domitian, around AD 95.
The early church also told an amazing story about John. Tertullian,

a Christian writer from about AD 200, wrote that John was thrown into a pot of boiling oil in Rome and came out unharmed, and was then sent to the island. No one can prove the story today, but it shows how the first Christians remembered him.
The Blessing for Reading
Revelation is the only book of the Bible that promises a blessing to the person who reads it.
“Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of
this prophecy, and keep those things which are written in it; for the time is near.” (Revelation 1:3, NKJV)
The blessing has three parts:
Read: “Blessed is he who reads.” In the early church, most believers did not own a copy of the Scriptures. One person read the book aloud to the whole church.
Hear: “And those who hear.” The blessing is for the listeners too. Hearing God’s Word read aloud counts.
Keep: “And keep those things which are written in it.” To keep means to hold on to it, guard it, and live by it.

That is the first of seven blessings in Revelation, and each one begins with the word “Blessed” (Revelation 1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). Near the end of the book, Jesus repeats the first one: “Blessed is he who keeps the words of the prophecy of this
book” (Revelation 22:7, NKJV). The book opens and closes with a blessing for those who keep it.
The Warning for Changing It
The book also ends with the strongest warning in the Bible:
“For I testify to everyone who hears the words of the
prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues that are written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this
prophecy, God shall take away his part from the Book of Life, from the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book.” (Revelation 22:18–19, NKJV)
Add to the book, and God adds its plagues. Take away from the
book, and God takes away that person’s part in the holy city. Moses gave a similar warning near the beginning of the Bible: “You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor take from it”
(Deuteronomy 4:2, NKJV). God guards His Word at both ends of the Bible.
Why People Are Afraid of It

Many believers never read Revelation. Some are scared of what they will find: beasts, plagues, earthquakes, and a dragon. Others tried once, got lost in the strange pictures, and put it down. So the one
book that promises a blessing for reading it is often the book people
skip.
But look at the very first thing Jesus did when John saw Him. John
fell at His feet as if he were dead. “But He laid His right hand on me, saying to me, ‘Do not be afraid; I am the First and the Last’” (Revelation 1:17, NKJV). Before Jesus showed John a single
judgment, He told him not to be afraid. That is how the book is meant to be read.
The Book Explains Itself
Revelation is not a secret code that only experts can crack. The
answer to a strange picture is very often found in the same chapter, or a few chapters later. If you keep reading, the book explains itself.
Jesus Himself starts the pattern in chapter 1. John sees seven stars
in Jesus’ hand and seven golden lampstands. Then Jesus tells him what they are: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands which you saw are the seven churches”
(Revelation 1:20, NKJV). Here are a few more examples:
What John Saw What It Means Where Revelation Says So
Seven stars The angels, or messengers, of the seven churches
Revelation 1:20
Seven golden lampstands
The seven churches Revelation 1:20
Golden bowls full of incense
The prayers of the saints Revelation 5:8
The great dragon The devil, Satan, the serpent from the garden
Revelation 12:9
The waters where the harlot sits
Peoples, crowds, nations, and languages
Revelation 17:15
The Bride’s fine linen The righteous acts of the saints Revelation 19:8
The Bride, the Lamb’s wife
The holy city, New Jerusalem Revelation 21:9–10
Why is a city called the Bride? Because of who lives in it. The Bride
is God’s people, and the New Jerusalem is her home, the place Jesus went to prepare (John 14:2). When you see the city, you see the Bride who lives there.
Jesus even gave John an outline of the whole book: “Write the

things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which will take place after this” (Revelation 1:19, NKJV). The things John had seen are in chapter 1. The things which are, the churches
of John’s day, are in chapters 2 and 3. The things after this fill
chapters 4 through 22. Keep that outline in mind, and you will always know where you are in the book.
One more fact makes this clear. Hundreds of years earlier, God told Daniel to “shut up the words, and seal the book until the time of the
end” (Daniel 12:4, NKJV). But at the end of Revelation, the angel told John the opposite: “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is at hand” (Revelation 22:10, NKJV).
Daniel’s book was sealed. John’s book was left open. God wants it read and understood.
Excited, Not Terrified
Revelation does describe terrible judgments on the earth. But the book was written to God’s servants (Revelation 1:1), and for them it

is good news from start to finish. The Bible says, “For God did not appoint us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:9, NKJV). We will study that promise in
Lesson 10.
Jesus told His followers how to feel when they see these things
begin: “Now when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near” (Luke 21:28,
NKJV). Not hide. Look up. Paul called the return of Jesus “the
blessed hope” (Titus 2:13, NKJV).
Think about how the story ends. Satan is defeated. Death is gone.
Every tear is wiped away. The Bride is with her Husband, and God lives with His people forever. A believer who reads to the last page
finds out that Jesus wins, and that His people win with Him.
That is why the last prayer in the Bible is not a cry of fear. It is a cry of joy. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming quickly,” and John answers,
“Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20, NKJV).
Facts About Revelation
The last book written: Revelation was the last book of the Bible to be written, about fifteen hundred years after Moses began writing the first.
Hundreds of echoes: Revelation never once says “as it is written,”
the way other books introduce a quotation. Yet it echoes the Old Testament hundreds of times, more than any other New Testament book. To understand Revelation, you need Genesis, Exodus, Isaiah,
Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zechariah.
The number seven: The word “seven” appears 54 times in Revelation in the New King James Version: seven churches, seven
lampstands, seven stars, seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls, and more. Seven is the number of completion.
The Lamb: Revelation calls Jesus “the Lamb” 28 times. The King
who rules over all is the same Lamb who was slain for us (Revelation 5:6).
The first and the last: Genesis opens with a garden, the tree of life,
and a river. Revelation closes with a city, the tree of life, and the river of life. We will look at that mirror in Lesson 12.
THE VISION OF THE LAMPSTANDS
Revelation chapter 1 gives us the key to the whole book.
“Write the things which you have seen, and the things which
are, and the things which will take place after this. The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in My right hand,
and the seven golden lampstands: The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands which you saw are the seven churches.” (Revelation 1:19–20,
NKJV)
In verse 19, Jesus gives John a simple outline of Revelation:
Part 1: “The things which you have seen.” That is John’s vision of the
glorified Christ in chapter 1.
Part 2: “The things which are.” That is the Church Age, in chapters 2
and 3.
Part 3: “The things which will take place after this.” That is the
Tribulation, the Second Coming, and the Kingdom, from chapter 4
on.
The Greek words for “after this” are meta tauta, which simply mean
“after these things.” The same words open chapter 4: “After these
things I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven” (Revelation 4:1, NKJV). The Church is the focus of chapters 2 and 3. Then John hears a voice like a trumpet say, “Come up here,” and
from that point on the word “church” does not appear again until
the end of the book. The Church is in heaven while the Tribulation unfolds on earth.
Jesus calls the churches golden lampstands. A lampstand has no
light of its own. Its job is to hold up the oil and the flame so light can
fill a dark room. When the oil runs dry, it fails its purpose.
WHO IS AN OVERCOMER?
Each letter ends with a promise “to him who overcomes.” Before we walk through the seven eras, we need to know who that is.
Some preachers teach that an overcomer is a super-Christian who
never sins, a special class of high achievers. If you believe that, you will think the promises in these letters are only for a few.
The same John who wrote Revelation tells us who overcomes:
“For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. And this
is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith. Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” (1 John 5:4–5, NKJV)
An overcomer is not an elite few. An overcomer is every true
believer, everyone who has been born of God through faith in Jesus.
If you belong to Jesus, you are an overcomer, and every promise in these seven letters belongs to you.
But notice what John says: whatever is born of God overcomes the
world. Real faith is alive. It shows itself by turning from sin. Someone who claims to believe but has no desire to repent should
ask whether he has truly been born of God (James 2:17).
Notice also how Jesus opens each letter. He describes Himself with
a part of the vision from chapter 1, choosing the very thing that church has lost or most needs.
THE CALL TO REPENT: NO CHEAP GRACE
Because these letters are written to believers, they answer a popular false teaching sometimes called hyper-grace or cheap grace.
It says a believer never needs to repent of ongoing sin, never needs
to look at the fruit of his life, and can live in open rebellion because
grace has covered it all. It turns God’s favor into a license to sin.
But look at what Jesus says to His own churches. Five of the seven
receive the same command: Repent!
Jesus does not offer soft grace with no accountability. He warns that if a church refuses to repent, He will remove its lampstand, fight
against its false teachers with the sword of His mouth, or spit it out
of His mouth.
Salvation is a free gift, received by faith alone. But real grace never leaves a person comfortable in sin. Real grace gives a believer the

power to live holy and the desire to repent quickly when he drifts. If someone says he belongs to the Bride but has no desire to turn from open rebellion, his faith is a fake, and it will fail the test.
THE SEVEN CHURCH AGES AT A GLANCE
The dates below are approximate. The name meanings are the meanings Larkin and other Bible teachers have long given. The eras
also overlap. Each age has its own main spirit, but churches like all
seven can still be found today.
Church Era Approximate Dates
Name Taught to Mean
Overcomer Promise
Ephesus The Apostolic Church
AD 33 to 100 Desirable Eat from the tree of life (2:7)
Smyrna The Persecuted Church
AD 100 to 313 Myrrh Not hurt by the second death (2:11)
Pergamos The Compromising Church
AD 313 to 606 Height, or mixed marriage
Hidden manna and a white stone (2:17)
Thyatira The Medieval Church
AD 606 to 1517 Continual sacrifice
Power over the nations and the morning star (2:26– 28)
Sardis The Reformation Church
AD 1517 to 1750 Those who escape, a remnant
White garments and a name kept in the Book of Life (3:5)
Philadelphia The Missionary Church
AD 1750 to 1900 Brotherly love
A pillar in God’s temple and God’s name written on him (3:12)
Laodicea The Lukewarm Church
AD 1900 to today
Rule of the people
Sit with Christ on His throne (3:21)
1. EPHESUS: THE APOSTOLIC
CHURCH (AD 33 TO 100)
The name Ephesus has been taught to mean “desirable.” This was
the first era of the Church, led by the apostles. It was a hard-working church that fought to keep its teaching pure.
“To the angel of the church of Ephesus write... ‘I know your
works, your labor, your patience, and that you cannot bear those who are evil... Nevertheless I have this against you, that you have left your first love. Remember therefore from
where you have fallen; repent and do the first works, or else I
will come to you quickly and remove your lampstand from its place—unless you repent.’” (Revelation 2:1–2, 4–5, NKJV)
Jesus introduces Himself as the One “who holds the seven stars in
His right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands” (Revelation 2:1, NKJV). He reminds this church that He is the center of it all, and He wants closeness with His people.
Ephesus did not lose its doctrine. It did not stop holding services. Its problem was that busy work had replaced burning love. It became a
church running a big operation, but it was no longer close to the
Bridegroom. Jesus warned that if their love was not restored, He would remove their lampstand.
Jesus also praised Ephesus for one thing: “You hate the deeds of the
Nicolaitans, which I also hate” (Revelation 2:6, NKJV). The name
Nicolaitan has long been explained as two Greek words: nikao, “to conquer,” and laos, “the people.” Put together: “conquering the
people.” Many teachers see it as a picture of a ruling class of clergy
lording it over ordinary believers. In this first era, it was only a set of deeds, and the true Church hated them.
The overcomer’s promise: “To him who overcomes I will give to eat
from the tree of life, which is in the midst of the Paradise of God”
(Revelation 2:7, NKJV). The Bride is given access to the Paradise of God, the eternal home of the family.
2. SMYRNA: THE PERSECUTED CHURCH (AD 100 TO 313)
The name Smyrna comes from the word for myrrh, a bitter spice used in burials. Myrrh had to be crushed to release its sweet smell.
This era covers the centuries when the Roman Empire tried again and again to wipe out Christianity. Church tradition counts ten great
waves of persecution, from Nero to Diocletian.
“And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write... ‘I know your works, tribulation, and poverty (but you are rich)... Do
not fear any of those things which you are about to suffer.
Indeed, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and you will have tribulation ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of
life.’” (Revelation 2:8–10, NKJV)
Jesus introduces Himself as “the First and the Last, who was dead,
and came to life” (Revelation 2:8, NKJV). He reminds people facing
death that He has already beaten the grave. Many Bible teachers see
the “ten days” of tribulation as a picture of those ten waves of persecution.
Smyrna is one of only two churches that receive no criticism at all
from Jesus. Thousands of believers were thrown to wild animals,
burned, and killed for their faith. But like myrrh, the more Rome crushed the Church, the sweeter its fragrance became. Persecution
burned away the fakes and left a body of true believers.
To this church Jesus promised the crown of life for those faithful until death, a victor’s crown. And the overcomer’s promise: “He who
overcomes shall not be hurt by the second death” (Revelation 2:11, NKJV). No matter what Rome did to their bodies, their souls were
safe forever.
3. PERGAMOS: THE COMPROMISING
CHURCH (AD 313 TO 606)
The name Pergamos is related to a word for “height” or “citadel.”
Many teachers have also explained it as per, meaning “mixed,” and
gamos, meaning “marriage.” Either way, this era begins with the
turning point we saw in Lesson 7. In 313, Emperor Constantine made Christianity legal with the Edict of Milan, and in 325 he called
the Council of Nicaea.
“And to the angel of the church in Pergamos write... ‘I know your works, and where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is...
But I have a few things against you, because you have there
those who hold the doctrine of Balaam... Repent, or else I will
come to you quickly and will fight against them with the sword of My mouth.’” (Revelation 2:12–14, 16, NKJV)
Jesus introduces Himself as “He who has the sharp two-edged sword” (Revelation 2:12, NKJV). The sword of His Word is the only
thing that can cut a pure church away from a corrupt government.
Why did Jesus call Pergamos the place “where Satan’s throne is”?
The city was a center of emperor worship, and it had a giant altar to the false god Zeus. Many Bible teachers believe that is what Jesus
meant.
When the devil could not destroy the Church by persecution in Smyrna, he changed his plan. He tried to join it. Constantine made a mixed marriage between the pagan Roman state and the Christian
church. The church gained legal protection, political power, and
money.
Once the church sat on an imperial throne, it began to compromise.
The doctrine of Balaam took root: mixing God’s Word with pagan
customs, pagan holidays, and political control. Balaam was the
prophet who showed Israel’s enemies how to trap God’s people, by luring them into idol feasts and sexual sin (Numbers 31:16,
Revelation 2:14). He could not curse Israel, so he taught Balak how
to lead Israel into compromise.
Jesus also says, “Thus you also have those who hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans” (Revelation 2:15, NKJV). What were only deeds in
Ephesus had become accepted doctrine in Pergamos. A ruling class
of clergy over a silent laity became the system. The pulpit became a political tool. Jesus warned that unless they repented, He would fight against them with the sword of His mouth.
The overcomer’s promise: “To him who overcomes I will give some of the hidden manna to eat. And I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written which no one knows except him
who receives it” (Revelation 2:17, NKJV). The hidden manna is
Jesus Himself, the true bread from heaven: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:51, NKJV). In the ancient
world, a white stone could serve as a ticket of admission to a feast, and judges used a white stone to vote “not guilty.” Either way, it is a
beautiful promise: the overcomer is declared innocent and
personally invited into the King’s banquet, with a new name known
only to him.
4. THYATIRA: THE MEDIEVAL
CHURCH (AD 606 TO 1517)
The name Thyatira has been taught to mean “continual sacrifice.”
This era covers the Middle Ages, when one church system controlled
most of Europe.
“And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write... ‘I know your works, love, service, faith, and your patience... Nevertheless I have a few things against you, because you
allow that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to
teach and seduce My servants to commit sexual immorality and eat things sacrificed to idols.’” (Revelation 2:18–20,
NKJV)
Jesus introduces Himself as “the Son of God, who has eyes like a
flame of fire, and His feet like fine brass” (Revelation 2:18, NKJV). His eyes see through everything, and His feet crush corruption.
Larkin’s map places the rise and rule of the Roman Catholic Church
system in this era. The ruling clergy of Pergamos grew into a single power under the pope. That church let the spirit of Jezebel take hold, mixing worship of God with idolatry.
The Roman Catholic system replaced the once-for-all sacrifice of
Christ with the Mass, offered over and over, a “continual sacrifice.” It taught people to earn salvation through works, frightened them
with purgatory, and sold indulgences, promising less time in
purgatory for money. It kept the Bible in Latin, a language most
ordinary people could not read. Jesus warned that He would throw Jezebel onto a sickbed and her followers into great tribulation
unless they repented (Revelation 2:22). Here “great tribulation”
means great trouble sent as a judgment, not the seven years of Daniel’s last week.
The overcomer’s promise: “And he who overcomes, and keeps My works until the end, to him I will give power over the nations... and I
will give him the morning star” (Revelation 2:26, 28, NKJV). The
Bride will reign alongside the Bridegroom over the nations. And the morning star is Jesus Himself, who calls Himself “the Bright and
Morning Star” (Revelation 22:16, NKJV). It is the same morning
star in the verse we read in Before You Begin (2 Peter 1:19), the star that shines just before the dawn.
5. SARDIS: THE REFORMATION
CHURCH (AD 1517 TO 1750)
The name Sardis has been taught to mean “those who escape” or “a
remnant.” This is the era of the Protestant Reformation, which began when Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in Wittenberg in 1517.
“And to the angel of the church in Sardis write... ‘I know your

works, that you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead. Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die, for I have not found your works perfect before God.’” (Revelation 3:1–2, NKJV)
Jesus introduces Himself as the One “who has the seven Spirits of
God and the seven stars” (Revelation 3:1, NKJV). He reminds them that He holds the fullness of the Holy Spirit, the source of life.
The reformers did a great work. They escaped the control of Rome
and recovered the truth that we are saved by faith alone. But they stopped short. As we saw in Lesson 7, they kept the poison of Replacement Theology. They held on to the idea of a state church,
and they persecuted believers who would not bow to it, like the Anabaptists, some of whom were drowned for their faith.
Jesus said it plainly: they had a name for being alive, but they were
dead. They had correct doctrine and thick books of theology, but little life, little closeness to God, and little power.
The overcomer’s promise: “He who overcomes shall be clothed in

white garments, and I will not blot out his name from the Book of Life; but I will confess his name before My Father and before His angels” (Revelation 3:5, NKJV). These are the white wedding garments the Bride will wear, which we will study in Lesson 11.
6. PHILADELPHIA: THE MISSIONARY
CHURCH (AD 1750 TO 1900)
Philadelphia means “brotherly love.” This is the great era of world missions.

“And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write... ‘I know your works. See, I have set before you an open door, and no one can shut it; for you have a little strength, have kept My word, and have not denied My name.’” (Revelation 3:7–8, NKJV)
Jesus introduces Himself as “He who is holy, He who is true, ‘He
who has the key of David, He who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens’” (Revelation 3:7, NKJV). He is the One who opens doors for the gospel. The key of David comes from Isaiah
22:22, where God gave the key of the king’s house to a faithful servant. Whoever holds the key decides who comes in. Jesus holds it now.
Philadelphia is the second church with no criticism from Jesus. Their love for the Word and for lost souls kept them pure.
In this era, God raised up men like John Wesley, who preached revival across England; William Carey, who sailed to India in 1793 and is called the father of modern missions; Charles Spurgeon, who
preached the gospel to millions; and Hudson Taylor, who carried the
gospel deep into China. They did not have political power or great wealth. They had “a little strength,” but they kept the Word and did not deny His name, and God opened doors no one could shut.
The overcomer’s promise: “He who overcomes, I will make him a
pillar in the temple of My God, and he shall go out no more. I will write on him the name of My God and the name of the city of My
God, the New Jerusalem... And I will write on him My new name” (Revelation 3:12, NKJV). The Bride is placed forever in the center of the Father’s house, marked as a citizen of the New Jerusalem.
7. LAODICEA: THE LUKEWARM
CHURCH (AD 1900 TO TODAY)
The name Laodicea is made of two Greek words: laos, “the people,”

and dike, “judgment” or “rights.” So the name has been taught to mean “the rule of the people” or “the people’s rights.” This is the era we are living in right now, the last stage before the trumpet sounds.
THE LIE OF HUMAN RIGHTS
We need to stop and expose a lie that drives this final era. The world
tells today’s generation that every person has the right to do whatever he wants, live however he wants, and even become
whoever he wants based on his feelings.

But search the Scriptures from Genesis to Revelation, and you will find something surprising. The Bible never gives anyone the right to do whatever he wants. Every right in Scripture comes from God, from the right of the firstborn (Deuteronomy 21:17) to justice for the needy (Jeremiah 5:28). And the greatest right of all is the right to
become a child of God.
“But as many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God, to those who believe in His name.” (John 1:12, NKJV)

And with that one right comes its reward: “the right to the tree of life” (Revelation 22:14, NKJV). Every right God gives comes through Jesus. Outside of Him, the Bible does not teach a list of personal
rights. It teaches stewardship, responsibility, and surrender to the Lordship of King Jesus. “For you were bought at a price; therefore
glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s” (1 Corinthians 6:20, NKJV). We belong to the Master.

This idol of human rights is the soil where cheap grace grows. Because Laodicea believes it has the right to rule itself and live in comfort, its preachers turn grace into a shield that protects sinful lifestyles. They teach that grace exists to serve our rights, instead of breaking our flesh so we can serve the King.
Jesus warned about this in Matthew 24: “And because lawlessness will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12,
NKJV). When a church trades the Lordship of Christ for the rule of the people, lawlessness grows and love grows cold.
“And to the angel of the church of the Laodiceans write... ‘I
know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. I could wish you were cold or hot. So then, because you are
lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will vomit you out of My mouth.’” (Revelation 3:14–16, NKJV)
How Jesus introduces Himself: “the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness, the Beginning of the creation of God” (Revelation 3:14, NKJV). He is the final word, no matter what the crowd thinks.
The crowd rules the pulpit: In the Laodicean age, the crowd rules the pulpit instead of God. The Word is watered down to fit political
correctness, popular opinion, entertainment, and globalist marketing. It is a rich, comfortable, high-tech church that brags
about its attendance and its money, saying, “I am rich, have become
wealthy, and have need of nothing” (Revelation 3:17, NKJV). Jesus answers that it is “wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked.”
Jesus is outside the door: Look at the saddest part of this letter.
Jesus is not even inside. He is standing outside the door of His own church, knocking, waiting to see if anyone will let Him in.
But look at the grace hidden in this last warning. The Laodicean

church as a whole is lukewarm and headed for rejection, but Jesus turns from the crowd to the individual: “If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me” (Revelation 3:20, NKJV).
That is the lesson for our generation. You do not have to let the cold
faith of this age decide how you walk with God. You can live with the fire and faithfulness of Philadelphia, even in a lukewarm Laodicean world.
The overcomer’s promise: “To him who overcomes I will grant to sit with Me on My throne, as I also overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne” (Revelation 3:21, NKJV). This is the highest
promise of all: to share the throne with the Bridegroom.
WHY THE MAP MATTERS
This map shows us where we stand on God’s calendar. We are not
drifting through a random moment in history. We are living at the end of the seventh lampstand.
There is no eighth church. Laodicea is the last era of the Church Age.
Notice something about the last four letters. Each one speaks of
Jesus’ coming. To Thyatira: “Hold fast what you have till I come” (Revelation 2:25, NKJV). To Sardis: “I will come upon you as a
thief” (Revelation 3:3, NKJV). To Philadelphia: “Behold, I am coming quickly!” (Revelation 3:11, NKJV). And to Laodicea, Jesus
stands at the door (Revelation 3:20). In the letters to Ephesus and
Pergamos, His coming is a warning of judgment on that one church, not a promise of His return. That is why many teachers see the last four churches lasting side by side until the Rapture.

But remember, the eras overlap. Faithful Philadelphia believers are still living inside the Laodicean age, and they will be here until the end. That is why Jesus’ promise to Philadelphia, “I also will keep

you from the hour of trial” (Revelation 3:10, NKJV), belongs to every true believer alive when He comes. Laodicea is the spirit of the age. It is not the true Bride. When it runs its course, the door in heaven will open, the voice like a trumpet will say, “Come up here!” (Revelation 4:1), and the Bride will be taken home before the wrath
falls.
Every promise in these seven letters is part of the Bride’s inheritance. In Lesson 11 we will meet them again as the seven

bridal blessings: the tree of life, the crown of life and safety from the second death, the white stone and the new name, authority over the nations, the white garments, the pillar in God’s temple, and a seat on the throne. Do not let this lukewarm culture cool your faith or tear down the God-given roles in your family.
Stand on the Word. The last era is ending. The King is at the door.
CHAPTER SUMMARY
One sentence: The seven letters of Revelation 2 and 3 were written
to real churches and also form a map of church history made famous by Clarence Larkin, ending in the lukewarm Laodicean age we live in now, with promises for every true believer before the Rapture.
Three truths:
1. After these things: Revelation 1:19 divides the book into three parts, and the Church is the focus of chapters 2 and 3 until the voice like a trumpet says “Come up here” in chapter 4.
2. Written to believers: Unlike the parables Jesus aimed at the leaders who rejected Him (Lesson 5), these letters are His review of
His own Church, and His call to repent answers cheap grace.
3. The one right: The greatest right the Bible gives is the right to become children of God, and the age that worships human rights is
the lukewarm age of Laodicea.

Lesson 9
The Rebirth of Israel
The Gathering of the Natural Branches, the Miracle of
Survival, and the Budding of the Fig Tree
MEMORY VERSE
“Shall the earth be made to give birth in one day? Or shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children.” (Isaiah 66:8, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

Picture yourself in the 1800s. Ask the smartest historians in the world a simple question: Can a people scattered across the earth for almost two thousand years ever return to their homeland, bring their dead language back to life, and become a nation again? They would tell you no. It has never happened.
History seemed to agree. When a nation was conquered and its people scattered, they usually blended into the countries around them. Their language died. Their identity faded away.

Yet on May 14, 1948, Israel was born again as a nation in a single day. Her people came back to their ancient homeland, just as the prophets wrote. This is not just a political headline. It is one of the greatest prophetic signs of our time. It proves that God keeps His promises.
In this lesson we will read what God promised, look at the history, and see why Israel’s rebirth is a starting signal for the end times.
A NATION BORN IN A DAY
Centuries before anyone drew the borders of the modern Middle East, Isaiah asked a question that sounded impossible:

“Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall the earth be made to give birth in one day? Or shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children.” (Isaiah 66:8, NKJV)
Nations usually grow slowly over hundreds of years. But Isaiah said a nation would be born at once, in one day.

Here is what happened. The British government had ruled the land since the end of World War I, and its rule was set to end at midnight, as May 14, 1948, came to a close. That afternoon, at four o’clock, Jewish leaders gathered in the Tel Aviv Museum. David Ben-Gurion stood up and read Israel’s Declaration of Independence out loud. At midnight, the State of Israel came into being. Just eleven minutes later, President Harry Truman announced that the United States recognized the new nation.
Zion had gone into labor, and a nation was born in a day.
A DEAD LANGUAGE COMES BACK TO LIFE

Something else happened that the historians said was impossible. For more than fifteen hundred years, Hebrew had not been anyone’s everyday language. Jewish people read it in prayer and studied it in the Scriptures, but no family spoke it at the dinner table. No child grew up speaking it as his first language. It was like Latin is today: read, but not spoken.

Then in 1881, a young man named Eliezer Ben-Yehuda moved to Jerusalem. He made a decision that people thought was crazy: his family would speak only Hebrew. His son Itamar became the first child in modern times to grow up with Hebrew as his first language. Ben-Yehuda spent the rest of his life writing a Hebrew dictionary, creating words for things the ancient language never had, like newspapers, dictionaries, and ice cream.

Others joined him, and the language spread through schools and homes. Today, millions of people speak Hebrew every day. It is the only language in history that has come back from being unspoken to being the everyday language of a nation.
God’s Word gives a picture of this too:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: ‘They shall again use this speech in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I bring back their captivity: “The Lord bless you, O home of justice, and mountain of holiness!”’” (Jeremiah 31:23, NKJV)

God promised that this blessing would be spoken again in the land of Judah when He brought His people home. Today it is spoken there in Hebrew, the language that came back to life. When God brought His people home, He brought their language home with them.
THE ORDER OF THE GATHERING IN EZEKIEL
God did not leave Israel’s return to guesswork. Through the prophet Ezekiel, He laid out the order of events.

“For I will take you from among the nations, gather you out of all countries, and bring you into your own land. Then I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean; I will cleanse you from all your filthiness and from all your idols.” (Ezekiel 36:24–25, NKJV)
Look at the order. God did not say He would cleanse them first while they were scattered and then bring them home. He set a clear sequence.
Step 1: God gathers them out of all countries and brings them into their own land.
Step 2: After they are in the land, He cleanses them spiritually.
That is exactly what we see today. God brought His people back to the land in 1948 while most of them still did not believe in Jesus. He is setting the stage for the final seven years.

Ezekiel’s vision of the valley of dry bones in chapter 37 shows the same order. When Ezekiel spoke to the bones, they did not come to life all at once. First there was a rattling noise, and the bones came together. Then muscles, flesh, and skin covered them. But the Bible says plainly, “there was no breath in them” (Ezekiel 37:8, NKJV). Only after the body was put together did the breath of God enter it.

God Himself told Ezekiel what the bones stand for: “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel” (Ezekiel 37:11, NKJV). That is a picture of Israel today. The body is back together in the land, but the breath of spiritual life has not yet come into the nation.

The Hebrew word for “return” and for “repentance” is the same word: teshuvah. It means to turn back. God is bringing His people back to the land first. One day that physical return will become a spiritual return, when “they will look on Me whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10, NKJV).
THE MIRACLE OF SURVIVAL:
THE YOM KIPPUR WAR OF 1973

Israel was attacked the day after she was born. In 1948, the armies of five Arab nations invaded to destroy her. Against all odds, Israel survived. But one of the hardest tests came twenty-five years later, in October 1973.

Before that, in June 1967, Israel fought the Six-Day War. In just six days she took back the Old City of Jerusalem and the Temple Mount, the hill where both temples stood (Lesson 3). For the first time in almost two thousand years, the Old City was under Jewish rule. Jesus had said, “And Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled” (Luke 21:24, NKJV). Many Bible teachers see 1967 as a sign that those times are running out.

On October 6, 1973, on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack from the south and the north. Much of the nation was fasting in synagogues. Many soldiers were home with their families. The attackers broke through Israel’s lines, and for several days it looked like the nation could be destroyed.
But the tide turned. Within about two weeks, Israeli forces pushed the attackers back, crossed the Suez Canal, and came within about 63 miles of Cairo and about 25 miles of Damascus.
Think about the day the attack came. The nation was nearly destroyed on Yom Kippur, the very day that pictures her future cleansing (Lesson 6). God kept her alive for that day.

Many Israelis did not see this as God’s hand. They gave the credit to their own military skill, their intelligence, and their planning. As we saw in Lesson 4, Israel today lives much like Jacob, leaning on her own strength. But her survival is God’s work. He is keeping His people alive so He can finish every promise He made to them.
THE SIGN OF THE FIG TREE
Jesus gave us a sign to watch. In His prophecy on the Mount of Olives, right after describing wars and troubles at the end of the age, He told a short parable:

“Now learn this parable from the fig tree: When its branch has already become tender and puts forth leaves, you know that summer is near. So you also, when you see all these things, know that it is near—at the doors! Assuredly, I say to you, this generation will by no means pass away till all these things take place.” (Matthew 24:32–34, NKJV)

In the Old Testament, the fig tree is often used as a picture of Israel. God said, “I saw your fathers as the firstfruits on the fig tree in its first season” (Hosea 9:10, NKJV). Joel spoke of an enemy that “has laid waste My vine, and ruined My fig tree” (Joel 1:7, NKJV). Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs that stood for the people of Judah (Jeremiah 24). The Hebrew word for fig tree is te’enah.

In Lesson 5 we saw that Jesus cursed a fig tree with leaves but no fruit during His last week. It withered. That was a picture of the nation’s leadership rejecting Him and the judgment that followed. But in Matthew 24, Jesus says the fig tree will put out tender leaves again.
Many Bible teachers see May 14, 1948, as the day the fig tree began to bud. After almost two thousand years, the nation of Israel came back to life.

Jesus said that the generation that sees these things will not pass away until all of them are fulfilled. The Greek word for generation is genea. It can mean the people living at the same time, and it can also mean a family line or race of people. Both meanings carry a promise.
First, the Jewish people will not be wiped out before the end. Hitler tried and failed. No one will succeed.
Second, the generation that saw the fig tree bud has watched the stage being set for the end of the age. We are living under the green leaves of that fig tree right now.

Some people have tried to turn “this generation” into a date by adding forty, seventy, or eighty years to 1948. Those dates came and went, and people lost faith in prophecy because of it. Jesus did not give us a number. He gave us a season. We do not count years. We watch.
God has not told us the day or the hour. But He has told us the season, and the leaves are out.
WHY ISRAEL’S RETURN MATTERS FOR YOU
Israel’s return in 1948 and her survival in 1973 are signs to our generation that the Church Age valley is coming to an end. The long pause is closing, and the final seven years are drawing near.

For almost two thousand years, Israel was missing from the map. Because of that, many church leaders and teachers could not imagine God keeping His promises to her. They turned the prophecies into symbols and said God had changed His mind. Israel’s absence made Replacement Theology seem believable, as we saw in Lesson 7.

But when Israel came back to her land, those old ideas fell apart. God had kept His word, literally, in front of the whole world. Israel’s return teaches us to read the rest of prophecy the same way: as real promises that will happen in real history.
God is preparing to take His Bride home to the Father’s house. Then He will turn to Israel and bring her through the fire of Jacob’s
trouble until she looks on the One she pierced and is made clean. The stage is set. The leaves are green. The Bridegroom is at the door.
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: Israel’s rebirth as a nation on May 14, 1948, the revival of the Hebrew language, and her survival in the 1973 Yom Kippur War are the budding of the prophetic fig tree, a sign that the final season of this age has come.
Three truths:
1. The order of the gathering: Ezekiel 36 and 37 show that God brings Israel back to the land first, while she is still in unbelief, and cleanses her spiritually later.
2. The fig tree sign: The fig tree is a picture of Israel, and its budding in 1948 is a sign that summer is near.
3. Promises kept literally: A nation born in a day and a dead language brought back to life prove that God’s promises to Israel are meant to be read literally.
Key Verses: Isaiah 66:8, Jeremiah 31:23, Ezekiel 36:24–25, Ezekiel 37:1–10, Matthew 24:32–34, Zechariah 12:10
