Lesson 10
Counted Worthy to Escape
Jesus’ Own Word for the Rescue of His Church
MEMORY VERSE
“Watch therefore, and pray always that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that will come to pass, and to stand before the Son of Man.” (Luke 21:36, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

Imagine a family asleep in a house when a fire starts. A firefighter breaks through the door, grabs the children, and carries them out before the roof falls in. Nobody says those children were weak or afraid. Nobody says they were running away from their duty. They were rescued. Rescue is what love does for children when a fire is coming.

In His last great teaching on the Mount of Olives, Jesus described the troubles that would come at the end of the age: wars, earthquakes, signs in the sky, and nations in fear. Then He gave His followers one word to hold on to. That word is “escape.”

“But take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with carousing, drunkenness, and cares of this life, and that Day come on you unexpectedly. For it will come as a snare on all those who dwell on the face of the whole earth. Watch therefore, and pray always that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that will come to pass, and to stand before the Son of Man.” (Luke 21:34–36, NKJV)

Read those verses slowly. Jesus did not say, “Pray that you may be strong enough to live through all these things.” He said, “Pray that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things.” And then He said where the rescued would be: standing “before the Son of Man.”
Some newer English Bibles read, “that you may have strength to escape.” Either way, the key word is the same: escape. Jesus asked His followers to pray to get out, not to get through.

In this lesson we will study that one word, gather every piece of evidence the Bible gives for it, and answer the most common questions people ask. Consider yourself as you read. Jesus spoke these words to you, so that you may escape.
THE WORD “ESCAPE”

The Greek word Luke uses is ekpheugō. It is made of two parts: ek, meaning “out of,” and pheugō, meaning “to flee.” Put together, it means to flee out of, to get away safely, to get clean out of danger.
The best way to understand a Bible word is to see how the Bible uses it in other places. Look at these:

In Acts 16:27, when an earthquake opened the doors of the prison in Philippi, the jailer pulled out his sword to kill himself, “supposing the prisoners had fled” (NKJV). The word is ekpheugō. He thought they had gotten clean out of the prison.

In 2 Corinthians 11:33, Paul tells how he got away from the governor of Damascus: “I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall, and escaped from his hands” (NKJV). Same word. Paul did not stay inside the city and fight his way through. He was lowered over the wall and gone.

In 1 Thessalonians 5:3, Paul uses the same word for the unbelieving world when the Day of the Lord comes: “For when they say, ‘Peace and safety!’ then sudden destruction comes upon them, as labor pains upon a pregnant woman. And they shall not escape” (NKJV).
In Hebrews 2:3, the writer asks, “How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation” (NKJV)?

Every time, the word means getting out. It does not mean staying in the middle of the danger and surviving. Jesus could have used a word that meant “endure” or “make it through,” but He chose the word that means to get out.

Notice also the two groups in these passages. Of the world, Paul says, “They shall not escape.” Of His followers, Jesus says, “Pray that you may be counted worthy to escape.” The same word divides the two.
GOD DID NOT APPOINT US TO WRATH
The word “escape” is not alone. Again and again, the New Testament promises that believers will be kept from the wrath to come.
“And to wait for His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead, even Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.” (1 Thessalonians 1:10, NKJV)
“For God did not appoint us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.” (1 Thessalonians 5:9, NKJV)
“Much more then, having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from wrath through Him.” (Romans 5:9, NKJV)

Look at where Paul put 1 Thessalonians 5:9. It comes right after his teaching on the Day of the Lord, when “sudden destruction” falls on the world. In that very setting he says God did not appoint us to wrath. The Tribulation is the time when God pours out His wrath on a world that has rejected Him. Revelation says that when the seals are opened, people cry out that “the great day of His wrath has come” (Revelation 6:17, NKJV). The Church was not appointed to that. Remember the verse from Before You Begin: the Day of the Lord cannot come until “He who now restrains” is “taken out of the way” (2 Thessalonians 2:7, NKJV). Many Bible teachers see the Holy Spirit, living in the Church, as that restrainer. When the Church is taken out, the restraint is lifted and the man of sin is revealed.
Jesus made the same promise to the faithful church in Philadelphia:
“Because you have kept My command to persevere, I also will keep you from the hour of trial which shall come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth.” (Revelation 3:10, NKJV)

Jesus did not promise to keep them through the hour. He promised to keep them from it. The Greek words mean to keep out of. And notice that this hour of trial comes “upon the whole world.” The only way to be kept out of something that covers the whole world is to be taken out of the world.
Peter sums it up: “The Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptations and to reserve the unjust under punishment for the day of judgment” (2 Peter 2:9, NKJV).
HIDDEN IN THE CHAMBER
The Old Testament prophets saw this too. Isaiah wrote:

“Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourself, as it were, for a little moment, until the indignation is past. For behold, the Lord comes out of His place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity.” (Isaiah 26:20–21, NKJV)

Look at the verse just before this one: “Your dead shall live; together with my dead body they shall arise” (Isaiah 26:19, NKJV). First the dead rise, then God’s people are hidden while the wrath passes, the same order Paul gives in 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17. God calls His people to come into their chambers and shut the door while He punishes the earth. The Hebrew word for “chambers” here, cheder, is the same word Joel uses for the bridegroom’s chamber on his wedding day: “Let the bridegroom go out from his chamber, and the bride from her dressing room” (Joel 2:16, NKJV). As you will see in Lesson 11, the bride and groom stayed in the chamber for seven days while the celebration went on outside. Isaiah’s “little moment” behind a shut door fits the seven years of Tribulation.

Zephaniah gives the same call: “Seek the Lord, all you meek of the earth, who have upheld His justice. Seek righteousness, seek humility. It may be that you will be hidden in the day of the Lord’s anger” (Zephaniah 2:3, NKJV).
THREE WITNESSES: ENOCH, NOAH, AND LOT
The Bible says a matter is settled “by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18:16, NKJV). God gave us three witnesses to show how He rescues His people before judgment falls.
Enoch, taken before the flood: “And Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24, NKJV). The book of

Hebrews explains: “By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death, ‘and was not found, because God had taken him’; for before he was taken he had this testimony, that he pleased God” (Hebrews 11:5, NKJV). Enoch was taken off the earth before the flood ever came. He is a picture of the Church caught up in the Rapture.

Noah, shut in the ark: Noah and his family went into the ark, “and the Lord shut him in” (Genesis 7:16, NKJV). God Himself closed the door. Noah was carried safely through the flood while the judgment fell outside. Peter says God “saved Noah, one of eight people, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood on the world of the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:5, NKJV). Many teachers see Noah as a picture of the Jewish remnant that God protects through the Tribulation.

Lot, led out of Sodom: The angels took Lot by the hand and led him out of the city. One of them said, “Hurry, escape there. For I cannot do anything until you arrive there” (Genesis 19:22, NKJV). Think about that. The angel could not let the fire fall until righteous Lot was out. Judgment had to wait for the rescue.
Jesus Himself pointed to these days:

“And as it was in the days of Noah, so it will be also in the days of the Son of Man: They ate, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. Likewise as it was also in the days of Lot: They ate, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they built; but on the day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all. Even so will it be in the day when the Son of Man is revealed.” (Luke 17:26–30, NKJV)
Notice the pattern. Life was going on as usual: eating, drinking, buying, selling, building, getting married. Then on the very day the
righteous were taken out or shut in, judgment fell. First the rescue, then the wrath. That is God’s pattern.
THE PROMISE OF THE BRIDEGROOM
Jesus promised to come back for His Bride Himself.
“And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to Myself; that where I am, there you may be also.” (John 14:3, NKJV)
Paul explains how it will happen:

“Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed—in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” (1 Corinthians 15:51–52, NKJV)

“For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And thus we shall always be with the Lord.” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17, NKJV)

The words “caught up” translate the Greek word harpazō, which means to snatch away, to seize, to carry off by force. It is the language of rescue. Then Paul adds, “Therefore comfort one another with these words” (1 Thessalonians 4:18, NKJV). A promise that the Church must first live through the wrath of God would not be much comfort. A promise of rescue is.

And in Revelation, right after the letters to the seven churches, John sees “a door standing open in heaven,” and a voice like a trumpet says, “Come up here” (Revelation 4:1, NKJV). As we saw in Lesson
8, the Church is not mentioned on earth again until the end of the book.
WHAT DOES “COUNTED WORTHY” MEAN?
Jesus said, “Pray that you may be counted worthy to escape.” Some people hear that and worry. Do I have to earn my place in the Rapture?
No. No one is worthy on his own. Our worthiness comes from Jesus. He paid the price, and He clothes us in His righteousness. Salvation is a gift (Ephesians 2:8–9).

But look at what Jesus put right before those words. “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with carousing, drunkenness, and cares of this life.” He was warning His followers not to let their hearts grow heavy and careless. The person who is counted worthy is the person who watches and prays, like the wise bridesmaids in Matthew 25 who had oil in their lamps. That is someone who has truly been born again and whose faith is alive.

The Bible says the Bride of Christ “has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7, NKJV). The believer watches, prays, and stays ready. “And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as He is pure” (1 John 3:3, NKJV). The hope of escape does not make us lazy. It makes us clean.
COMMON QUESTIONS
People often raise questions about the Rapture. Here are short, plain answers to the ones you will hear most.
“The word ‘rapture’ isn’t in the Bible.”
The English word is not in most English Bibles, but the teaching is. In 1 Thessalonians 4:17, Paul writes that we will be “caught up.” The

Greek word is harpazō. When the Bible was translated into Latin many centuries ago, the word used there was rapiemur, from the Latin verb rapio, which means “to snatch away.” Our English word “rapture” comes from that Latin word. The word “Trinity” isn’t in the Bible either, but the truth it names is.
“Isn’t this just escapism, a way to run from hard times?”

No. Jesus Himself told us to pray to escape, so it cannot be wrong to hope for it. And the hope of His coming does not make believers lazy or afraid. It makes them holy (1 John 3:3) and busy in His work. Paul calls it “the blessed hope” (Titus 2:13, NKJV). The early Christians who looked for Jesus to come at any moment were the same Christians who carried the gospel across the Roman Empire.
“Won’t Christians suffer?”

Yes. Jesus said, “In the world you will have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33, NKJV). Believers have always been persecuted, and many are suffering for their faith around the world today. But the persecution of men is one thing. The wrath of God is something else. Christians may suffer the anger of the world, but God “did not appoint us to wrath” (1 Thessalonians 5:9, NKJV). The Tribulation is the time of His wrath poured out on a world that rejected His Son.
“Can anyone be saved after the Rapture?”

Yes, but at a terrible cost. John saw “a great multitude which no one could number” and was told, “These are the ones who come out of the great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9, 14, NKJV). Many of them will die for their faith (Revelation 20:4). God will still be calling people, but they will have to refuse the Antichrist and his mark in the worst days the world has ever seen. Do not wait for that. “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2, NKJV).
“Didn’t the early church believe something different?”

The early church lived every day expecting that Jesus could come at any time. Paul wrote to the Thessalonians as if he might be alive when it happened: “We who are alive and remain” (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Around AD 180, a church leader named Irenaeus wrote that “when in the end the Church shall be suddenly caught up from this,” there would be tribulation such as never had been. He was not the only one. Here are some of the voices from long before the 1800s:

The Shepherd of Hermas, around AD 140 to 150: This was one of the most widely read Christian books in the early church. In a vision, a great beast is called “a type of the great tribulation that is coming,” and believers are told, “If then you prepare yourselves, and repent with all your heart, and turn to the Lord, it will be possible for you to escape it.”

Irenaeus of Lyons, around AD 180: Irenaeus learned from Polycarp, and Polycarp learned from the apostle John. He wrote that the Church “shall be suddenly caught up” before a tribulation like no other.

Victorinus of Pettau, who died around AD 304: He wrote the oldest Latin commentary on Revelation that we still have. When the sky rolls up like a scroll in Revelation 6:14, he explained it this way: “that the Church shall be taken away.”

A sermon long credited to Ephraem the Syrian, from somewhere between AD 373 and 627 (scholars disagree on the date): “For all the saints and elect of God are gathered, prior to the tribulation that is to come, and are taken to the Lord lest they see the confusion that is to overwhelm the world because of our sins.”
Brother Dolcino, Italy, AD 1304: A record of his teaching says he believed that he and his followers would be carried up to Paradise, where Enoch and Elijah are, while the Antichrist ruled.
Morgan Edwards, a Welsh Baptist who later became a pastor in Philadelphia, written in 1744 while he was a student in England and
printed in 1788: He taught that the dead saints would be raised and the living changed at Christ’s “appearing in the air” (1 Thessalonians 4:17), years before He comes back to reign.

To be honest, not every early church leader saw the order of events the same way, and many expected the Church to face hard persecution. Teachers in later centuries laid out the order of events in more detail. But the hope of being caught up and escaping the wrath to come was there from the very beginning, and it comes straight from the apostles.
“Didn’t John Darby make up the Rapture in the 1800s?”

No. John Nelson Darby was a Bible teacher in Ireland and England who taught the order of events clearly in the 1830s, and many people learned it from him. But he did not invent the hope. Paul wrote it down in the first century, and Irenaeus wrote about the Church being “suddenly caught up” around AD 180, more than sixteen hundred years before Darby was born. As you just read, Hermas, Victorinus, the Ephraem sermon, and Morgan Edwards all spoke of it before Darby too.
“What happens to little children at the Rapture?”

The Bible does not answer this in one verse, so we speak carefully. But it shows a God who loves little children. Jesus said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not forbid them; for of such is the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:14, NKJV). When King David’s baby died, David said, “I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23, NKJV). Many Bible teachers believe that children too young to understand and believe will be taken with the Bride. What we know for sure is this: the Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25).
“Why can’t anyone set a date?”
Because Jesus said no one can. “But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but My Father only”

(Matthew 24:36, NKJV). Just before He went up to heaven, He told His disciples, “It is not for you to know times or seasons which the Father has put in His own authority” (Acts 1:7, NKJV). Anyone who announces the date of the Rapture is going against the words of Jesus. As we saw with the Feast of Trumpets, the day is hidden. We are not told to know the day. We are told to know the season, as we saw in Before You Begin, and to be ready. “Therefore you also be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect” (Matthew 24:44, NKJV).
CONSIDER YOURSELF
So far this course has walked through God’s plan from the first word of Genesis to the edge of the Rapture. Before we go on to the wedding and the Kingdom, it comes down to you.
Jesus said, “Watch therefore, and pray always that you may be counted worthy to escape.” Ask yourself these questions honestly:
Have I truly received Jesus as my Savior and Lord? Is there oil in my lamp?
Is my heart weighed down with the cares of this life, or am I watching?
Am I keeping my garments clean while I wait for the Bridegroom?

The same word that promises rescue to the Church warns the world: “They shall not escape.” There is no middle ground. Every person either belongs to Jesus or does not. Every person is either behind the shut door with the Groom or outside it. If you are not sure where you stand, the How to Be Ready page near the end of this book will show you how to settle it today.
The signs are all around us. The fig tree is in leaf. The last lampstand is burning low. The Bridegroom is at the door. Look up, for your redemption draws near (Luke 21:28).
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: Jesus’ own word “escape” in Luke 21:36, backed by the promises that God did not appoint us to wrath and by the witnesses of Enoch, Noah, and Lot, shows that the Church will be taken out before the wrath of the Tribulation, and calls every believer to watch, pray, and be ready.
Three truths:
1. The word means “get out”: The Greek word ekpheugō means to flee out of and get away safely, as when Paul was let down over the wall of Damascus, and Jesus chose it for the rescue of His followers.
2. Rescue comes before wrath: God promised to keep His people from the hour of trial, and in the days of Enoch, Noah, and Lot, the righteous were taken out or shut in before judgment fell.
3. Counted worthy means ready: No one earns the Rapture, but true believers show their faith by watching, praying, and keeping their garments clean.
Key Verses: Luke 21:34–36, 1 Thessalonians 1:10, 1 Thessalonians 5:9, Revelation 3:10, Isaiah 26:20–21, Luke 17:26–30, 1 Corinthians 15:51–52, 1 Thessalonians 4:16–18

Lesson 11
The Ancient Wedding
The Eleven Steps of the Ancient Marriage, the Seven Bridal
Blessings, and the Roma Wedding
MEMORY VERSE
“Let us be glad and rejoice and give Him glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His wife has made herself ready.” (Revelation 19:7, NKJV)
A NOTE BEFORE YOU BEGIN
Take your time with this lesson. It is the longest one in the book. Scripture, history, and culture sit side by side on these pages, so do not rush.

This lesson ties the whole course together. The wedding is the golden thread that connects Bible prophecy, the history of Israel, and the Gospel of your salvation. Once you see the wedding, everything else falls into place: the feasts, the seven churches, and the Rapture.
Read slowly and take good notes. Watch for the seven bridal blessings as they come alive, one at a time.
INTRODUCTION
Will the Church go through the Tribulation? That question is the hinge the whole prophetic timeline turns on.

Jesus promised that believers would face trouble and persecution in this world (John 16:33). That is one thing. The poured-out wrath of Almighty God is something else. There is a clear line between the persecution of men and the wrath of God. Keep that line in mind as you read.

Jesus told His followers to pray “that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that will come to pass, and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36, NKJV). God has already shown us His pattern through three witnesses. Enoch was taken before the flood. Noah was shut in the ark and carried safely through it. Lot was led out of Sodom before the fire fell. We studied the word “escape” and each of these witnesses in Lesson 10.

In this lesson we look at the clearest picture God gave of how He will rescue His people: a wedding. Marriage is the oldest covenant on earth, given in the Garden of Eden. When we walk through the steps of the ancient marriage, the Rapture comes into view.

Even more amazing, many of these same steps are still alive in our own Gypsy Roma weddings today. The eleven steps below follow the order of a Roma wedding, and the Gospel meaning is given at each step. Keep one thing in mind: on God’s calendar a few of these steps come in a different order. First comes the Rapture (Step 10). Then, in heaven, come the Judgment Seat of Christ and the wedding (Steps 8 and 9). Then comes the marriage supper of the Lamb (Step 7). Last of all, the Bride returns to earth with the King (Step 11).
STEP 1: THE OPENED SIDE

“And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam, and he slept; and He took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place. Then the rib which the Lord God had taken from man He made into a woman, and He brought her to the man. And Adam said: ‘This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.’” (Genesis 2:21–23, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

The story of the Bride begins in Genesis. God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam. In the Bible, deep sleep is often a picture of death. God did not make Eve out of the dirt the way He made Adam. He opened Adam’s side while he slept, took a rib, and built a bride out of that wound.

This points straight to the cross. Jesus, the Last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45), fell into the sleep of death. While He hung there, “one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John 19:34, NKJV). Blood and water come with every birth, and from the wounded side of Christ the Church was born.
From the first Adam came a bride of flesh. From the Last Adam came a Bride bought with blood. God wrote the wedding into creation before Israel ever stood at Mount Sinai.
The Ephesus Wedding Blessing

Here we see the first of seven bridal blessings, taken from the overcomer promises we studied in Lesson 8. When Eve was formed, she was given a share in the whole garden, which held the tree of life. Jesus promises the same thing to His Bride: “To him who overcomes I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the midst of the Paradise of God” (Revelation 2:7, NKJV). The Bride has a place in the Father’s home forever.
STEP 2: THE MESSENGER AND THE TEST

“Then he said, ‘O Lord God of my master Abraham, please give me success this day, and show kindness to my master Abraham. Behold, here I stand by the well of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water. Now let it be that the young woman to whom I say, “Please let down your pitcher that I may drink,” and she says, “Drink, and I will also give your camels a drink”—let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac.’” (Genesis 24:12–14, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

When it was time to find a bride for Isaac, Abraham did not send his son into the far country. He sent his oldest and most trusted servant. Genesis 24 never gives his name, but he is traditionally known as Eliezer, the servant named in Genesis 15:2. The name Eliezer means “God is help,” which makes him a picture of the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus called the Helper (John 14:26).

The servant traveled to a far country, sat by a well, and asked God for a test to show him the right woman. He was looking for a servant’s heart. A woman who would offer to water ten thirsty camels was willing to do hard work for a stranger. Rebekah passed the test.

In the whole story, the servant never talks about himself. He talks only about the wealth, the greatness, and the love of his master’s son. That is still the work of the Holy Spirit. He does not point to Himself. He lifts up Jesus.
John the Baptist played a similar part, pointing everyone to Jesus as the Bridegroom.

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:29–30, NKJV)
The Roma Wedding

In our traditional Roma culture, we follow this same pattern. A marriage never starts as a random dating game. It starts with a messenger, a trusted friend who knows both families well. He speaks with both households to make sure the match is right, both in family and in character, before the parents ever meet. This humble messenger sets up the meeting so the family line stays protected.
STEP 3: THE GLASS OF WATER AND THE WILLING HEART

“Then they called Rebekah and said to her, ‘Will you go with this man?’ And she said, ‘I will go.’ So they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse, and Abraham’s servant and his men.” (Genesis 24:58–59, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

God never forces anyone into a relationship with Him. He wants a willing heart. Back at her family’s home, after the servant told his story, Rebekah’s family asked her one question: “Will you go with this man?” She did not stall or bargain. She simply said, “I will go.”

Rebekah agreed to leave her homeland and marry a man she had never seen. She trusted the servant’s word and the gifts in her hand. That is exactly where the Church is now. We have never seen Jesus with our eyes, yet we love Him (1 Peter 1:8). We have given Him our lives because of the testimony of the Word.
The Roma Wedding
This heart test is still kept in our Roma culture. When we want to know if a girl wants to come into our family, we ask her to bring a glass of water right before any talks begin.

If she hands over a glass that is half empty, it means go look somewhere else. She is saying no. But if she walks in and hands over a glass that is completely full, she is saying yes with her whole heart.

That full glass of water is a beautiful picture of a sinner’s prayer. It is the moment a person chooses to receive the living water of Jesus Christ. Jesus said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:37, NKJV).
STEP 4: THE CONTRACT AND THE PRICE

“Knowing that you were not redeemed with corruptible things, like silver or gold, from your aimless conduct received by tradition from your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” (1 Peter 1:18–19, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

Once the bride agreed, the betrothal began. In Hebrew this binding betrothal is called kiddushin, from the word for “holy” or “set apart.” As the Galilean custom is taught, the groom and his father traveled to the bride’s town and met with her parents. With witnesses present, they drew up a marriage contract called a ketubah.
The groom paid a bride price, called the mohar, to the bride’s father (Genesis 34:12, Exodus 22:16–17). It was a large amount. It showed how much the bride was worth to him.
This is the heart of the Gospel. “For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son” (John 3:16, NKJV). Jesus paid the
highest price ever paid for a bride: His own life. Not silver. Not gold. Blood. That is how much the Bride is worth to Him.

To seal the agreement, the groom poured a cup of wine and offered it to the bride. If she drank it, she was saying yes to the covenant. Jesus did this in the Upper Room. He lifted the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20, NKJV). When you receive that cup by faith, you accept the contract. Communion is not an empty ritual. It is a reminder of a signed covenant.
The Roma Wedding
After the glass of water, the fathers of both families sit down to settle the bride price. Each family has someone experienced to speak for it.

The groom’s family does not come into the bride’s house emptyhanded. When we go to seek our daughter-in-law, we walk in carrying a bottle. Jesus came to us the same way: “for the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10, NKJV).

When the price is agreed, the families stand up, shake hands, and seal it with a toast from that bottle. The price is settled, and the cup seals it. The night before Jesus paid the price for His Bride, He lifted the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20, NKJV). Remember that bottle. We will see it again.
STEP 5: THE GIFTS AND THE TOKEN
“Then the servant brought out jewelry of silver, jewelry of gold, and clothing, and gave them to Rebekah.” (Genesis 24:53, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

After the bride price was paid, the groom gave gifts to the bride herself. These were called the mattan. They were not part of the price paid to her father. They were hers to keep, often gifts of gold, to remind her of his love while she waited. That is exactly what Abraham’s servant did for Rebekah.

Jesus did the same for His Church. He gave His Bride the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Paul lists nine of them in 1 Corinthians 12:8–10. The Holy Spirit Himself “is the guarantee of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:14, NKJV), a down payment on everything that is coming. The Bride is never left empty-handed or powerless while she waits for the Groom.
The Pergamos Wedding Blessing

Here we see the second bridal blessing. Jesus promised the overcomer in Pergamos “a white stone, and on the stone a new name written which no one knows except him who receives it” (Revelation 2:17, NKJV). In the ancient world, a white stone could be used as a ticket into a feast. Judges also used a white stone to vote “not guilty.” Both pictures fit the Bride. She is declared innocent, and she holds her personal invitation to the wedding banquet.
The Roma Wedding

In our Roma culture, as soon as the talks are finished and the handshake seals the price, the gold gifts are given to the bride. A gold chain with a gold coin is placed around the neck of the new daughter-in-law, along with gold earrings and a bracelet. The gold coin is the token of engagement.

In our culture, this token carries great weight. When you see that gold chain and coin on your daughter-in-law, you know how much she wants to be part of your family, and that she is waiting patiently to get there.

The coin is a badge that says she belongs to someone. If a bride is seen in public without her coin, it is a sign of disrespect, and the parents could even break the engagement. In the same way, a true believer walks through the world marked by the Holy Spirit, showing that he belongs to Christ. Paul says we “were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise” (Ephesians 1:13, NKJV). Every time we take Communion, it is like touching our engagement token and remembering the price Jesus paid.
STEP 6: THE SEPARATION

“In My Father’s house are many mansions; if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to Myself; that where I am, there you may be also.” (John 14:2–3, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

When Jesus spoke these words, He was not being mysterious. He was using wedding language that everyone in the room understood. Once the price was paid and the gifts were given, the hardest part of the covenant began: the separation.

As the custom is taught, the groom would say to his bride, “I am going to my father’s house to prepare a place for you.” He would leave a bottle of wine with her, promising not to drink it again until they were together in the wedding chamber. Jesus said the same thing at the Last Supper: “I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it new with you in My Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 26:29, NKJV).

Many teachers also tell the custom of the folded napkin. It may not have been the same everywhere, but the picture is a good one. When a master was finished with his meal, he would crumple his napkin and leave it on the table. But if he folded it neatly and set it aside, it

meant he was coming back. Many teachers link this picture to the empty tomb, where Peter and John saw the cloth that had been around Jesus’ head “folded together in a place by itself” (John 20:7, NKJV). Jesus left a message His Bride could understand: I am not finished. I am coming back.

The groom then went back to his father’s house to build the bridal room, often called the chuppah. It could take about a year. The groom did not decide on his own when the room was finished. His father did. When people asked the groom when the wedding would be, he would answer, “I don’t know. Only my father knows.”

Jesus used those same words about His return: “But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but My Father only” (Matthew 24:36, NKJV). The Father sets the day. The Son keeps the promise.
The Bride Gets Ready

The bride used this time to get ready. First, she went through a ceremonial washing in water, called a mikvah. It showed she was leaving her old life behind and belonged to her groom, a picture of Christian baptism. She often wore a veil in public so every other man knew she was promised to someone.

Then she prepared her own wedding clothes. This is important. The groom paid the price, but the bride had work to do. She had to get her garments ready and keep them clean. That is exactly what the Bible says about the Bride of Christ.

“Let us be glad and rejoice and give Him glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His wife has made herself ready. And to her it was granted to be arrayed in fine linen, clean and bright, for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.” (Revelation 19:7–8, NKJV)

Notice the two sides of that verse. The fine linen is “granted to her.” It is a gift. We are saved by grace through faith, not by our own works (Ephesians 2:8–9). But it also says “His wife has made herself ready.” Once we are saved, we have a part to play. The fine linen is “the righteous acts of the saints.”

Jesus praised the few believers in Sardis “who have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with Me in white, for they are worthy” (Revelation 3:4, NKJV). And He warned, “Behold, I am coming as a thief. Blessed is he who watches, and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Revelation 16:15, NKJV). James tells us what this looks like day to day: “Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their trouble, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world” (James 1:27, NKJV).

So the Bride does not sit and wait doing nothing. She prays. She reads the Word. She serves others. She turns away from sin and asks for forgiveness quickly when she falls. She keeps her dress clean, because she wants to be ready when the Groom comes.
The Midnight Cry

Jesus told a parable about this waiting time, the parable of the ten bridesmaids in Matthew 25. The ten young women in this story are not the bride. They are bridesmaids, waiting with their lamps to meet the groom. Five were wise and brought extra oil. Five were foolish and brought none.
“And at midnight a cry was heard: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him!’” (Matthew 25:6, NKJV)

When the cry came, there was no time left to get ready. The wise went in with the groom to the wedding, “and the door was shut” (Matthew 25:10, NKJV). When the foolish came knocking later, the groom said, “Assuredly, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12, NKJV).

Why bridesmaids, and not the bride? In a parable, Jesus uses one picture to teach one main point. All of us together, the whole Church, are the Bride. But readiness is personal. Each person must have his own oil. No one can borrow it from a parent, a husband, a wife, or a pastor. The wise bridesmaids could not share their oil, and no one else can believe for you. So Jesus shows us as individuals, each one holding a lamp and waiting for the Groom. (Some Bible teachers believe the ten bridesmaids stand for Israel waiting for the Messiah at the end of the Tribulation. Either way, the lesson for us is the same: be ready, because the door will be shut.)

Pay close attention to those words: “I do not know you.” The groom did not say, “You are late.” He said he never knew them. The foolish bridesmaids are a picture of people who carried a lamp and looked the part, but never had the oil of the Holy Spirit in their lives. They said the right words, but they were never truly born again. As we saw in Lesson 8, every true believer is an overcomer. The midnight cry does not catch a true believer unready. It shows who was real all along.
That is why this lesson calls you to check your heart now. Do you have the oil? Is Jesus truly your Lord? Once the cry goes out, the door will be shut.
The Roma Wedding
In our Roma culture, we follow this same pattern during the separation. After the price is settled and the gold gifts are given, the guests and family always ask when we are having the wedding.

Then the groom’s family does something that means the very same thing as the Galilean groom’s wine. When they leave, they do not take the bottle with them. They leave it with the bride’s family. It stays in her house as a promise: we are coming back for her, and we will drink from this again. It waits, just like the bride waits.

Jesus did the same. At the Last Supper He said, “I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it new with you in My Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 26:29, NKJV). And He left the cup with His Bride: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death till He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26, NKJV). Every time the Church takes Communion, it is like the bride’s family looking at that bottle. He paid the price, and He is coming back for us.

The groom and his father then leave to prepare everything for the wedding. They find the banquet hall, buy what is needed for the celebration, and buy the white wedding dress the bride will wear. That dress is the groom’s gift, and his family guards it. They make sure it does not get dirty or touched by anyone who has been married more than once. In our tradition, the wedding dress is very important, and it must stay clean.

Why only someone who has been married once? Because the dress is a picture of a pure, faithful covenant: one bride for one groom, for life. That is how God planned marriage from the beginning: “a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24, NKJV). It is also how God sees His people. Paul told the church, “For I have betrothed you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2, NKJV). When the Bible lists who should lead and serve in God’s house, it says a leader must be “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2, NKJV). So our custom keeps the dress and the crown in the hands of people whose own lives show that onecovenant picture.

This custom is a picture, not a judgment on anyone. If you have been divorced or widowed, Jesus does not love you less, and His blood washes every believer completely clean (1 John 1:7). The custom is simply our way of honoring what the wedding stands for: Christ has one Bride, and He will never leave her.

While they are away, the bride stays ready too. In our culture there is no secret day. The date is set and everyone knows it. Here our custom is different from the Bible picture, because for the Bride of Christ the day is hidden. What our custom keeps is the readiness: the bride must still be made ready beforehand. The father has the final say over the day. During this time of separation, the bride must keep a strict standard of modesty and keep herself pure. Her own family prepares the outfit she will wear when she walks into the wedding hall, and she gets it ready and keeps it clean while she waits for the wedding.
So there are two outfits in a Roma wedding. The bride prepares one with her family. The groom and his family prepare the other, the white dress. We will see both on the wedding day.
STEP 7: THE WEDDING DAY
AND THE BANQUET HALL
“Then he said to me, ‘Write: “Blessed are those who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb!”’” (Revelation 19:9, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

After the long time of waiting, the bride is brought out of the house where she prepared and into the groom’s celebration. She is surrounded by her companions. The waiting is over, and she is brought before the groom’s whole household.

This is not a quiet, private moment. It is a public and joyful entry into the celebration. The covenant that began with a contract, a cup, and a promise now becomes a feast. Waiting ends. Being together begins. On God’s calendar this feast comes after the Rapture (Step 10) and the Judgment Seat (Steps 8 and 9), just before the King returns (Revelation 19:7–9).
The Roma Wedding

On the long-awaited wedding day, the bride walks into the wedding hall in an outfit her family prepared for her. Her father, her whole family, and her closest friends come with her. As she steps through the door, the groom’s family meets her with joy. Her old home is behind her. Her new family and the banquet are in front of her.

Then comes one of the most beautiful moments of the day. The bride’s family gives the bottle back to the groom’s family. They kept it the whole time she waited, and now they hand it back. It is set on the groom’s family’s table, and they drink from it again. The promise has been kept.

This is the marriage supper of the Lamb. The Bride does not come empty-handed either. She brings back what He left with her, the covenant she kept “till He comes.” Jesus told the faithful in Thyatira, “Hold fast what you have till I come” (Revelation 2:25, NKJV). And Jesus drinks the fruit of the vine new with His Bride in His Father’s kingdom, just as He promised. The Last Supper and the marriage supper are two ends of one promise, like one bottle drunk from twice.

Why a bottle of wine? In the Bible, wine is the drink of celebration. The psalm thanks God for “wine that makes glad the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15, NKJV). When Jesus did His very first miracle, He did it at a wedding. The wine had run out, and He turned water into wine. The master of the feast told the groom, “You have kept the good wine until now!” (John 2:10, NKJV). That is a picture of the marriage supper of the Lamb. God has saved the best for last.

Wine also comes from grapes that have been crushed. The joy of the wedding came through the crushing of the cross. Jesus “for the joy that was set before Him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2, NKJV). And the prophets saw that joy spreading over the whole earth in the Kingdom: “The Lord of hosts will make for all people a feast of choice pieces, a feast of wines on the lees” (Isaiah 25:6, NKJV). In
the same passage God promises, “He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord God will wipe away tears from all faces” (Isaiah 25:8, NKJV).
So when the bottle is set on the table and the families drink from it again, it is more than a toast. The price is paid, the waiting is over, and it is time to celebrate.

In the old days, a Roma wedding lasted seven days, the same length as a wedding feast in Bible times. Later it became three days, and today most of our weddings last one day. But the old seven-day wedding shows how closely our tradition once followed the Bible’s pattern. We will see in Step 10 why those seven days matter so much in prophecy.
STEP 8: THE WHITE DRESS, THE
CROWN, AND THE TIED HANDS

“Now if anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become clear; for the Day will declare it, because it will be revealed by fire; and the fire will test each one’s work, of what sort it is. If anyone’s work which he has built on it endures, he will receive a reward.” (1 Corinthians 3:12–14, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

In heaven, after the Church is gathered, believers stand before the Judgment Seat of Christ. The Greek word for this seat is bema, the platform where a judge gave out prizes to winners of a race. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10, NKJV). This judgment is not to decide who is saved. That was settled at the cross. It is to give out rewards. The Bride is presented clothed in white, and her works are tested by fire. What was done for Christ lasts and becomes her reward.
The Sardis and Smyrna Wedding Blessings
Two bridal blessings appear here.

The Sardis Wedding Blessing is the white garment. Jesus promised, “He who overcomes shall be clothed in white garments” (Revelation 3:5, NKJV). This is the dress without spot or wrinkle. Christ will “present her to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27, NKJV).

The Smyrna Wedding Blessing is the crown. To the church in Smyrna Jesus promised, “Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10, NKJV), and “He who overcomes shall not be hurt by the second death” (Revelation 2:11, NKJV). The crown is the victor’s crown, and the Bride is safe forever.
The Roma Wedding
Once inside the hall, the bride changes from her family’s outfit into the white wedding dress the groom and his family prepared for her, and she is presented to her father.
Look at the two outfits, because they show the two sides of Revelation 19:7–8 that we read in Step 6.

The outfit her family prepared is the one she worked on and kept clean while she waited. That is “His wife has made herself ready.” It pictures our faithful life while we wait for Jesus: praying, reading the Word, serving, and turning from sin. We are told to keep our garments clean (Revelation 3:4, 16:15).

But she does not get married in the outfit she prepared. At the wedding she puts on the dress the groom provided. That is “to her it was granted to be arrayed in fine linen, clean and bright.” Our best efforts walk us to the door, but the garment we are married in is His gift. Isaiah said it this way: “He has clothed me with the garments of salvation, He has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorns

herself with her jewels” (Isaiah 61:10, NKJV). When the high priest Joshua stood before God in filthy clothes, the Lord said, “Take away the filthy garments from him... See, I have removed your iniquity from you, and I will clothe you with rich robes” (Zechariah 3:4, NKJV).

Remember the parable of the wedding feast in Lesson 5. The king provided the wedding garment, and the man who came in his own clothes was thrown out (Matthew 22:11–13). No one gets into the wedding of the Lamb dressed in his own goodness. His righteousness is ours the moment we believe (Romans 3:22). At the Judgment Seat, what we prepared is tested, and the Bride is shown to all in the dress He gave her.

Then the ceremony begins. A crown is placed on her head. The person who places it must be a trusted family member who has never been married more than once, for the same reason we saw with the dress in Step 6. This is a picture of believers receiving their crowns when they arrive in heaven. The greatest crown of all is our eternal salvation.

After the crown is placed, the bride’s and groom’s hands are tied tightly together with a red cloth, and a prayer is spoken to bless the marriage. The red cloth is a clear picture of the blood of Christ. The covenant is bound and sealed in the blood of the Lamb.
STEP 9: THE DOWRY WALK
“And behold, I am coming quickly, and My reward is with Me, to give to every one according to his work.” (Revelation 22:12, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture
The Bride of Christ does not enter her new life empty-handed. She brings the fruit of her faithful life on earth.

Our works are not judged to decide our salvation. Jesus already paid for that on the cross. Our works are judged for rewards. Wood, hay, and straw stand for selfish things done for this world. They burn up in a moment. Gold, silver, and precious stones stand for things done in faith, love, and sacrifice. They last forever. Jesus Himself brings these rewards and hands them to His Bride. You do not earn the wedding. But you do bring fruit into it.
The Roma Wedding

In our Roma culture, we act this out in a way everyone can see. With their hands still tied together in the red cloth, a picture of the blood of Christ, the bride and groom begin the ceremony known as “Darhgo.” They do not sit at the front of the room. They walk around the whole banquet hall, from table to table where the guests are eating dinner, and they gather their dowry as they go.

The guests do more than say congratulations. They place real money into a loaf of bread. In the old days, it was literally silver and gold. That is why, when gathering the “Darh-go,” we say, “Oh Nickalas dell 500 on do rupe, hai soon uh kai,” which represents someone giving 500 dollars’ worth of gold and silver.

Why bread? The bread can remind us of Jesus, who said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35, NKJV). Every reward the Bride receives comes to her through Him. Remember the afikomen from Lesson 6: the hidden bread that is found and brought back, with a reward given for it. Here too, the reward comes in the bread.

This custom is a living picture of the Judgment Seat of Christ and the wedding feast. The true Bride is honored and rewarded in front of the Father’s guests. The gold and silver placed in her hands go with her into her new home.
STEP 10: THE SHOFAR AND
THE ESCAPE FROM THE HALL

“For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And thus we shall always be with the Lord.” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

This is the high point of the whole wedding. The father of the groom decided when the bridal room was ready. When people asked the groom when the wedding would be, he answered, “Only my father knows.”

As we saw in Lesson 6, that phrase fits the Feast of Trumpets, called Yom Teruah. It comes on Tishrei 1, which falls in our September or October. Trumpets is the only feast that begins on a new moon, and no one could know the exact day until witnesses saw the first thin sliver of the new moon. Jewish tradition calls it the hidden day, reading Psalm 81:3, “Blow the trumpet at the time of the New Moon, at the full moon, on our solemn feast day” (NKJV). The Hebrew word that the NKJV translates “full moon” is keseh, and Jewish tradition reads it as “covered” or “hidden.” That is why many teachers hear in Trumpets the words of Jesus: no one knows the day or the hour. When the new moon was confirmed, the shofar was blown.

As the custom is taught, when the father finally said the room was ready, the groom came for his bride suddenly, often late at night. A friend ran ahead with a shout, and a shofar was blown: “The bridegroom is coming!” The bride had to be ready to go at once, and he carried her away to his father’s house. Paul describes the same sounds in the verse at the top of this step: a shout and a trumpet.

Paul uses a strong Greek word for “caught up” in 1 Thessalonians 4:17: harpazō. It means to grab, to snatch away, to carry off by force. It is a rescue. The Bridegroom snatches His Bride out of a world that is about to fall under judgment.

Then the bride and groom stayed in the wedding chamber for seven days. That was the length of a wedding feast in Bible times. When Jacob married Leah, Laban told him, “Fulfill her week” (Genesis 29:27, NKJV), and Samson’s wedding feast lasted “the seven days of the feast” (Judges 14:12, NKJV). Those seven days are a picture of the seven years of the Tribulation. While God’s wrath is poured out on the earth, the Bride is safe inside the Father’s house.
The Philadelphia Wedding Blessing

At the moment of escape, we see the Philadelphia Wedding Blessing. “He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of My God, and he shall go out no more” (Revelation 3:12, NKJV). When the shofar sounds and the Bride is snatched into the Father’s house, she is placed there forever. To this same church Jesus promised, “I also will keep you from the hour of trial which shall come upon the whole world” (Revelation 3:10, NKJV). She is marked with the name of God and made a citizen of the New Jerusalem, completely out of reach of the storm on earth.
The World’s Cover Story

The world is already getting ready to explain away the Rapture. In the 2018 movie Avengers: Infinity War, half of all life, billions of people, vanishes at the snap of a finger. A whole generation has watched people turn to dust on the big screen and called it entertainment. Fiction comes first, so the real thing will feel familiar.
It goes deeper than movies. Look at the news about Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, known as UAPs, the government’s newest name for UFOs. In July 2023, a committee of the U.S. House of

Representatives held a public hearing where a former intelligence officer testified under oath that the government has recovered craft of “non-human” origin. The Pentagon denied his claims, but the headlines spread around the world. Over and over, the public hears the same message: “We are not alone.”

This is not just a sudden interest in science fiction. When the trumpet sounds and millions of believers disappear, the world will not give credit to the Word of God. It will reach for the story it has been told for years. Some will say, “We warned you we were not alone. This was an alien harvest, a cleansing of the planet.” That lie will blind many hearts and open the door for the Antichrist to rise in the name of world peace and unity.
The Red Heifer and October 7
Look at what is happening in Israel right now, and you can see how close we are.

“Speak to the children of Israel, that they bring you a red heifer without blemish, in which there is no defect and on which a yoke has never come. You shall give it to Eleazar the priest, that he may take it outside the camp, and it shall be slaughtered before him.” (Numbers 19:2–3, NKJV)

Under the Law of Moses, the ashes of a perfect red heifer that has never worn a yoke were needed to make people, including the priests, ceremonially clean. Without them, temple worship could not start again. The heifer was burned outside the camp, like the sin offerings described in Hebrews: “For the bodies of those animals, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that He might sanctify the people with His own blood, suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:11–12, NKJV). In later times, Jewish tradition says the heifer was burned on the Mount of Olives, facing the temple.

For almost two thousand years, Israel has not had a red heifer that qualified. Then in September 2022, five red heifers were flown from Texas to Israel. By 2024 they were old enough to be used under Jewish law. No heifer has been burned for the ceremony yet, but the preparations are underway.

On October 7, 2023, Hamas attacked Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking about 250 hostages. That attack started a war that spread across the region, and in 2024 and 2025 Iran and Israel struck each other directly.

On January 14, 2024, the 100th day of the war, the Hamas military spokesman Abu Obeida gave a televised speech. He listed the reasons for the attack, and among them he named “the bringing of red cows.” Then he said, “Thus came the epic of October 7th.”

I promise you, this is not a coincidence. Too much lines up. The enemy launched a war to stop a prophetic clock. If the tools for a third temple are being made ready, and nations go to war over a red heifer, then the stage for the Tribulation is being set.

While Israel prepares for an earthly temple, the true Bride sits in her separation season, watching the headlines line up with the Word. If the earthly shadow is this close, the heavenly Bridegroom is already standing at the door. Stay ready. Keep your lamp burning. The Father alone knows the hour, but the signs are not silent.
The Roma Wedding

As soon as the bride and groom finish walking the hall and gathering their gold and silver, our Roma custom acts out this very thing. The groom’s family suddenly runs the daughter-in-law straight out of the hall! We do not walk out slowly. We snatch her away with sudden speed, running her past the shouting crowd, even though her father brought her there. She almost always goes straight to the safety of the groom’s father’s house.

This sudden exit is a living picture of the Rapture. The Bridegroom does not linger in the hall of this world. He grabs His Bride and carries her away in the twinkling of an eye, before judgment falls on the earth.
STEP 11: THE THREE-DAY RETURN
“And in that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east... Thus the Lord my God will come, and all the saints with You.” (Zechariah 14:4–5, NKJV)
The Jewish and Gospel Picture

Many people think the story ends inside the wedding chamber. It does not. When the seven days are over, which matches the end of the seven-year Tribulation, the doors of the Father’s house open. The Bridegroom comes back to earth, and He brings His Bride with Him. “And the armies in heaven, clothed in fine linen, white and clean, followed Him on white horses” (Revelation 19:14, NKJV). The wedding does not cancel the Kingdom. The wedding leads into the Kingdom.
The Thyatira and Laodicea Wedding Blessings
As the Bride comes back to earth beside her Husband, she receives the last two bridal blessings.

The Thyatira Wedding Blessing is the scepter. “And he who overcomes, and keeps My works until the end, to him I will give power over the nations” (Revelation 2:26, NKJV). The Bride will reign beside her Groom and rule with Him with a rod of iron (Psalm 2:9, Revelation 2:27).
The Laodicea Wedding Blessing is the shared throne. “To him who overcomes I will grant to sit with Me on My throne, as I also overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne” (Revelation
3:21, NKJV). The Bride and the Groom will rule the Millennial Kingdom together.
The Roma Wedding

Our Roma wedding has one last step. After three days in the groom’s home, the groom’s family must take the daughter-in-law back to her father’s house for a visit. In the Jewish custom the couple stayed in the chamber for seven days. In ours, it is three days, and then the bride goes back. Both point to the same truth: the Bride is hidden away for a set time, and then she returns.

This custom is a picture of the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. Just as the daughter-in-law goes back to her first home after her time in the groom’s house, the Church will come back to earth with her Husband after her time in the Father’s house. The Bride does not stay hidden forever. She comes back with the King to reign.

In Lesson 12 we will see that return in full: the Mount of Olives splitting, the rod of iron, and the thousand-year reign. Keep the wedding steps in mind as you go. They show that the Bride is safe in the Father’s house while the wrath falls.
CHAPTER SUMMARY

One sentence: The ancient wedding, seen through Scripture, the Gospel, and our Roma customs, shows the Church Age as a season of separation where the Bride keeps herself ready, ending with a sudden rescue at the sound of the trumpet and the seven bridal blessings of her inheritance.
Three truths:
1. The opened side and the price: The Bride was born from the pierced side of Christ and bought with His blood, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the white stone are her token while she waits.

2. The Bride makes herself ready: The Bride keeps her garments clean during the separation, but she is married in the white dress the Groom provides, and the midnight cry shows who truly had the oil of the Holy Spirit.

3. The escape and the return: The sudden run out of the hall pictures the Rapture before the wrath, the seven days in the chamber picture the seven years of Tribulation, and the return visit pictures the Second Coming when the Bride reigns with Christ.
