Lesson 12
The Millennial Kingdom
The Thousand-Year Reign of Christ on Earth and Satan’s
Final Test
MEMORY VERSE

“Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection. Over such the second death has no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with Him a thousand years.” (Revelation 20:6, NKJV)
INTRODUCTION

In Lesson 11, the Bride was hidden away in the Father’s house for seven days, a picture of the seven years of Tribulation. Now the doors swing open. In this lesson we walk through the thousand-year Kingdom: the King’s return to the Mount of Olives, His rule from Jerusalem, the peace that fills the earth, and the final revolt at the very end.

The view this book teaches is called premillennialism. The word is easy to break apart. Pre means “before.” Mille means “thousand.” Annus means “year.” Put together, it means Jesus returns to earth before the thousand-year Kingdom begins. The order is right there in Revelation. In chapter 19 Christ rides out of heaven and defeats His enemies. Then in chapter 20 the words “a thousand years” come six times, all after His return. This view takes the words of the Old
Testament prophets and the Book of Revelation at face value, and it keeps God’s promises to Israel and to the throne of David just as He gave them.

Other views turn the Kingdom into a vague spiritual idea. Amillennialism (the “a” means “no”) teaches there will be no real thousand-year reign on earth. Postmillennialism (the “post” means “after”) teaches that the Church will make the whole world Christian first, and then Christ will return. But the Word of God describes a real period of a thousand years when Jesus Christ sits on the throne of David in Jerusalem.
THE RAPTURE AND THE SECOND
COMING ARE TWO DIFFERENT EVENTS
Before we go further, we have to keep two events apart. They are not the same. If you mix them together, the whole timeline gets confused.
The Rapture The Second Coming
When Before the Tribulation At the end of the Tribulation
Where Jesus comes
In the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17)
To the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4)
Who sees Him His Church Every eye (Revelation 1:7)
Why He comes To take His Bride to the Father’s house
To defeat His enemies and set up His Kingdom
What the Church does
Is caught up to meet Him Comes back with Him (Revelation 19:14)
Can we know the day?
No one knows the day or the hour
Seven years after the treaty is confirmed
The Rapture comes as a surprise. Christ does not set foot on the earth. He meets His Bride in the air and takes her home before the wrath falls. No one knows the day or the hour.

The Second Coming ends the seven-year Tribulation. Once the Antichrist confirms his treaty with Israel, the seven years can be counted, so this day is not hidden the way the Rapture is. And everyone on earth will see Him.
“Behold, He is coming with clouds, and every eye will see Him.” (Revelation 1:7, NKJV)

Nothing is hidden at the Second Coming. Christ comes down, makes war on the armies of the beast, and stands on the Mount of Olives. The Rapture hides the Bride away. The Second Coming shows the King to the whole world.
ARMAGEDDON AND THE KING’S RETURN

At the very end of the Tribulation, the Antichrist gathers the armies of the world into northern Israel, and from there they march on Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:2). John tells us, “And they gathered them together to the place called in Hebrew, Armageddon” (Revelation 16:16, NKJV). The name comes from the Hebrew Har Megiddo, the hill of Megiddo. It overlooks the Valley of Jezreel, where armies have fought for thousands of years. The Antichrist has two goals: to wipe out the Jewish people, and to fight the returning King.

It is not a long war. Heaven opens, and Christ rides out on a white horse with the armies of heaven behind Him, dressed in fine linen (Revelation 19:11–14). With the sharp sword that comes from His mouth, His spoken word, the armies of the Antichrist fall. “The beast” is another name for the Antichrist (Revelation 13:1–8). The false prophet is his partner, who makes the world worship the beast and take his mark (Revelation 13:11–17). Now the beast and the false prophet are captured and “cast alive into the lake of fire burning with brimstone” (Revelation 19:20, NKJV). Armageddon clears away the last of man’s empires so the Kingdom can begin.
THE MOUNT OF OLIVES SPLITS

“And in that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east. And the Mount of Olives shall be split in two, from east to west, making a very large valley; half of the mountain shall move toward the north and half of it toward the south... Thus the Lord my God will come, and all the saints with You.” (Zechariah 14:4–5, NKJV)

At the Rapture, Christ stays in the air. At the Second Coming, He comes all the way down. His feet touch the Mount of Olives, the same mountain He left from when He went up to heaven (Acts 1:11– 12). The angels told the disciples that day, “This same Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will so come in like manner as you saw Him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11, NKJV).

This is the day Jesus promised in Lesson 5, when He said Jerusalem would not see Him again until she says, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Matthew 23:39, NKJV). The surviving people of Israel “will look on Me whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10, NKJV), the national Day of Atonement we studied in Lesson 6. Jerusalem finally welcomes her King.

When His feet touch the mountain, it splits from east to west, and a great valley opens. The land of Israel changes shape. The valley gives the Jewish survivors a way to escape (Zechariah 14:5). It also prepares the land for the living water that will flow out of Jerusalem.

“And in that day it shall be that living waters shall flow from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and half of them toward the western sea; in both summer and winter it shall occur.” (Zechariah 14:8, NKJV)
Ezekiel saw that same river flowing down into the Dead Sea and making its salty water fresh: “And it shall be that every living thing
that moves, wherever the rivers go, will live” (Ezekiel 47:9, NKJV). The Dead Sea will come alive.
The King does not come back alone. The Bride who was taken in the Rapture rides with Him in white linen, stepping out of the wedding chamber and into her place of rule.
THE NATIONS ARE JUDGED
When Jesus returns, He gathers the people who lived through the Tribulation and judges them.

“When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the holy angels with Him, then He will sit on the throne of His glory. All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate them one from another, as a shepherd divides his sheep from the goats. And He will set the sheep on His right hand, but the goats on the left. Then the King will say to those on His right hand, ‘Come, you blessed of My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’” (Matthew 25:31–34, NKJV)

The “sheep” are those who came to faith during the Tribulation and lived through it. They go into the Kingdom in their natural, human bodies. They will marry, have children, and fill the earth again. This is very important for understanding the end of the thousand years. The “goats” are those who rejected Him, and they do not enter the Kingdom (Matthew 25:41, 46).
CHRIST RULES WITH A ROD OF IRON

“And I saw thrones, and they sat on them, and judgment was committed to them. Then I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for their witness to Jesus and for the word of God, who had not worshiped the beast or his image, and had not received his mark on their foreheads or on their hands. And they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. But the rest of the dead did not live again until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection. Over such the second death has no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with Him a thousand years.” (Revelation 20:4–6, NKJV)

The Millennial Kingdom is a real government that lasts a thousand years. Jesus Christ sits on the throne of David in Jerusalem. This keeps the promise God made to King David: “And your house and your kingdom shall be established forever before you. Your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16, NKJV). Jerusalem becomes the capital of the whole world. This Kingdom does not run by popular vote or by laws that people make up. It runs by the word of the King.
David, the Forefather of Jesus

When the angel spoke to Mary, he said, “the Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David” (Luke 1:32, NKJV). Some people read that and ask, “Wait, is David Jesus’ father?” No. In the Bible, “father” often means forefather, an ancestor from long ago. Abraham is called the father of Israel in the same way. David lived about a thousand years before Jesus was born.
Jesus had no human father by birth. He is the eternal Son of God, born of the virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35). But Joseph, who raised Him as His legal father, came from David’s royal line

(Matthew 1:6–16), and many Bible teachers believe the family line in Luke 3 traces Mary back to David too. That is why Jesus is called “the Son of David” (Matthew 1:1, NKJV), and it is how He has the legal right to David’s throne. Jesus Himself said, “I am the Root and the Offspring of David” (Revelation 22:16, NKJV). As God, He is the Root, the One who made David. As a man, He is the Offspring, born into David’s family. David is His ancestor. God is His Father.
What It Means to Reign

To reign means to rule as a king. When Revelation 20:6 says believers “shall reign with Him a thousand years,” it means real responsibility in a real government. Christ rules the nations “with a rod of iron” (Revelation 19:15, NKJV). That means His laws are enforced everywhere, and disobedience is dealt with right away. Believers who received their new bodies help Him rule as kings and priests. They carry out His decisions over the people who entered the Kingdom in natural bodies and over their children.

Paul wrote, “If we endure, we shall also reign with Him” (2 Timothy 2:12, NKJV). Jesus told the faithful servant in His parable, “Well done, good servant; because you were faithful in a very little, have authority over ten cities” (Luke 19:17, NKJV). How faithful you are now with small things shows what you will be trusted with then. That is the reward given at the Judgment Seat, which we studied in Lesson 11.

Do not mix up reign with rain. But the two words do meet in one verse. Zechariah says that during the Kingdom, the nations will go up to Jerusalem every year to worship the King. Then he adds, “And it shall be that whichever of the families of the earth do not come up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, on them there will be no rain” (Zechariah 14:17, NKJV). Under this King, even the weather answers to His reign. And that verse shows something else: some people in the Kingdom will still refuse to obey.
WILL ANYONE STILL SIN OR DIE?
This is one of the most common questions about the Millennium. If Jesus is ruling and Satan is locked away, how can anyone still sin? And can anyone still die?
The answer depends on which kind of body a person has. Two groups of people live in the Kingdom.

The first group is every believer who received a new, resurrected body: the Church raised or changed at the Rapture, the Old Testament saints, and the Tribulation believers who died for their faith. These people can never sin again, never get sick, and never die. “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53, NKJV). They reign with Christ.

The second group is the “sheep” who lived through the Tribulation and entered the Kingdom in natural, human bodies, along with all the children born to them over the thousand years. They still have a sinful nature, because the devil was never the only source of sin. Jesus said, “For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts” (Mark 7:21, NKJV). Each child born in the Kingdom still needs to be born again, just like every child today.

So yes, people in natural bodies can still die. Isaiah describes it: “No more shall an infant from there live but a few days, nor an old man who has not fulfilled his days; for the child shall die one hundred years old, but the sinner being one hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isaiah 65:20, NKJV).

Here is what that means. People will live so long, like the people before the flood, that someone who dies at one hundred years old will seem like a child who died young. Isaiah also says, “For as the days of a tree, so shall be the days of My people” (Isaiah 65:22, NKJV). Babies will not die. Death will be rare, and when someone dies that young, it will usually be a judgment on open sin. That is
what “the sinner being one hundred years old shall be accursed” means.

The Bible does not tell us everything. It does not say whether a believer born during the Millennium will grow old and die or will be changed at the end. Where Scripture is quiet, we stay quiet too. It also does not give every detail of where the believers with resurrected bodies live during the thousand years. It tells us they reign with Christ (Revelation 20:6), and that afterward the New Jerusalem comes down to the new earth.

Death is finally gone only after the thousand years. “The last enemy that will be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26, NKJV). After the Great White Throne, death itself is thrown into the lake of fire, and in the New Jerusalem “there shall be no more death” (Revelation 21:4, NKJV). The Millennium is a world with far less death. The New Jerusalem is a world with no death at all.
WHAT IS THE SECOND DEATH?
Look again at the promise in Revelation 20:6: “Over such the second death has no power.” What is the second death?

The first death is the death of the body. It comes to nearly every person, because all of us were born into a fallen world. (Believers who are alive at the Rapture will be changed without dying, 1 Corinthians 15:51.) The second death is something far worse. It is being separated from God forever. Revelation 20 tells us that at the end, everyone whose name is not written in the Book of Life is thrown into the lake of fire. “This is the second death” (Revelation 20:14, NKJV).

The first resurrection includes the Church at the Rapture, the Old Testament saints, and those who die for their faith during the Tribulation. But how can the Rapture and the end of the Tribulation both be “the first” resurrection? Because the first resurrection is like

a harvest that comes in stages, as we saw in Lesson 6. Christ the Firstfruits rose first. The Church rises at the Rapture. The Tribulation martyrs and, as many teachers believe, the Old Testament saints rise when Christ returns (Daniel 12:2). All of them together are the first resurrection, the resurrection of life. If you have part in the first resurrection, you are called “blessed and holy.” Your sins were already judged and paid for by the blood of the Groom at Calvary. The second death has no power over you at all. You will rule with the King through the thousand years and on into forever.
THE PEACE OF THE KINGDOM
Under Christ’s rule, even nature changes.

“The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them... They shall not hurt nor destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea.” (Isaiah 11:6, 9, NKJV)

The cow and the bear will eat grass side by side. A baby will play safely near a cobra’s hole (Isaiah 11:7–8). This is the peace of the Millennium: real animals, real safety, and the knowledge of the Lord covering the whole earth while the King sits on David’s throne.
THE FEAST OF TABERNACLES FULFILLED
In Lesson 6, we learned that the seventh and last feast of the Lord, the Feast of Tabernacles, is still waiting to be fulfilled. Now we can see it come true.

“And it shall come to pass that everyone who is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles.” (Zechariah 14:16, NKJV)

For seven days every year, Israel lived in booths, small shelters made of branches (Leviticus 23:42). The feast reminded them that God lived among them in the wilderness. It came at the end of the harvest, when every crop was gathered in. It was the most joyful feast of the year.
The Millennium is that feast come to life, in four ways:

1. God lives among His people: The King is not far away. He sits on His throne in Jerusalem, and the nations come to see Him face to face. John wrote about Jesus’ birth this way: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14, NKJV). The Greek word for “dwelt” means “pitched His tent” or “tabernacled.” At His first coming He tabernacled among us for a short time. In the Kingdom He stays.

2. The harvest is gathered in: Tabernacles was the Feast of Ingathering. Before the Kingdom begins, the Church has been gathered at the Rapture, Israel has turned back to her Messiah, and the Tribulation believers have been brought in. Every crop is in the barn.
3. The nations keep the feast: Zechariah says the nations will go up to Jerusalem every year to keep this very feast. It is the only feast the Bible says the whole world will celebrate.
4. Rest and joy: The booths remind us that this world was always a temporary shelter. In the Kingdom, God’s people finally rest under the rule of their King.
But the Millennium is not the end of the picture. Tabernacles lasted seven days, and then came an eighth day, a holy day of its own (Leviticus 23:36). Many Bible teachers see that eighth day as a

picture of eternity, the new beginning after the thousand years. At the very end of the Bible, John hears the final fulfillment: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3, NKJV). The Millennium is Tabernacles on this earth. The New Jerusalem is Tabernacles forever.
SATAN IS LOCKED AWAY

“Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, having the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain in his hand. He laid hold of the dragon, that serpent of old, who is the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years; and he cast him into the bottomless pit, and shut him up, and set a seal on him, so that he should deceive the nations no more till the thousand years were finished. But after these things he must be released for a little while.” (Revelation 20:1–3, NKJV)

Before the thousand-year reign begins, the source of so much evil is taken away. An angel comes down from heaven with a great chain, grabs Satan, and locks him in the bottomless pit for the whole thousand years.
The earth gets a fresh start. For a thousand years, the devil cannot push nations into war or whisper his lies into people’s minds (Revelation 20:3). The world lives under the King who can be seen.
THE FINAL REVOLT

“Now when the thousand years have expired, Satan will be released from his prison and will go out to deceive the nations which are in the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them together to battle, whose number is as the sand of the sea.” (Revelation 20:7–8, NKJV)

“Gog and Magog” here is the name John gives to the nations Satan gathers for one last revolt against God. The prophet Ezekiel also spoke of Gog and Magog (Ezekiel 38–39). Many Bible teachers see Ezekiel’s battle as an earlier war, and John uses the old name for this last revolt.
Why would God let the devil out after a thousand years of peace? And how could so many people living under the rule of Jesus Christ Himself turn against Him?

First, remember what Satan has already done. He led a third of the angels in rebellion. John saw that “his tail drew a third of the stars of heaven and threw them to the earth” (Revelation 12:4, NKJV). If Satan could turn angels who stood in the very glory of God, then deceiving human beings with a sinful nature is easy for him.

Second, remember where these people come from. The “sheep” from Matthew 25 entered the Kingdom in natural bodies. Over a thousand years of long life and peace, their families grow until their number is “as the sand of the sea.”
These children grow up in a perfect world. They never lived through the Tribulation. They have never heard the devil’s whispers, because Satan has been locked in the pit.

But obeying the rules on the outside is not the same as having a new heart. Many of these people obey the King only because they have to, not because they love Him. They do not have the willing heart Rebekah showed when she said, “I will go” (Lesson 11). Their sinful nature lies quiet, waiting. When Satan is released, he does not need a new trick. He just goes to the four corners of the earth and fans the hidden coals of rebellion. This proves that a perfect world cannot fix a broken heart. Only a new birth through Jesus can do that.
FIRE FROM HEAVEN

“They went up on the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them. The devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone where the beast and the false prophet are. And they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.” (Revelation 20:9–10, NKJV)

This is not a battle like Armageddon. The rebels march across the earth and surround Jerusalem. The saints do not lift a sword. Fire comes down from God out of heaven and devours them. Just as fire fell on Sodom, judgment falls from God’s throne in a single moment, and the revolt is over.

Then the devil himself is thrown into the lake of fire. Notice who is already there: “the beast and the false prophet.” They were thrown in before the thousand years began, and a thousand years later they are still there. That shows the lake of fire does not burn people up so that they stop existing. It is a place of punishment that lasts forever. Satan’s power to deceive is finished for good.
THE GREAT WHITE THRONE
After the final revolt comes the last courtroom in history: the Great White Throne Judgment.

“Then I saw a great white throne and Him who sat on it, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away. And there was found no place for them. And I saw the dead, small and great, standing before God, and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their works, by the things which were written in the books. The sea gave up the dead who were in it, and Death and Hades delivered up the dead who were in them. And they were judged, each one according to his works. Then Death and Hades were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And anyone not found written in the Book of Life was cast into the lake of fire.” (Revelation 20:11–15, NKJV)

No born-again believer stands in this line. The Bride was gathered at the Rapture, received her rewards at the Judgment Seat of Christ, and has been reigning with the King for a thousand years. This courtroom is for “the rest of the dead,” the unsaved of all history.

Every unsaved person from Cain to the last rebel of the Millennium is raised to stand before Christ the Judge. The grave gives up the body, and Hades gives up the soul. “The sea gave up the dead who were in it,” including those lost in the flood of Noah’s day. No one is forgotten, and no one escapes.
Two kinds of records are opened.

The books of works: These hold a record of every thought, word, and deed. These people refused the payment Jesus made at the cross, so they must stand on their own works. Their works decide how severe their punishment will be. But no human works can meet the standard of a holy God.
The Book of Life: This book does not list good deeds. It holds only the names of those who received the gift of salvation by grace through faith.

Here is the good news for every believer: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1, NKJV). The Bride does not stand trembling before the books of works. Her name is written in the Book of Life.

The verdict is final. Anyone whose name is not found in the Book of Life is thrown into the lake of fire. Then Death and Hades themselves are thrown in. Sin, death, and rebellion are locked away forever from God’s clean new creation. That is the second death.
GENESIS AND REVELATION: THE MIRROR
The first three chapters of the Bible and the last three chapters answer each other like a mirror.

Genesis 1 to 3, paradise lost: God makes a perfect world. The tree of life is planted. Man walks with God. The serpent slips into the garden and lies. Sin brings a curse. Man is driven away from the tree of life, and death begins to rule.

Revelation 20 to 22, paradise restored: The serpent is judged and thrown into the lake of fire forever. The curse is gone. The tree of life stands on both sides of the river of life (Revelation 22:2). “Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54, NKJV).

What began in Genesis is finished in Revelation. History is not a circle that goes around and around. It is a straight line drawn by the One who says, “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, the First and the Last” (Revelation 22:13, NKJV). Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. He started the story, and He will finish it.
THE NEW JERUSALEM
When the courtroom closes, where will God’s people live forever? Many people picture eternity as floating on a cloud. The Bible shows something much richer: heaven and earth joined together.

“Now I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away. Also there was no more sea. Then I, John, saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying, ‘Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them, and they shall be His people. God Himself will be with them and be their God.’” (Revelation 21:1–3, NKJV)

God makes a new heaven and a new earth. The old creation, scarred by sin, passes away. Jesus told us this would happen: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will by no means pass away” (Matthew 24:35, NKJV). The world changes. His Word does not.

Then the New Jerusalem comes down out of heaven. This is the place Jesus went to prepare when He told His disciples, “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2, NKJV). Revelation 21:16 measures the city at 12,000 furlongs (an old unit of distance), about 1,400 to 1,500 miles long, wide, and high. The city is pure gold, like clear glass. Its wall is jasper, and each of its twelve gates is a single pearl (Revelation 21:18, 21).
Three things mark that forever home:

1. God lives with His people: “But I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. The city had no need of the sun or of the moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illuminated it. The Lamb is its light” (Revelation 21:22–23, NKJV). We do not go off to live with God in some far-away sky. God comes down to live face to face with His people.

2. No more tears, death, or pain: “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4, NKJV). God does not just manage our suffering. He ends it. Everything that has hurt people since Genesis is gone, and it will never come back.

3. The nations walk in His light: “And the nations of those who are saved shall walk in its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory and honor into it” (Revelation 21:24, NKJV). Believers will not sit around bored. We will walk in the light of the Lamb, explore the new earth, serve Him, and worship Him, and it will never end.
WILL THE ROMA HAVE A HOME?

Our people often ask, “Will the Roma finally have their own land? Will we have our own city?” For hundreds of years our people have moved from country to country, often without a land to call our own and often unwelcome where we stopped. So this is a fair question, and it deserves an honest answer from the Word.

The Bible does not name the Roma, and it does not promise a separate Roma city. God made specific land promises to Israel, and He will keep them. But for every other people on earth, God promises something even better than a country of our own.

First, our people will be there. In heaven they sing to the Lamb, “You were slain, and have redeemed us to God by Your blood out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9, NKJV). John saw “a great multitude which no one could number, of all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes” (Revelation 7:9, NKJV). Every Roma believer will stand in that crowd, washed by the same blood, in the same white robes.

Second, the nations keep who they are. “The nations of those who are saved shall walk in its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory and honor into it” (Revelation 21:24, NKJV). God does not erase the peoples He made. Our families, our faith, and the good things God has given our people can be brought into His city as honor to the King.

Third, the wandering ends. The men and women of faith in Hebrews 11 “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.” Then the Bible says, “But now they desire a better, that is, a heavenly country. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them” (Hebrews 11:13, 16, NKJV). Abraham lived in tents all his life because “he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10, NKJV).

That is the answer for a people who have traveled so long. We will not get a city built by human hands that someone could take away. We will be citizens of the New Jerusalem, the city God Himself built, with a home inside it that Jesus prepared, and no one will ever tell us to move on again. And remember Luke 19:17: faithful servants will be given authority over cities. Roma believers will not just have a home. They will reign with the King.

The Bridegroom Is Coming. Are You Ready?
You opened this book looking for a clearer map of prophecy. If the Holy Spirit has done His work in these pages, you are leaving with more than a map. You are leaving with Jesus in sharper focus.

“For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” (Revelation 19:10, NKJV). That is not just a nice line for a book cover. It is the center of everything we studied. From the first Hebrew word of Genesis to the last chapters of Revelation, the Bible tells one story with one heartbeat: Jesus keeps His Word, He rules over history, and He is coming back for His Bride.
Look at what you have already walked through.

You saw that before creation began, the Cross was already in view. You saw that the Old Testament did not guess about Jesus. It named Him so clearly that chance cannot explain it. You learned how the prophets often saw something near and something far in the same line of sight, with the long valley of the Church Age hidden between. You watched Daniel’s seventy weeks count down to the very days of the Messiah, and you saw why God’s clock still has one final week set aside for Israel.

You stood in the temple during the last week of Jesus’ life and heard the parables of the King, as the Lawyer turned His accusers’ own verdict back on them. You saw why Israel and the Church must stay in the places God gave them, and how Replacement Theology brought confusion

and centuries of suffering when those lines were erased. You heard the letters to the seven churches as more than old mail, as warnings and promises that still speak to us in the lukewarm age of Laodicea. You stood inside the ancient wedding and saw why the Bride is not appointed to the poured-out wrath of God. And you looked ahead to the Millennial Kingdom, when the King returns, the devil is bound, and the earth finally knows the righteous rule of Christ, until the Great White Throne closes history and God lives with His people forever in the New Jerusalem.
That is not trivia. That is preparation.

God did not give prophecy so the Church could brag about charts. He gave it so the Church would wake up. Jesus did not tell His disciples to argue forever about dates. He told them to watch, pray, and live ready. The early church staked their lives on prophecy that had already come true. You are called to stake your life on the same God, who still has promises left on the calendar.
So here is the question every lesson has been pushing toward: Are you ready?

Ready does not mean you understand every symbol in Revelation. Ready does not mean you won every argument online. Ready means your lamp has oil. Ready means your wedding clothes are clean. Ready means you belong to Jesus by faith, you walk in repentance, and you live like someone expecting the shout, the trumpet, and the gathering of the Bride.

The Bridegroom is coming.

How to Be Ready
Settling It Today

The Conclusion ended with one question: Are you ready? Knowing about God’s plan is not the same as being part of it. The most important question in this book is not “When is Jesus coming?” It is “Am I ready if He comes today?”
If you are not sure, you can settle it right now. God made it simple.
1. EVERYONE HAS SINNED
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23, NKJV)

Every person has broken God’s law. We have lied, been selfish, disobeyed, and gone our own way. Sin is not just doing bad things. It is living as if God is not our King. Being a good person, going to church, or growing up in a Christian family cannot erase it.
2. SIN HAS A PRICE
“For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:23, NKJV)

A wage is what you earn. What sin earns is death, being separated from God forever. That is the second death we read about in Lesson 12. But notice the second half of the verse. Eternal life is not a wage. It is a gift.
3. JESUS PAID THE PRICE
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8, NKJV)

God did not wait for us to clean ourselves up. While we were still sinners, Jesus died on the cross in our place. He paid the bride price with His own blood. Three days later He rose from the dead, just as the prophets said He would.
4. RECEIVE HIM BY FAITH

“That if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” (Romans 10:9–10, NKJV)

You cannot earn salvation. You receive it. Like Rebekah, you hear the message about the Son and answer, “I will go.” Turn away from your sin, believe that Jesus died and rose again for you, and call on Him as your Lord. “For ‘whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved’” (Romans 10:13, NKJV).
A PRAYER YOU CAN PRAY
The words of a prayer do not save you. Jesus does. But if you are ready to trust Him, you can tell Him so in words like these:

Lord Jesus, I know that I have sinned and that I cannot save myself. I believe that You died on the cross for my sins and that God raised You from the dead. I turn away from my sin, and I turn to You. Come into my life. Forgive me, wash me clean, and make me Yours.
I receive You as my Savior and my Lord. Help me to live ready for the day You come for Your Bride. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

If you prayed that prayer and meant it, the Bible says you belong to Him. “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13, NKJV).

Glossary
Hard Words Made Plain
Abomination of desolation: The terrible act Daniel and Jesus spoke of, when the Antichrist sets himself up in the temple in the middle of the seven-year Tribulation (Daniel 9:27, Matthew 24:15).
Afikomen: A piece of matzah hidden during the Passover meal and found later by the children. It is a later Jewish custom that many Christians see as a picture of Jesus buried and raised.
Aleph and Tav: The first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet, like Alpha and Omega in Greek.
Alhambra Decree: The order signed by Ferdinand and Isabella on March 31, 1492, that forced every Jew in Spain to convert or leave.
Alpha and Omega: The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. Jesus uses this name to say He is the Beginning and the End (Revelation 22:13).
Amillennialism: The view that there will be no real thousand-year reign of Christ on earth. The “a” means “no.”
Anabaptists: Believers in the 1500s who taught baptism after a person believes. Both Catholic and Protestant state churches persecuted them.
Antichrist: The coming world ruler who will oppose Christ, make a treaty with Israel, and set himself up as God during the Tribulation.
Apokalypsis: The Greek word behind the name Revelation. It means “an unveiling,” like pulling back a curtain.
Ark of the Covenant: The gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the Law. It stood in the Most Holy Place, and its lid was the mercy seat.
Armageddon: From the Hebrew Har Megiddo, “the hill of Megiddo,” in northern Israel. The place where the armies of the world gather at the end of the Tribulation (Revelation 16:16).
Atonement: “At-one-ment,” bringing two who were separated back together as one. In Hebrew, kaphar, which means “to cover” or “to wipe clean.”
Beast: Another name for the Antichrist in the Book of Revelation (Revelation 13:1–8).
Bedikat chametz: The search for leaven in a Jewish home the night before Passover.
Beh ray SHEET: The way the first Hebrew word of the Bible sounds. It means “In the beginning.”
Bema: The Greek word for the judge’s platform at a race. The Judgment Seat of Christ, where believers receive rewards (2 Corinthians 5:10).
Bereshit: The first Hebrew word of the Bible, said Beh ray SHEET. It means “In the beginning.”
Book of Life: God’s record of the names of everyone who has received salvation through faith in Jesus (Revelation 20:15).
Bridal blessings: The seven overcomer promises to the churches in Revelation 2–3, seen in Lesson 11 as the Bride’s inheritance.
Bride of Christ: The Church, all true believers in Jesus, who are promised to Him like a bride to a groom.
Cheap grace: The false teaching that grace lets a believer keep living in sin without repenting. Also called hyper-grace.
Chuppah: The bridal room the groom prepared at his father’s house. Today it also means the canopy at a Jewish wedding.
Church Age: The time from Pentecost until the Rapture, when the Gospel goes to every nation and God builds His Church.

Council of Nicaea: A church council called by Emperor Constantine in AD 325. It set the date for celebrating the resurrection apart from the Jewish calendar, which helped cut the Church off from its Jewish roots.
Covenant: A binding promise or agreement, like a contract, made before witnesses. God’s covenants cannot be broken.
Crypto-Judaism: Keeping the Jewish faith in secret behind a Christian mask, as many Spanish Jews did during the Inquisition.
Darh-go: In the Roma wedding, the walk of the bride and groom from table to table to gather their dowry.
Day of Atonement: See Yom Kippur.
Day of the Lord: The time when God pours out His wrath on the earth and the King returns. It comes after the Church is taken out (1 Thessalonians 5:2–9; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–7).
Days of Awe: The ten days from the Feast of Trumpets to the Day of Atonement, a time of looking back over the year and asking God for forgiveness.
Dead Sea Scrolls: Ancient scrolls found in caves at Qumran, near the Dead Sea, starting in 1947. They include the Great Isaiah Scroll.
Dowry: Money or gifts that go with the bride into her new home.
Edict of Milan: The agreement of AD 313 that made Christianity legal in the Roman Empire.
Ekklesia: The Greek word for “church.” In Greek cities, it was the assembly of citizens who met to run the city’s business.
Ekpheugō: The Greek word Jesus uses for “escape” in Luke 21:36. It means to flee out of, to get away safely.
Ephesus: The first of the seven churches of Revelation, the apostolic church. Its name has been taught to mean “desirable.”
False prophet: The Antichrist’s partner, who makes the world worship the Antichrist and take his mark (Revelation 13:11–17).
Feast of Tabernacles: See Sukkot.
Feast of Trumpets: See Yom Teruah.
First Gospel: The first announcement of the Good News, God’s promise in Genesis 3:15 that the Seed of the woman would crush the serpent’s head.

First resurrection: The resurrection of life for all God’s people. It comes in stages: Christ first, then the Church at the Rapture, then the Tribulation martyrs and Old Testament saints when Christ returns (Revelation 20:5–6).
Firstfruits: The first part of the harvest, given to God. Jesus rose from the dead on the Feast of Firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Genea: The Greek word for “generation” in Matthew 24:34. It can mean the people living at one time, or a family line or race.
Gentile: Any person who is not Jewish.
Gog and Magog: In Revelation 20:8, the name John gives to the nations Satan gathers for his final revolt at the end of the thousand years.
Great Tribulation: The last three and a half years of the seven-year Tribulation, after the Antichrist sets himself up in the temple (Matthew 24:21).
Great White Throne: The final judgment, where the unsaved dead of all history are judged (Revelation 20:11–15).
Hades: The place where the souls of the unsaved dead are held until the final judgment.
Harpazō: The Greek word for “caught up” in 1 Thessalonians 4:17. It means to snatch away or carry off by force.
High priest: The chief priest of Israel. Only he could go behind the veil into the Most Holy Place, once a year on the Day of Atonement.
Holocaust: The murder of more than six million Jewish men, women, and children by the Nazis during World War II.
Indulgence: A paper sold by the medieval church that promised less punishment in purgatory for money.
Inquisition: Church courts that hunted down, tortured, and punished people accused of false belief. The Spanish Inquisition began in 1478.
Jacob’s trouble: Another name for the Tribulation, from Jeremiah 30:7.
Judgment Seat of Christ: See Bema.
Keseh: The Hebrew word in Psalm 81:3 that the NKJV translates “full moon.” Jewish tradition reads it as “covered” or “hidden,” a name for the Feast of Trumpets.
Ketubah: The written marriage contract in a Jewish wedding.
Kiddushin: The Hebrew word for the betrothal, the binding engagement. It comes from the word for “holy” or “set apart.”
Kristallnacht: “The night of broken glass,” November 9 and 10, 1938, when synagogues across Germany were burned.
Lake of fire: The place of final, everlasting punishment for Satan, his angels, and all whose names are not in the Book of Life (Revelation 20:10, 15).
Lampstand: A stand that holds up an oil lamp. In Revelation, a picture of a church.
Laodicea: The last of the seven churches of Revelation, the lukewarm church. Its name has been taught to mean “the rule of the people.”
Last Adam: A name for Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:45). The first Adam brought sin and death; the Last Adam brings life.
Leaven: Yeast, which makes dough rise. In Scripture it is a picture of sin.
Mark of the beast: The mark the Antichrist will require on the right hand or forehead in order to buy or sell (Revelation 13:16–17).
Marriage supper of the Lamb: The wedding feast of Christ and His Bride (Revelation 19:9).
Mashach: The Hebrew word for “anointed.” The word Messiah comes from it.
Mashiach: The Hebrew word for Messiah, the Anointed One. It comes from mashach.
Mattan: The gifts a groom gave to his bride herself, often gifts of gold.
Matzah: Flat bread made without yeast, eaten at Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
Matzah tash: The cloth pouch with three pockets that holds the unleavened bread at the Passover meal.
Memory Verse: The short verse at the start of each lesson to learn by heart during the week.
Mercy seat: The gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant, where the high priest sprinkled the blood on the Day of Atonement.
Messiah: “The Anointed One.” In Greek, Christ.
Meta tauta: Greek for “after these things” (Revelation 1:19, 4:1).
Mikvah: A ceremonial washing in water. A picture of baptism.
Millennium: The thousand-year reign of Christ on earth (Revelation 20:4–6).
Miqra: The Hebrew word for “holy convocation.” A calling together, a rehearsal.
Moed: The Hebrew word for “feast.” An appointed time, a set meeting with God.
Mohar: The bride price the groom paid to the bride’s father.
Most Holy Place: The inner room of the tabernacle and the temple, behind the veil, where the Ark of the Covenant stood.
Mystery: In the Bible, a truth God kept hidden in the Old Testament and has now made known, such as Gentiles and Jews joined in one body, the Church (Ephesians 3:6).

Nicolaitans: A group whose deeds and teaching Jesus hated (Revelation 2:6, 15). The name has long been explained as “conquering the people,” a picture of a ruling class of clergy over ordinary believers.
Nisan: The first month of the Hebrew religious year. It falls in our March or April.
Olivet Discourse: Jesus’ great teaching about the end times, given on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24–25, Mark 13, Luke 21).
Overcomer: Every true believer, who overcomes the world through faith in Jesus (1 John 5:4–5).
Parable: A short story Jesus told to teach a truth.
Passover: The feast that remembers the night God spared Israel in Egypt through the blood of a lamb. Jesus died as our Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Patmos: A small rocky island in the Aegean Sea where John was a prisoner when he saw the Revelation (Revelation 1:9).
Pentecost: The Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Firstfruits. The day the Holy Spirit was poured out and the Church was born (Acts 2).
Pergamos: The third of the seven churches of Revelation, the compromising church. Its name is related to a word for “height,” and has also been explained as “mixed marriage.”
Philadelphia: The sixth of the seven churches of Revelation, the missionary church. Its name means “brotherly love.”
Pleroo: The Greek word for “fulfill.” To fill all the way to the top.
Porajmos: The Romani word for the murder of the Roma people by the Nazis. It means “the devouring.”
Postmillennialism: The view that the Church will make the whole world Christian first, and then Christ will return. The “post” means “after.”
Premillennialism: The view that Christ returns before the thousandyear Kingdom. The view this book teaches.
Purgatory: A place of suffering after death that the Roman Catholic Church teaches. It is not found in the Bible.
Rapiemur: The Latin word for “we shall be caught up” in 1 Thessalonians 4:17. Our word “rapture” comes from it.
Rapture: The moment Jesus comes in the air and catches up His Church, living and dead, to meet Him before the Tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17).
Red heifer: A perfect red young cow whose ashes were needed to make people, including the priests, ceremonially clean after contact with death (Numbers 19).
Reformation: The movement that began in 1517, when Martin Luther and others broke away from Rome and taught salvation by faith alone.
Remnant: A small group God keeps faithful to Himself when most people turn away.
Replacement Theology: The false teaching that the Church has permanently replaced Israel and that God’s promises to Israel are canceled. Also called Supersessionism.
Rosh Hashanah: “Head of the year,” the Jewish New Year, which falls on the Feast of Trumpets.
Sardis: The fifth of the seven churches of Revelation, the Reformation church. Its name has been taught to mean “those who escape” or “a remnant.”
Scapegoat: The live goat that carried Israel’s sins away into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:21–22).
Second Coming: The return of Jesus to the earth at the end of the Tribulation, with His saints, when every eye will see Him.
Second death: Being separated from God forever in the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14).
Second Temple: The temple rebuilt after the Jews came home from Babylon. Jesus walked in it, and Rome destroyed it in AD 70.
Seventy Weeks: Daniel’s prophecy of seventy sets of seven years for Israel. Sixty-nine are finished, and the last seven years are the Tribulation (Daniel 9:24–27).
Shavu’im: The Hebrew word for “sevens” or “weeks” in Daniel 9.
Shavuot: The Feast of Weeks, called Pentecost in Greek.
Sheep and goats: The judgment of the nations when Jesus returns. The sheep, who came to faith during the Tribulation, enter the Kingdom. The goats do not (Matthew 25:31–46).
Shevarim: Three short, broken shofar blasts that sound like sighing, the sound of repentance.
Shofar: A trumpet made from a ram’s horn.
Sinti: A branch of the Roma people, living mostly in Germany and nearby lands.
Smyrna: The second of the seven churches of Revelation, the persecuted church. Its name comes from myrrh, a spice that gives its sweet smell when crushed.
Sukkot: The Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths.
Supersessionism: Another name for Replacement Theology.
Talmud: A large collection of ancient Jewish teaching and discussion about the Law.
Te’enah: The Hebrew word for fig tree.
Tekiah: One long, straight shofar blast, the sound used to crown a king.
Tekiah Gedolah: “The great blast,” the last and longest blast of the shofar on the Feast of Trumpets.
Temple Mount: The hill in Jerusalem where the First and Second Temples stood.
Teruah: Nine or more quick, sharp shofar blasts, an alarm and a wake-up call.
Teshuvah: The Hebrew word for both “return” and “repentance.”
Third Temple: The temple that will be rebuilt in Jerusalem, where the Antichrist will stand in the holy place. Solomon built the First
Temple; the Second was the one Jesus walked in, destroyed in AD 70.
Thyatira: The fourth of the seven churches of Revelation, the medieval church. Its name has been taught to mean “continual sacrifice.”
Times of the Gentiles: The long time Jerusalem is under Gentile rule, until the end of the age (Luke 21:24).
Tishrei: The seventh month of the Hebrew religious year. It falls in our September or October.
Tribulation: The seven years of God’s judgment on the earth after the Rapture, Daniel’s seventieth week. The word comes from the Latin tribulum, a threshing board.
Triumphal Entry: The day Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey as King, now remembered as Palm Sunday. Daniel’s sixty-nine weeks ended on that day.
Unleavened Bread: The seven-day feast after Passover, when Israel ate bread made with no yeast.
Veil: The heavy curtain in front of the Most Holy Place. It tore from top to bottom when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51).
Ya’aqov: The Hebrew name for Jacob. It comes from the Hebrew word for “heel,” because he was born holding his brother’s heel (Genesis 25:26).
Yadah: The Hebrew word behind “confess” in Leviticus 16:21. It means “to throw” or “to cast.”
Yom Kippur: The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.
Yom Teruah: The Feast of Trumpets.
